items.title: Anthropic launches Claude Sonnet 5, an agentic AI model with improved reasoning, tool use, and safety, available across all plans with introductory pricing through August 2026 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Claude Sonnet 5
items.summary:
Anthropic has launched Claude Sonnet 5, an advanced agentic AI model designed to improve reasoning, tool use, and safety. This model can autonomously plan and execute tasks using tools like browsers and terminals, offering performance close to larger, more expensive models but at a lower cost. Claude Sonnet 5 is now available across all subscription plans, including Free and Pro, with introductory pricing available through August 2026.

The new model shows significant improvements over its predecessor, Sonnet 4.6, particularly in coding, knowledge work, and agentic capabilities. Safety assessments indicate a lower rate of undesirable behaviors, and it has limited ability to perform cybersecurity tasks compared to Opus models. Early users have praised its ability to complete complex, multi-step tasks efficiently and safely, making it suitable for a range of applications from software engineering to legal research and insurance workflows.

Claude Sonnet 5 is accessible via the Claude API and is positioned as a cost-effective option for developers seeking powerful, autonomous AI assistance. Its release marks a notable step forward in agentic AI technology, balancing enhanced functionality with improved safety and affordability.

items.title: Claude launches Claude Science, an AI-powered research platform for reproducible scientific analysis and manuscript drafting, available on macOS and Linux [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Claude Science
items.summary:
Claude has launched Claude Science, an AI-powered research platform designed to support rigorous scientific analysis and manuscript drafting. Available on macOS and Linux, the platform enables researchers to run analyses, search databases, and trace every step from data processing to publication, ensuring full reproducibility and transparency.

The app features native visualization tools for proteins, molecules, and genomic data, along with built-in fact-checking to flag inconsistencies. It supports domain-specific workflows across life sciences, including genomics, proteomics, and cheminformatics, and manages computing resources from local machines to high-performance clusters. Claude Science also integrates manuscript drafting with analysis, allowing researchers to write and revise results alongside their data in a single environment.

By connecting to over 60 scientific databases and offering reusable pipelines, Claude Science aims to streamline complex research projects and enhance collaboration. Early users have praised its ability to facilitate reproducible research and accelerate discovery, highlighting its potential to transform scientific workflows.

items.title: Meta AI releases Brain2Qwerty v2, a non-invasive AI system decoding brain waves into text with up to 78% word accuracy in real time [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From brain waves to words: a new path to communication without surgery
items.summary:
Meta AI has introduced Brain2Qwerty v2, an advanced non-invasive AI system that decodes brain waves into text with up to 78% word accuracy in real time. This technology builds on the previous version by using end-to-end deep learning to interpret raw brain signals recorded via magnetoencephalography (MEG), enabling coherent sentence reconstruction without surgical implants.

The system was trained on data from nine volunteers who typed while wearing MEG devices, allowing the AI to leverage semantic context through fine-tuned large language models. Brain2Qwerty v2 significantly outperforms other non-invasive methods, achieving a 61% average word accuracy and demonstrating potential to narrow the gap with invasive brain decoding techniques through further data scaling.

Meta AI has released the full training code and datasets to encourage open research and collaboration, aiming to accelerate neuroscience breakthroughs and improve communication options for individuals with brain lesions. This effort is part of a broader initiative to develop foundational brain models and stimulate open datasets within the Digital Brain Project.

items.summary:
Mistral has released Leanstral 1.5, a formal proof engineering model designed to enhance automated theorem proving and autoformalization. The model features 119 billion parameters, with 6.5 billion active, and is based on the Lean 4 formal proof system.

This update aims to improve the efficiency and accuracy of formal proof tasks, supporting advancements in automated reasoning and formal verification processes. Leanstral 1.5 is part of Mistral's broader suite of models, which also includes Mistral Medium 3.5 and Voxtral TTS.

items.title: arXiv to spin out from Cornell University and become an independent nonprofit organization on July 1, 2026, maintaining free access and community support [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ArXiv's Next Chapter
items.summary:
On July 1, 2026, arXiv will become an independent nonprofit organization, separating from Cornell University after 25 years. Despite this change, arXiv will continue to provide free access to scientific papers and maintain its commitment to supporting the global scientific community. The transition aims to offer greater flexibility and growth opportunities while ensuring uninterrupted service for authors and readers.

The decision to spin out has been carefully planned, with staff and volunteers working to ensure a smooth transition. arXiv will uphold its mission, vision, and values, remaining a community-driven platform. To keep users informed, arXiv has launched a dedicated FAQ page and will release a series of blog posts detailing leadership updates, milestones, and policy changes, emphasizing transparency throughout the process.

items.title: Researchers study LearnStop, a learned stopping rule for reasoning models, finding its effectiveness depends on task type and is most beneficial when scalar confidence or convergence signals are unreliable [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Does Learning to Stop Help? A Cost-Aware Study of Early Exits in Reasoning Models
items.summary:
Researchers investigated LearnStop, a learned stopping rule designed to optimize computation in reasoning language models by predicting when to halt processing based on multiple online features. Their study across 18 task-model settings revealed that the effectiveness of LearnStop varies by task type, showing significant improvements in free-form math problems but less advantage in multiple-choice or very challenging tasks where simpler scalar confidence or entropy measures perform comparably or better. The findings suggest that learned stopping is most beneficial when no single reliable scalar stopping signal exists, but its advantages diminish when confidence or answer convergence already provide clear stopping cues.

The study evaluated LearnStop's performance using various metrics and conditions, including validation-selected operating points, risk calibration, and robustness checks, across diverse datasets such as GSM8K, MATH-500, and MMLU-Pro. The researchers emphasize that learned stopping should be viewed as a complementary tool rather than a universal replacement for scalar exit strategies, with its value depending on the structure of the reasoning process and the nature of the task.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30852v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reasoning models spend different amounts of useful computation across instances, but it remains unclear when a learned stopping rule improves over simple confidence or convergence thresholds. We study this question with LearnStop, a hidden-state-free checkpoint stopper for reasoning language models. At fixed budget checkpoints, LearnStop probes a short answer from the current reasoning prefix and predicts prefix correctness from online features such as answer confidence, entropy, prefix vote share, answer stability, and backtracking-marker density. Across 18 task-model settings spanning GSM8K, MATH-500, MMLU-Pro, AIME-90, GPQA, Qwen3, and DeepSeek-R1 distillations, the answer is task-dependent. On free-form math, learned multi-feature stopping improves the fixed-budget frontier and often beats scalar exits: on GSM8K with Qwen3-32B, the empirical frontier reaches a post-hoc peak adapt gain of +0.157, validation-selected operating points preserve positive gains, and the paired gain over the strongest scalar baseline is +0.028. On multiple-choice and very hard settings, scalar confidence, entropy, or stability rules are competitive or stronger. We therefore frame learned stopping not as a universal replacement for scalar exits, but as a tool whose value depends on trajectory structure. We further provide validation-selected operating points, paired bootstrap tests, finite-grid lost-correct risk calibration, cost accounting under KV-fork, prefix-cache, and black-box regimes, H100 serving profiles, checkpoint-schedule sweeps, transfer analyses, and robustness checks. The main practical finding is that learned stopping is useful when many questions become correct before full budget but do not exhibit a single reliable scalar stopping signal; its benefits largely disappear when confidence or answer convergence already solves the stopping problem.

Their study across 18 task-model settings revealed that the effectiveness of LearnStop varies by task type, showing significant improvements in free-form math problems but less advantage in multiple-choice or very challenging tasks where simpler scalar confidence or entropy measures perform comparably or better. The findings suggest that learned stopping is most beneficial when no single reliable scalar stopping signal exists, but its advantages diminish when confidence or answer convergence already provide clear stopping cues.

The study evaluated LearnStop's performance using various metrics and conditions, including validation-selected operating points, risk calibration, and robustness checks, across diverse datasets such as GSM8K, MATH-500, and MMLU-Pro. The researchers emphasize that learned stopping should be viewed as a complementary tool rather than a universal replacement for scalar exit strategies, with its value depending on the structure of the reasoning process and the nature of the task.

items.title: New ARC-AGI-2 solver uses modality-driven search and holistic trace judging to achieve 72.9% accuracy on ARC Prize semi-private set, outperforming GPT-5.2 Pro and Gemini 3 Pro by over 18 points [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Modality-Driven Search with Holistic Trace Judging for ARC-AGI-2
items.summary:
A new solver for the ARC-AGI-2 visual reasoning benchmark achieves a 72.9% accuracy on the ARC Prize semi-private evaluation set, outperforming leading models like GPT-5.2 Pro and Gemini 3 Pro by over 18 percentage points. The solver uses a modality-driven search approach that generates diverse candidate solutions across text, image, and code channels, combined with a holistic judging method that evaluates all candidate reasoning traces together to select the best answer. This method effectively recovers correct minority hypotheses where majority voting fails.

The solver also attains 76.1% accuracy on the public evaluation set at a lower cost per task. The developer has released the full source code and reported that certain techniques, such as prescriptive prompting and iterative refinement, reduce hypothesis diversity and negatively impact performance. This advancement highlights the importance of diverse candidate generation and comprehensive evaluation in improving abstract reasoning tasks with large language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31543v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models can produce fluent, internally coherent reasoning traces for abstract reasoning tasks while still being confidently wrong - making selection among candidates, not just generation, the central challenge. I present a solver for ARC-AGI-2, a few-shot visual reasoning benchmark, built around two principles: (i) treating reasoning modalities as search operators, generating diverse candidates independently across text, image, and code channels, and (ii) context-preserving holistic judging, in which a judge model jointly compares all candidate reasoning traces within a single long-context prompt. Unlike self-consistency or majority voting, this approach reliably recovers correct minority hypotheses on tasks where the modal answer is wrong. On the ARC Prize semi-private evaluation set, the solver achieves 72.9 percent at USD 38.99 per task - the highest score on the verified leaderboard at the time of writing, exceeding the best standalone frontier models, GPT-5.2 Pro at 54.2 percent and Gemini 3 Pro at 54.0 percent, by +18.7 percentage points. On the public evaluation set, it achieves 76.1 percent at USD 19.69 per task. I release the full source code and document extensive negative results, including the finding that prescriptive prompting templates and iterative refinement systematically reduce hypothesis diversity and degrade performance.

items.title: Researchers present MetaFlow, a meta-learning approach to train large language models as zero-shot workflow generators with strong generalization across tasks and operator sets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: From Search to Synthesis: Training LLMs as Zero-Shot Workflow Generators
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced MetaFlow, a meta-learning approach designed to train large language models (LLMs) as zero-shot workflow generators that generalize effectively across various tasks and operator sets. MetaFlow addresses the challenge of creating consistent, reusable workflows by learning to compose solution strategies from task and operator inputs, improving reliability and interpretability compared to instance-specific solutions. The model is trained through supervised fine-tuning on synthetic data followed by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, enabling it to produce effective workflows for both trained and novel tasks.

MetaFlow was evaluated on benchmarks including question answering, code generation, and mathematical reasoning, where it matched state-of-the-art performance on in-domain tasks and demonstrated strong zero-shot generalization to out-of-domain tasks and new operator sets. This approach offers a scalable alternative to manual workflow design, potentially enhancing the deployment and robustness of LLM-based solutions across diverse applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30704v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel across a wide range of tasks, yet their instance-specific solutions often lack the structural consistency needed for reliable deployment. Workflows that encode recurring algorithmic patterns at the task level provide a principled framework, offering robustness across instance variations, interpretable traces for debugging, and reusability across problem instances. However, manually designing such workflows requires significant expertise and effort, limiting their broader application. While automatic workflow generation could address this bottleneck, existing methods either produce instance-specific solutions without learning task-level patterns, or cannot generalize beyond their training configurations. We present MetaFlow, which casts workflow generation as a meta-learning problem: given a task and an operator set, the model learns to compose solution strategies. MetaFlow trains in two stages: supervised fine-tuning on synthetic workflow data, followed by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) that uses execution feedback across problem instances in the task to improve end-to-end success. The resulting model produces effective workflows for trained tasks and exhibits strong generalization to untrained tasks and novel operator sets. Across benchmarks in question answering, code generation, and mathematical reasoning, MetaFlow achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art baselines on in-domain tasks with single inference, while demonstrating remarkable zero-shot generalization capabilities on out-of-domain tasks and operator sets.

items.title: Researchers propose ComplianceGate, a classifier-gated multi-tier routing system for large language models that enforces data residency and reduces latency and costs in regulated industries [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: ComplianceGate: Classifier-Gated Multi-Tier LLM Routing for Inference in Regulated Industries
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced ComplianceGate, a classifier-gated multi-tier routing system designed for large language models (LLMs) used in regulated industries. This system addresses compliance and cost efficiency by using a trained encoder classifier to evaluate each query's complexity and data sensitivity before any model inference. Queries containing personally identifiable information (PII) are routed to local endpoints, ensuring data residency compliance, while simpler queries are directed to smaller, faster models, reducing resource use and costs.

Testing on 600 queries showed that ComplianceGate reduces median latency by 39%, cuts costs by 33-52% depending on query distribution, and improves generation throughput significantly compared to baseline models. The encoder classifier achieves 99.2% accuracy with near-perfect recall for PII, operating with minimal inference overhead, demonstrating a practical approach to compliance-by-design in LLM deployment.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31163v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models deployed in regulated industries operate under two constraints: compliance enforcement and cost efficiency. Personally identifiable information (PII) in user queries can reach model endpoints before the system determines whether that data should leave its jurisdictional boundary. Serving all queries through a single large model consumes full GPU capacity regardless of query complexity while offering no mechanism for geographic routing. Mixture-of-Experts architectures do not address this routing occurs between expert layers within the model after data has already arrived at the endpoint, with all experts loaded in memory regardless of query complexity. We propose a classifier-gated routing architecture that enforces compliance by design. A trained encoder classifier sits before any decoder inference, evaluating each query for complexity and data sensitivity, then routing it to an appropriately sized dense model in the appropriate geographic location. PII-containing queries route to local endpoints before any LLM computation begins, making data residency violations structurally impossible. Simple queries reach small, fast models at a fraction of the cost. Our evaluation on 600 queries demonstrates 39% median latency reduction, 33-52% cost savings depending on query distribution, and generation throughput of 122-200 tokens/second versus 50-64 for the baseline. The encoder classifier achieves 99.2% accuracy with near-perfect PII recall at 7ms inference overhead, establishing pre-inference classification as a practical path to compliance-by-design LLM deployment.

items.title: Researchers introduce MoralAltDataset to evaluate 15 LLMs on generating and preferring moral alternatives beyond binary dilemmas, finding LLM-generated options often surpass human ones in ethical and structural quality [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Can LLMs Imagine Moral Alternatives Beyond Binary Dilemmas?
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced MoralAltDataset, a collection of 307 moral dilemmas enhanced with compromise and reframed alternatives, to evaluate how large language models (LLMs) handle moral decision-making beyond binary choices. Testing 15 LLMs, the study found that these models often prefer compromise alternatives over original options, significantly influencing moral judgments. The research also compared LLM-generated alternatives to human-authored ones, revealing that LLMs frequently produce options that better meet detailed ethical and structural standards.

The dataset includes both narrative Advisor dilemmas and AI-facing Agent dilemmas, reflecting diverse moral scenarios. Evaluations involved pairwise preference tests and expert assessments, highlighting trade-offs between the structural quality of alternatives and their practical feasibility. This work underscores the potential of LLMs to generate nuanced moral options that extend beyond traditional binary frameworks, offering insights into their role as moral advisors and agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31213v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as moral advisors and agents, they need to address dilemmas between two competing values. However, existing research on LLMs with moral dilemmas overlooks a central aspect of human moral cognition: the ability to imagine alternatives that move beyond the given options. We introduce MoralAltDataset, a dataset of 307 moral dilemmas spanning narrative Advisor dilemmas and AI-facing Agent dilemmas, each augmented with compromise and reframed alternatives. We first examine whether humans and LLMs shift their judgments when such alternatives are introduced. Across 15 LLMs, we find that compromise alternatives are often preferred over either original option, substantially reshaping moral choice. We then evaluate the quality of LLM-generated alternatives against human-authored ones using pairwise preference and expert-based criteria. Results show that LLM-generated alternatives are often preferred and better satisfy fine-grained structural and ethical criteria, while revealing trade-offs between structural quality and practical feasibility.

items.title: Researchers propose failure-driven self-improvement for computer-use agents using LLMs to diagnose and patch errors, improving OpenCUA-72B success rate from 42.3% to 48.9% without extra training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning from Failure: Inference-Time Self-Improvement for Computer-Use Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a failure-driven self-improvement approach for computer-use agents that utilize multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to perform tasks on computers. Unlike traditional methods that focus only on successful task completions, this new method leverages failed attempts by using an LLM to diagnose errors, suggest solutions, and generate code patches that improve the agent's performance. Testing this approach on the OpenCUA-72B model with the OSWorld benchmark increased the success rate from 42.3% to 48.9% without additional training and with minimal inference overhead.

This approach complements existing success-based training pipelines by extracting valuable insights from failure cases, which are typically discarded. The process involves human verification of generated patches to ensure quality improvements. The results demonstrate that incorporating failure analysis can lead to more efficient and effective enhancements in agent capabilities, offering a promising direction for future development of computer-use agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31270v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Computer-use agents, which leverage multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to operate computers and complete tasks, have attracted significant attention for their utility and versatility. A major challenge in developing these agents is collecting large-scale, high-quality trajectories. The standard approach generates synthetic data through a self-improving loop: an agent is placed in a verifiable environment and iteratively fine-tuned on its successful trajectories. Despite its effectiveness, this paradigm exploits only successful trajectories and discards the failed ones, even though failures carry rich information about a model's weaknesses. In this work, we explore a complementary failure-driven self-improvement loop, a data-centric paradigm that turns failed trajectories into agent improvements. Specifically, we employ an LLM to diagnose failure modes, propose inference-time solutions, and generate code patches -- lightly verified by humans -- that upgrade the agent. items.title: Researchers find probability calibration reduces evaluator preference coupling in LLM agent feedback loops by up to 49%, improving strategy learning accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Calibrating the Evaluator: Does Probability Calibration Mitigate Preference Coupling in LLM Agent Feedback Loops?
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that applying probability calibration to evaluator feedback in large language model (LLM) agent training can significantly reduce evaluator preference coupling, a bias where evaluator judgments skew the agent's learned strategies. In a controlled experiment comparing standard binary feedback with confidence-calibrated updates, calibration lowered the coupling coefficient by 20-49% and reduced divergence measures by 45-67%, indicating more accurate strategy learning.

The study used DeepSeek-V4-Pro as the executor and GLM5.2 as the evaluator, confirming that the improvements were not due to reduced update asymmetry through a symmetric logistic regression control. The authors have released the calibrated training protocol and suggest it as an effective, lightweight method to mitigate evaluator bias in LLM feedback loops, enhancing the reliability of LLM-as-judge deployment systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31371v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When large language model (LLM) agents adapt their behavior through evaluator feedback, systematic evaluator biases propagate into the agent's learned strategy distribution - a phenomenon termed evaluator preference coupling. Prior work has documented this coupling and established a diagnostic framework (EPC) to measure it, but has not investigated whether calibration techniques can mitigate the effect. We present the first study of evaluator calibration as mitigation: applying probability calibration to the evaluator's pairwise judgments to reduce spurious preference propagation. In a controlled within-subjects experiment (N=5) comparing standard binary TTRL (win/loss) with confidence-calibrated TTRL (probability-weighted updates) using DeepSeek-V4-Pro as executor and GLM5.2 as evaluator, we find that calibration reduces the coupling coefficient gamma by 20-49% and Jensen-Shannon divergence by 45-67%. A symmetric-LR control confirms the effect is not due to reduced update asymmetry. We release the calibrated TTRL protocol and recommend it as a lightweight mitigation for LLM-as-judge deployment pipelines.

items.title: Researchers introduce STEB, an open-source Style Text Embedding Benchmark covering 96 datasets in 7 languages to standardize style embedding evaluation across multiple tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: STEB: Style Text Embedding Benchmark
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced the Style Text Embedding Benchmark (STEB), an open-source framework designed to standardize the evaluation of style embeddings across various tasks. STEB includes 96 datasets in seven languages and covers applications such as authorship verification, authorship retrieval, AI-text detection, and linguistic feature probing. The benchmark reveals that semantic embeddings generally perform poorly on stylistic tasks and that no single style embedding excels universally across all evaluated tasks.

STEB aims to address the fragmented nature of style embedding evaluation by providing a comprehensive and consistent testing ground. The researchers have made the STEB codebase publicly available to facilitate further research and development in this area.

To bridge this gap, we introduce the Style Text Embedding Benchmark, a comprehensive open-source benchmark intended to standardize the evaluation of style embeddings. STEB encompasses 96 datasets across 7 languages, spanning applications such as authorship verification, authorship retrieval, AI-text detection, probing of linguistic features, and others. We find that semantic embeddings consistently fail in stylistic tasks, and that there is no style embedding that is universally superior across all tasks evaluated. We open-source the STEB code base at: https://github.com/rrivera1849/STEB.

items.title: Researchers introduce QVal, a training-free testbed to cheaply evaluate dense supervision signals for long-horizon LLM agents across 21 methods and multiple environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: QVal: Cheaply Evaluating Dense Supervision Signals for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced QVal, a training-free testbed designed to evaluate dense supervision signals for long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents. QVal assesses how well a method's scoring aligns with the Q-values of a strong reference policy, enabling direct comparison of supervision signals without the need for costly training pipelines. This approach addresses the challenge of sparse outcome-only rewards by providing a way to evaluate intermediate action quality across various methods and environments.

QVal-v1.0 benchmarks 21 dense supervision methods spanning seven methodological families across four diverse environments and six open-weight model backbones, conducting over 1,200 evaluation experiments. The study found that simple prompting baselines often outperform recent dense supervision techniques, with performance clustering by method family. QVal is designed for easy extension to new environments and methods, facilitating iterative development of dense supervision approaches prior to training.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.32034v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents increasingly act over long horizons, where a single trajectory can contain hundreds or thousands of actions. In these settings, outcome-only rewards provide too sparse guidance, failing to inform the model about the goodness of intermediate actions. Dense supervision methods aim to solve this problem by scoring intermediate steps, from intrinsic confidence to self-distillation and embedding similarities. However, it is common practice to evaluate them by measuring the downstream performance of a training pipeline that integrates them. This is expensive, conflates supervision quality with training engineering confounders, and renders different methodological families requiring distinct training setups incomparable. As a result, dense supervision methods are rarely benchmarked on common ground. We introduce QVal, a training-free testbed for directly evaluating dense supervision signals. Given a state-action pair, QVal measures how well a method's score is Q-aligned: whether it orders actions according to the Q-values of a strong reference-policy. This lets us compare signals before any training run and separate signal quality from other engineering choices. We instantiate QVal as QVal-v1.0, benchmarking 21 dense supervision methods across four diverse environments and seven methodological families, with over 1.2K evaluation experiments across six open-weight model backbones. We find that simple prompting baselines consistently outperform recent dense supervision methods from the literature, and that performance clusters strongly by family. These findings hold across model sizes, environments, and observation modalities. QVal is designed to be easily extensible to new environments and methods, enabling researchers to iterate on dense supervision methods before any training run.

items.title: Researchers find language models trained on fixed counterfactual explanations produce introspective behavior tracking shifts without updated supervision across multiple tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Introspective Coupling: Self-Explanation Training Tracks Behavioral Change Despite Fixed Supervision
items.summary:
Researchers have found that language models (LMs) trained to generate explanations of their predictions using fixed counterfactual explanations from earlier model checkpoints or similar models can produce explanations that more accurately reflect their current behavior than the original training targets. This phenomenon, termed "introspective coupling," occurs when the training explanations remain correlated with the model's evolving behavior, allowing explanations to track behavioral changes even without updated supervision. The effect was observed across multiple tasks, including sycophancy and refusal, and demonstrated robustness to label noise.

The study shows that fixed datasets of counterfactual explanations can serve as scalable and generalizable signals for post-training introspection, enabling LMs to adapt their explanations alongside shifts in behavior when trained concurrently with other objectives. This insight suggests a promising approach for improving the faithfulness of model-generated explanations without requiring continuous retraining on updated supervision data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.32038v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When does training language models (LMs) to generate explanations of their predictions yield faithful introspection, rather than superficial imitation? We study LMs trained to explain which features of their inputs influenced their behavior, using models' counterfactual behavior on modified inputs as supervision. Surprisingly, we find that LMs trained on fixed counterfactual explanations derived from earlier checkpoints of themselves, or even from behaviorally similar models in different families, frequently produce explanations more faithful to their own current behaviors than to those of their training targets. This "introspective" coupling between LM explanations and behaviors occurs when training explanations remain sufficiently correlated with current behaviors over the course of training, even as behaviors themselves shift. We also show that introspective coupling tracks behavior shifts: when explanation training is provided concurrently with other post-training objectives, explanations track those shifts without requiring updated supervision. This phenomenon appears in multiple tasks, including sycophancy and refusal, and is robust to label noise. Overall, our results show that even fixed datasets of counterfactual explanations can provide scalable and generalizable post-training signal for introspection.

items.title: Researchers introduce DeXposure-Claw, an agentic system using forecast-grounded LLM supervision for DeFi risk management with regulator-aligned evaluation on five years of data [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: DeXposure-Claw: An Agentic System for DeFi Risk Supervision
items.summary:
Researchers have developed DeXposure-Claw, an agentic supervision system designed to manage risks in decentralized finance (DeFi) by using forecast-grounded large language model (LLM) supervision aligned with regulatory standards. The system integrates a graph time-series foundation model to predict future exposure networks, deterministic monitors and stress scenarios to generate alerts and evidence, and confidence gates to control escalation, ultimately producing auditable supervisory tickets with clear rationales. This approach addresses the limitations of general-purpose LLM agents, which tend to overreact to weak evidence and recommend unnecessary high-stakes interventions.

The team also introduced DeXposure-Bench, a comprehensive evaluation framework that measures the system's decisions against regulator-aligned criteria, including absolute loss and false-intervention rates. Experiments conducted on five years of weekly real-world data demonstrate the effectiveness of DeXposure-Claw in providing reliable and accountable DeFi risk supervision. The code for the system is publicly available for further research and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.19501v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Decentralized finance exposes supervisors to fast-moving, networked credit risks. General-purpose LLM agents fit this setting poorly: they over-read weak evidence and recommend high-stakes interventions, while existing evaluations offer no regulator-aligned way to measure the resulting false alarms. We introduce DeXposure-Claw, a forecast-grounded agentic supervision system that routes LLM decisions through structured evidence: (1) DeXposure-FM, a graph time-series foundation model, forecasts future exposure networks; (2) deterministic monitors and stress scenarios then turn those forecasts into typed alerts, attribution signals, and scenario evidence; and (3) data-health and confidence gates constrain escalation before DeXposure-Claw emits auditable supervisory tickets with rationales. We further develop DeXposure-Bench, a six-axis evaluation harness, whose decision axis scores tickets against a regulator-aligned absolute-loss ground truth and an explicit false-intervention rate. Experiments on five years of weekly real data fully support our system. Code is at https://github.com/EVIEHub/DeXposure-Claw.

items.title: Researchers propose GUI-AIMA, an attention-based fine-tuning framework aligning intrinsic multimodal attention for efficient GUI grounding with state-of-the-art accuracy on multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: GUI-AIMA: Aligning Intrinsic Multimodal Attention with a Context Anchor for GUI Grounding
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced GUI-AIMA, a novel attention-based fine-tuning framework designed to improve graphical user interface (GUI) grounding by aligning intrinsic multimodal attention in large language models. Unlike traditional methods that generate precise screen coordinates from visual inputs, GUI-AIMA identifies relevant visual patches first and then determines exact click locations, enhancing efficiency and accuracy without relying on coordinate generation. This approach leverages the native grounding ability found in the attention maps of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and adapts patch-wise grounding signals through multi-head aggregation.

Trained on a relatively small dataset of 509,000 samples, GUI-AIMA-3B demonstrates exceptional data efficiency and achieves state-of-the-art performance among 3B parameter models across multiple benchmarks, including ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, OSWorld-G, MMBench-GUI-L2, and UI-Vision. Its coordinate-free design also supports an optional zoom-in stage, further enhancing its flexibility and precision in GUI grounding tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2511.00810v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) grounding is a key capability for computer-use agents, mapping natural-language instructions to actionable regions on the screen. Existing Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) approaches typically formulate GUI grounding as a text-based coordinate generation task. However, directly generating precise coordinates from visual inputs is challenging and often data-intensive. A more intuitive strategy is to first identify instruction-relevant visual patches and then determine the exact click location within them. Motivated by recent observations that general MLLMs exhibit native grounding ability embedded in their attention maps, we propose GUI-AIMA, an attention-based and coordinate-free supervised fine-tuning framework for efficient GUI grounding. GUI-AIMA aligns the intrinsic multimodal attention of MLLMs with patch-wise grounding signals. These signals are calculated adaptively for diverse user instructions by multi-head aggregation on simplified query-visual attention matrices. Besides, its coordinate-free manner can easily integrate a plug-and-play zoom-in stage. GUI-AIMA-3B was trained with only 509k samples (around 101k screenshots), demonstrating exceptional data efficiency and verifying that light training can trigger the native grounding capability of MLLMs. It achieves state-of-the-art performance among 3B models, attaining an average accuracy of 61.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro, 92.1% on ScreenSpot-v2, 68.1% on OSWorld-G, 79.1% on MMBench-GUI-L2, and 60.0% on UI-Vision. Project page: https://github.com/sjz5202/GUI-AIMA .

items.title: Researchers introduce TaNOS, a self-supervised pretraining framework that improves numerical reasoning robustness and transferability on expert-domain tables, outperforming GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro in FinQA benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Generalizing Numerical Reasoning in Table Data through Operation Sketches and Self-Supervised Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed TaNOS, a self-supervised pretraining framework designed to enhance numerical reasoning over expert-domain tables by improving robustness and transferability. TaNOS employs header anonymization, operation sketches, and a program-first self-supervised approach to reduce reliance on superficial cues and promote structural reasoning. When applied to an 8-billion-parameter instruction-tuned model, TaNOS achieved 80.13% execution accuracy on the FinQA benchmark using only 10% of the training data, outperforming traditional supervised fine-tuning methods and proprietary models like GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro.

TaNOS also demonstrated strong resilience to domain shifts, showing less than a 2 percentage point drop in accuracy across different domains, compared to over 10 points for standard fine-tuning approaches. These findings suggest that combining structural guidance with header-agnostic representations and correctness-guaranteed self-supervision can significantly improve the robustness and generalization of numerical reasoning models across diverse expert tables.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.21495v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Numerical reasoning over expert-domain tables often exhibits high in-domain accuracy but limited robustness to domain shift. Models trained with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on specific datasets tend to rely on header-operation shortcuts rather than structural reasoning. We introduce TaNOS, a continual pre-training framework comprising three components: (i) header anonymization to reduce lexical memorization, (ii) operation sketches that provide minimal structural cues, and (iii) self-supervised pretraining that constructs correctness-guaranteed program-question pairs from given tables in a program-first manner. By decoupling domain semantics and numerical operation structure, TaNOS improves the transferability of numerical reasoning. Applied to an 8B instruction-tuned model, TaNOS achieves 80.13% execution accuracy on FinQA with only 10% train data, outperforming SFT baseline (73.97%) with full train data and proprietary models such as GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro. Furthermore, in the domain-shift experiments, TaNOS displays nearly-negligible cross-domain gap (<2pp) when standard SFT shows over 10pp gap. These results suggest that structural guidance with operation sketches, header-agnostic representations, and correctness-guaranteed self-supervision can improve the robustness of numerical reasoning across diverse expert-domain tables.

items.title: Researchers identify shared lexical task-specific attention heads in LLMs that explain behavioral variability across instruction-based and example-based prompts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Shared Lexical Task Representations Explain Behavioral Variability In LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers have identified specific attention heads in large language models (LLMs) that consistently represent task information across different prompting styles, such as instruction-based and example-based prompts. These "lexical task heads" appear to underlie the models' ability to perform tasks and explain why their behavior varies depending on how prompts are presented. The study shows that the activation level of these heads correlates with performance, and failures can result from competing task signals that weaken the intended task representation.

By comparing two common prompting methods, the researchers found that despite performance fluctuations, LLMs engage shared internal mechanisms to process tasks. This discovery sheds light on the internal representations driving LLM behavior, offering a clearer understanding of prompt sensitivity that has often seemed unpredictable to users and developers. The findings contribute to explaining how LLMs interpret and respond to different prompt formulations, potentially guiding improvements in model reliability and interpretability.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.22027v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: One of the most common complaints about large language models (LLMs) is their prompt sensitivity -- that is, the fact that their ability to perform a task or provide a correct answer to a question can depend unpredictably on the way the question is posed. We investigate this variation by comparing two very different but commonly-used styles of prompting: instruction-based prompts, which describe the task in natural language, and example-based prompts, which provide in-context few-shot demonstration pairs to illustrate the task. We find that, despite large variation in performance as a function of the prompt, the model engages some common underlying mechanisms across different prompts of a task. Specifically, we identify task-specific attention heads whose outputs literally describe the task -- which we dub lexical task heads -- and show that these heads are shared across prompting styles and trigger subsequent answer production. We further find that behavioral variation between prompts can be explained by the degree to which these heads are activated, and that failures are at least sometimes due to competing task representations that dilute the signal of the target task. Our results together present an increasingly clear picture of how LLMs' internal representations can explain behavior that otherwise seems idiosyncratic to users and developers.

items.title: Researchers introduce INFUSER, an influence-guided self-evolution framework that improves reasoning in language models with over 20% performance gain on Olympiad and SuperGPQA benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: INFUSER: Influence-Guided Self-Evolution Improves Reasoning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed INFUSER, a novel influence-guided self-evolution framework designed to enhance reasoning capabilities in pretrained language models. INFUSER employs an iterative co-training approach involving a Generator that creates questions and answers from unstructured documents, and a Solver that improves by training on these generated examples. This method uses an optimizer-aware influence score to reward the Generator for producing questions that effectively improve the Solver, resulting in over 20% performance gains on Olympiad and SuperGPQA benchmarks compared to existing self-evolution techniques.

The framework introduces DuGRPO, a dual-normalized variant of GRPO, to better handle the noisy influence scores during training. INFUSER's adaptive curriculum prioritizes questions that are beneficial to the Solver rather than merely difficult ones. Experiments demonstrate that an 8-billion-parameter INFUSER Generator surpasses a frozen 32-billion-parameter baseline on math and coding tasks. Additional tests confirm the necessity of each component, and extensions show the framework's flexibility and generalizability. The code for INFUSER is publicly available for further research and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.09052v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-evolution offers a scalable path to stronger reasoning: a pretrained language model improves itself with only minimal external supervision. Yet existing methods either depend on extensively curated or teacher-generated training data, or, when the generator runs unsupervised, reward it by a difficulty heuristic that need not improve the solver. We introduce INFUSER, an iterative co-training framework with two co-evolving roles: a Generator that drafts questions and reference golden answers from a pool of unstructured, automatically collected documents, and a Solver that improves by training on them. The solver is trained with standard correctness rewards against the generator-provided answers, while the generator is rewarded by an optimizer-aware influence score that measures whether each proposed question would actually improve the solver on the target distribution. Because this continuous, noisy influence score is poorly served by standard GRPO, we propose DuGRPO, a dual-normalized variant of GRPO, for generator training. Together, these turn the document pool into an adaptive curriculum that favors questions useful to the current solver, not just hard ones. On Qwen3-8B-Base, INFUSER outperforms strong self-evolution baselines with over 20% relative improvement on Olympiad and SuperGPQA benchmarks, and an 8B INFUSER co-evolving generator outperforms a frozen 32B thinking generator on math and coding. Ablations confirm each design choice is necessary, and two extensions, applying INFUSER to an instruction-finetuned anchor and augmenting it with rule-verifiable RLVR data, further demonstrate the flexibility and generalizability of the framework. Code is available at https://github.com/FFishy-git/INFUSER.

items.title: Researchers introduce Sibling-Guided Credit Distillation to improve long-horizon tool-use reinforcement learning by guiding credit assignment while maintaining policy gradient control [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Keep Policy Gradient in Charge: Sibling-Guided Credit Distillation for Long-Horizon Tool-Use Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Sibling-Guided Credit Distillation (SGCD), a new method to enhance long-horizon tool-use reinforcement learning by improving credit assignment while maintaining policy gradient control. SGCD uses distillation to provide bounded credit weighting rather than competing with the actor loss, leveraging dynamic sampling of mixed successful and failed rollouts and an external language model to guide training. This approach leads to better performance on benchmark tasks compared to existing methods.

SGCD was tested on the AppWorld and tau^3-airline environments, showing improvements in held-out evaluation scores over GRPO-family comparators. items.title: Researchers present HASTE, a hierarchical multi-agent system that organizes ML engineering skills across global, domain, and competition tiers to improve transfer efficiency and medal rates in Kaggle competitions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Why Solve It Twice? Hierarchical Accumulation of Skills for Transfer-Efficient ML Engineering
items.summary:
Researchers have developed HASTE, a hierarchical multi-agent system designed to improve machine learning engineering efficiency by organizing skills across global, domain, and competition-specific tiers. This system coordinates specialized agents and uses large language model-driven abstraction to facilitate knowledge transfer, significantly increasing medal rates in Kaggle competitions compared to flat skill loading methods. HASTE achieved a 77.3% medal rate on the MLE-Bench Lite benchmark, demonstrating its effectiveness in both cold-start and warm-start scenarios.

The system maintains a 159-skill inventory and shows that tiered loading leads to a 100% medal rate across eight competitions, outperforming flat loading which only reached 62.5%. Warm-start runs, which reuse skills from previous competitions, require 52% fewer refinement iterations and result in a higher acceptance rate of proposed changes by the agents. These findings suggest that structured knowledge organization can enhance ML engineering performance, potentially reducing the need for stronger models or larger compute budgets.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30911v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: ML engineering agents waste compute rediscovering known techniques because every competition is a cold start. We present HASTE, a hierarchical multi-agent system that organizes cross-competition knowledge into three scope tiers (global, domain, and competition-specific), each coupled to a matching agent level. An orchestrator coordinates domain specialists and promotes learning between tiers via LLM-driven abstraction. A controlled ablation provides evidence for scoped loading: holding a 159-skill inventory constant across 8 competitions, tiered loading achieves a 100% medal rate while flat loading reaches only 62.5%, the same medal rate as loading no skills, and consumes 2x the output tokens. On the full MLE-Bench Lite benchmark (22 Kaggle competitions), HASTE reaches a medal rate of 77.3% using Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 12h per competition. In a cold-start run, the system begins with no accumulated skills. In warm-start runs, it reloads skills learned from earlier competitions, using only global and domain-level skills for transfer across competitions. Warm starts use 52% fewer refinement iterations, and the fraction of proposed changes kept by the agent rises from 42% at low inventory to 85% once 50+ skills are available. These results suggest that better knowledge organization can partly substitute for model strength and compute budget in ML-engineering agents.

items.title: Researchers propose RoPoLL, a robust panel of LLM judges using geometric median aggregation, outperforming traditional PoLL under biased contamination across multiple benchmarks and corruption regimes [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: RoPoLL: Robust Panel of LLM Judges
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced RoPoLL, a robust panel of large language model (LLM) judges that improves upon the traditional Panel of LLM Evaluators (PoLL) by using geometric median aggregation to achieve greater resistance to biased contamination. Unlike PoLL, which can suffer unbounded bias when even a single judge exhibits typical LLM failures such as mode collapse or sycophancy, RoPoLL employs a robust mean estimator that maintains accuracy under various corruption scenarios. This approach has been tested across multiple benchmarks, judge sizes, and corruption regimes, demonstrating superior performance especially against biased and heavy-tailed adversarial attacks.

The study formalizes the LLM Jury under the Huber contamination model and provides theoretical error bounds that align with information-theoretic limits. Experiments involving 13 open-weight judges and several reward-model benchmarks show that RoPoLL consistently outperforms PoLL, achieving up to 19% improvement on cross-dimensional attacks and significantly better results against Byzantine adversaries. Notably, a small RoPoLL committee with fewer parameters outperformed a much larger model on a benchmark with substantial corruption, confirming its robustness to biased contamination rather than mere noise.

These findings suggest that RoPoLL offers a more reliable and computationally feasible method for aggregating LLM evaluations, potentially enhancing the robustness of AI model assessment in the presence of adversarial or biased inputs. This advancement could influence future evaluation protocols and improve the trustworthiness of consensus-based LLM judgments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30931v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The LLM Jury, a Panel of LLM Evaluators (PoLL) reporting consensus scores, has become a practical alternative to single-judge LLM evaluation, yet its statistical behavior remains poorly understood. We formalize the LLM Jury under the Huber contamination model and show that PoLL incurs unbounded bias under any positive contamination, regardless of jury size, whenever a single judge fails in a biased, LLM-typical way (mode collapse, sycophancy, safety refusal). Framing jury consensus as classical robust mean estimation, we propose RoPoLL (Robust Panel of LLM-as-Judge), which preserves the PoLL panel but replaces the aggregation function with a robust mean estimator, instantiated with the geometric median (GM): tuning-free, with the optimal finite-sample breakdown point 1/2. A finite-sample error bound and a matching information-theoretic minimax lower bound agree on the parametric rate sigma*sqrt(d/N) and differ on the breakdown floor by a factor of sqrt(d), a statistical-computational gap that polynomial-time RoPoLL pays relative to the intractable Tukey halfspace median. Across 13 open-weight judges (4B-675B), three reward-model benchmarks, and four corruption regimes at rates up to 50%, RoPoLL dominates PoLL on every biased corruption type: by about 19% on cross-dimensional attacks at matched compute, and by orders of magnitude on heavy-tailed Byzantine adversaries. A 3-judge RoPoLL committee at 38B beats Mistral-Large-3 (675B) by 1.31x on HelpSteer-2 under 30% bimodal-random corruption, an 18x parameter advantage at better accuracy; a Noisy-GT control confirms the premium is paid against biased contamination, not benign imprecision.

items.title: Researchers introduce Neuro-Bayesian-Symbolic Residual Attention Shallow Network for explainable cybersecurity risk assessment, validated on 20 open-source projects with confidence scores of 0.79-0.97 [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Neuro-Bayesian-Symbolic Residual Attention Shallow Network: Explainable Deep Learning for Cybersecurity Risk Assessment
items.summary:
Researchers have developed the Neuro-Bayesian-Symbolic Residual Attention Shallow Network (NBS-RASN), a hybrid neural architecture designed for explainable cybersecurity risk assessment in open-source ecosystems. This shallow network integrates domain knowledge, causal reasoning, and expert judgment through 80 interpretable neurons across 12 layers, enforcing five epistemological axioms to ensure precision, causality, falsifiability, transparency, and completeness. Unlike traditional deep models, NBS-RASN maintains interpretability while learning complex risk patterns using residual attention and feedback loops, producing fully decomposable risk scores that include expert adjustments linked to specific risk amplifiers.

The model was validated on 20 open-source projects covering all OWASP Top 10:2025 categories and various language risk classes, achieving confidence scores between 0.79 and 0.97. This approach challenges the notion that deep learning requires deep networks by demonstrating that shallow networks with embedded deep reasoning can outperform opaque models in cybersecurity contexts where interpretability is critical.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce the Neuro-Bayesian-Symbolic Residual Attention Shallow Network (NBS-RASN), a hybrid neural architecture for explainable cybersecurity risk assessment in open-source ecosystems. Unlike deep models that trade interpretability for accuracy, our shallow network encodes domain knowledge, causal reasoning, and expert judgment as differentiable components. It uses 80 interpretable neurons across 12 layers, including a gatekeeper that enforces five epistemological axioms - precision, causality, falsifiability, transparency, and completeness - as hard constraints before propagation. Despite limited depth, the network exhibits deep-learning traits via residual attention and feedback loops, learning complex risk patterns without becoming a black box. It produces fully decomposable scores: a deterministic weighted component plus an expert adjustment, with each adjustment traceable to named amplifiers (blast radius, propagation speed, structural nature, default exposure, exploitation pattern, institutional criticality). We validate on 20 open-source projects covering all OWASP Top 10:2025 categories and language risk classes, achieving confidence scores of 0.79-0.97, and show that explainability is guaranteed by design, not by a training algorithm. This challenges the assumption that deep learning requires deep networks, proving that shallow networks with deep reasoning can outperform opaque models in high-stakes cybersecurity, where interpretability is essential.

items.title: Researchers evaluate natural-language-to-Lean statement formalization on a 400-entry graduate-level benchmark, finding 89.5% compilation but only 60.5% consensus faithfulness, highlighting gaps in current formalizer models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Compilation: Evaluating Faithful Natural-Language-to-Lean Statement Formalization
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated the process of converting natural language statements into formal Lean language on a 400-entry graduate-level benchmark covering topics like real analysis, complex analysis, topology, and algebra. Their study revealed that while 89.5% of the formalized statements compiled successfully, only 60.5% were deemed faithful to the original meaning by consensus, highlighting a significant gap between syntactic validity and semantic accuracy.

The evaluation combined Lean compilation checks, cross-model semantic judgments, and expert human calibration to assess faithfulness. Human audits confirmed that most consensus-positive outputs were indeed faithful, while many compile-passing but consensus-negative outputs contained semantic errors. The study also analyzed the impact of different formalization pipeline components, finding that elaboration feedback improved validity but increased semantic failures, search enhanced grounding and selectivity, and expert drafting was largely replaceable when feedback and grounding were present.

These findings suggest that formal validity, proof-oriented Lean competence, and faithful statement generation are distinct challenges that should be evaluated separately. Current one-shot formalizer models and prover-oriented Lean models show limited performance in faithful statement generation, indicating room for improvement in natural-language-to-formal-language translation tools.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Theorem-proving benchmarks evaluate proof search against fixed formal statements, but natural-language-to-Lean formalization must generate the formal statement itself. In this setting, compilation is only a validity check: a Lean declaration may type-check while omitting hypotheses, changing domains, or expressing a vacuous claim. We study faithful statement formalization as both an evaluation problem and a bottleneck-attribution problem. On a 400-entry graduate-level benchmark spanning real analysis, complex analysis, topology, and algebra, our protocol combines Lean compilation, cross-model semantic judging, and human expert calibration. The resulting picture is different from compile-rate evaluation: a full tool-augmented agent reaches 89.5% compilation but only 60.5% consensus faithfulness, exposing a 29.0-point compile-pass but consensus-unfaithful gap. Targeted human audits support the metric as a conservative decision boundary: across available case-level audits, 96.0% of consensus-positive outputs are human-confirmed faithful, while 82.4% of compile-pass consensus-negative outputs are human-confirmed semantic failures. Under this metric, existing one-shot formalizer models and prover-oriented Lean models remain low, suggesting that formal validity, proof-oriented Lean competence, and faithful statement generation should be reported separately. We then use a full $2^3$ factorial design to decompose three recurring interventions in formalization pipelines: parametric expert drafting, Mathlib/context search, and Lean elaboration feedback. Elaboration feedback is the largest validity intervention, but it also exposes a larger compile-pass semantic-failure bucket; search mainly improves grounding and selectivity; and fine-tuned drafting is largely substitutable in this tool stack once feedback and grounding are available.

items.title: Researchers introduce HealthAgentBench, a benchmark suite of 54 realistic healthcare AI tasks across 7 categories, revealing current frontier agents achieve only about 42% success rate [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: HealthAgentBench: A Unified Benchmark Suite of Realistic Agentic Healthcare Environments for Challenging Frontier AI Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed HealthAgentBench, a comprehensive benchmark suite comprising 54 realistic healthcare AI tasks across seven categories designed to evaluate the capabilities of advanced AI agents in clinical workflows. The suite challenges agents to perform complex, multi-step reasoning using raw healthcare data in diverse environments, reflecting real-world patient care scenarios. Testing leading AI models revealed a modest overall success rate of about 42%, highlighting the difficulty of these tasks and the current limitations of frontier AI agents in healthcare applications.

HealthAgentBench covers a wide range of healthcare workflows and modalities, including electronic health records and medical imaging. While some agents showed promise in automating research modeling pipelines with EHR data, medical imaging tasks remain particularly challenging. The benchmark also identified that tasks requiring extensive search and compositional reasoning are difficult for all tested agents, indicating areas needing further development.

The introduction of HealthAgentBench provides a rigorous and realistic platform for assessing AI progress in healthcare, emphasizing significant room for improvement. By releasing this benchmark publicly, the researchers aim to foster advancements in AI agents capable of handling complex clinical tasks, ultimately supporting better healthcare outcomes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI agents become increasingly capable of complex, long-horizon reasoning, rigorous and holistic evaluation is essential for measuring progress toward real-world healthcare applications. We introduce HealthAgentBench, a suite of 54 agentic healthcare tasks across 7 categories each with its unique environment. The benchmark suite spans diverse workflows throughout the patient journey and a broad range of modalities. Each task is designed to replicate an end-to-end clinical workflow: given minimal instructions, an agent must explore raw healthcare data, operate within a complex environment, and execute multi-step solutions that go beyond naive prompting. A final task success rate is reported to provide a single, interpretable metric for HealthAgentBench overall performance for each agent. Evaluating frontier agents on HealthAgentBench, we find that overall task success rate remains low, underscoring the difficulty of the suite. The strongest and the most cost effective agent, Codex GPT-5.5, achieves only approximately 42% success rate. Beyond aggregate performance, HealthAgentBench reveals nuanced strengths and weaknesses across task categories. Frontier agents show promise in automatically developing research modeling pipelines over EHR data, but medical imaging remains especially challenging, particularly for Claude Code models, while Codex GPT-5.5 shows emerging capability. Tasks that combine large search spaces with compositional reasoning requirements remain difficult for all current agents. Together, these results suggest that HealthAgentBench provides a challenging and realistic benchmark with substantial room for future progress. We release our benchmark at https://github.com/microsoft/HealthAgentBench.

items.title: Researchers propose Hard-Routed MoR-LoRA, a two-stage framework for composing frozen reasoning LoRA experts with hard top-1 routing, reducing trainable parameters and preserving expert behavior across benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning to Select, Not Relearn: Hard-Routed Mixtures of Reasoning LoRAs
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Hard-Routed MoR-LoRA, a two-stage framework designed to compose frozen reasoning LoRA experts using hard top-1 routing. This approach enables the integration of independently trained domain-specific LoRA adapters into a single large language model while preserving their original behavior and significantly reducing the number of trainable parameters compared to soft-routing mixture methods.

The method involves first training domain-specific LoRA adapters with reinforcement learning to develop reasoning experts. These experts are then frozen, and a lightweight shared router along with a small attention LoRA is trained to select exactly one expert per token through hard routing. Experiments across multiple benchmarks and model scales demonstrate that Hard-Routed MoR-LoRA maintains expert performance efficiently, with analysis indicating that hard unit-scale routing offers a simpler and more effective way to compose frozen LoRA experts than normalized soft mixtures.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31413v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Composing independently trained LoRA adapters into a single large language model is useful for multi-domain adaptation, especially when the original training data cannot be shared. A common approach is to use MoE-style routing over LoRA experts, but for frozen pretrained adapters, soft weighted combinations can change the unit-scale additive update under which each LoRA module was originally trained. We propose \textbf{Hard-Routed MoR-LoRA}, a two-stage framework for composing frozen reasoning LoRA experts through unit-scale hard selection. First, domain-specific LoRA adapters are trained independently using reinforcement learning from verifiable feedback to obtain reasoning experts. Then, all experts are frozen, reasoning traces are distilled from them, and only a lightweight shared router together with a small attention LoRA is trained for integration. The router selects exactly one expert per token using hard top-1 routing, while a straight-through estimator enables gradient-based training. Experiments across five benchmarks, multiple model scales, and additional model families show that Hard-Routed MoR-LoRA preserves expert behavior while requiring substantially fewer trainable parameters than soft-routing mixture baselines. Our analysis further shows that normalized soft mixtures often concentrate most routing mass on a single expert, suggesting that hard unit-scale routing provides a simple and efficient abstraction for frozen LoRA expert composition.

items.title: Researchers introduce CDR-Bench, a benchmark with 3,462 tasks to evaluate LLMs' execution of compositional, order-sensitive data refinement recipes, revealing sharp performance drops in complex settings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CDR-Bench: Evaluating Faithful Execution of Compositional, Order-Sensitive Data Refinement Recipes
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced CDR-Bench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on their ability to execute compositional, order-sensitive data refinement tasks. The benchmark includes 3,462 tasks across four real-world domains and 29 operators, assessing models in atomic, order-agnostic, and order-sensitive scenarios with deterministic reference outputs for precise evaluation. Testing over ten state-of-the-art LLMs revealed significant performance declines in complex, compositional settings, especially when task order mattered, indicating current models struggle with procedural accuracy in data refinement.

CDR-Bench addresses a gap in existing evaluations by focusing specifically on multi-step data refinement recipes where both the composition and sequence of operations impact the final result. Unlike prior benchmarks that separate text editing from code or tool execution, this benchmark provides a comprehensive and exact framework to measure LLMs' faithful execution of these tasks. The findings highlight consistent failure patterns, emphasizing the need for improved model capabilities in handling procedural and order-dependent data processing.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31435v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data refinement involves executing multi-step recipes over evolving text states, where both composition and execution order of processing operators determine the outcome. While existing benchmarks either isolate text editing or entangle it with code and tool execution, it remains unclear whether LLMs can directly and faithfully execute these compositional, order-sensitive data refinement recipes. To fill this gap, we introduce CDR-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark featuring 3,462 high-quality tasks spanning four real-world data refinement domains and 29 distinct operators. Our benchmark evaluates models across atomic, order-agnostic, and order-sensitive settings, leveraging deterministic reference outputs to enable exact evaluation. Experiments on 10+ state-of-the-art LLMs reveal consistent failure patterns: performance degrades sharply in compositional settings, and order-sensitive recipe success collapses. These findings underline that current LLMs lack the procedural faithfulness required for reliable compositional data refinement.

items.title: Researchers propose a prediction-error surprise signal to gate plasticity and support metacognition in episodic memory and vision-language models, demonstrating improved retention and concept recognition [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Surprise as a Signal for Plasticity and Metacognition
items.summary: Researchers have proposed a prediction-error surprise signal that functions as both a gate for neural plasticity and a basis for metacognition in artificial intelligence systems. This approach was tested in two settings: an episodic memory system that selectively writes new concepts when surprise is high and consolidates them through offline replay, and a vision-language model that uses the surprise signal to modulate its responses based on familiarity with concepts. The episodic memory system demonstrated improved retention and few-shot learning performance on ImageNet classes, while the vision-language model effectively distinguished known from novel concepts and learned new concepts from single user interactions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a single idea across two settings: that a prediction-error signal, computed by a small predictor over the latent space of a frozen encoder, can serve both as a gate on plasticity and as a substrate for metacognition. In the first system, a non-parametric episodic memory writes a new concept only when this surprise is high, and a periodic offline replay phase consolidates recent traces into a slow linear readout. On a continual stream of 1000 ImageNet classes with a frozen DINOv2 or I-JEPA backbone, the consolidation phase recovers 17.7 points of retention on the oldest classes for DINOv2 and 51.3 points for I-JEPA (single-seed runs), and an ablation shows that replaying only a recent window is worse than no replay at all. In few-shot evaluation the same memory reaches 91.6% on 5-way 1-shot mini-ImageNet, above a task-specific baseline, while a harder 500-way regime exposes the true difficulty. In the second system, the same surprise signal, computed in a shared text-image space, modulates the behaviour of a vision-language model: it answers assertively when a concept is known, hedges when it is partially familiar, and refuses to identify the object and asks for an explanation when it is novel, learning the concept from a single user utterance. The external detector separates known from novel concepts at an AUROC of 0.966 (95% CI +/-0.024), far above the model's own verbalised confidence (0.618), while its token-level confidence sits below chance under greedy decoding; after a sleep phase that empties the fast store, the system recalls 99.2% of fifty taught facts from the consolidated store while a base model recovers none. We report both systems as proof-of-concept, with explicit limitations, and position the second against recent episodic-memory and personalised-VLM work.

items.title: Cohere and LG CNS develop LuckyStar 111B, a 111B-parameter multilingual reasoning model for Korean-English enterprise agents with efficient tool use and memory-constrained deployment [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Think in English, Answer in Korean: Efficient Adaptation of Multilingual Tool-Using Agents
items.summary:
Cohere and LG CNS have developed LuckyStar 111B, a 111-billion-parameter hybrid reasoning model designed for Korean-English enterprise agents that operate under practical memory and serving constraints. The model builds on Cohere's post-trained Command A model and employs preamble conditioning to alternate between concise non-reasoning and extended tool-oriented reasoning modes. It incorporates multilingual supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, language-consistency rewards for Korean responses, and 4-bit quantization to enable efficient single-GPU deployment.

The adapted model enhances mathematical reasoning, function calling, and natural-language-to-SQL (NL2SQL) capabilities while maintaining strong instruction-following performance in both Korean and English. This work offers a practical approach and analysis for adapting post-trained multilingual models to verifiable agentic workflows within memory-limited environments, supporting more effective enterprise applications.

items.title: Researchers introduce Modality-Agnostic Refusal Steering (MARS) to improve multimodal large language model safety using textual refusal directions without multimodal safety data [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Harnessing Textual Refusal Directions for Multimodal Safety
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Modality-Agnostic Refusal Steering (MARS), a novel approach to enhance safety in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) without relying on multimodal safety data. MARS leverages textual refusal directions extracted from the language model backbone, which generalize across different modalities such as images and videos. The approach operates by re-centering activations, selecting optimal intervention layers, and applying steering at the first generated token, enabling consistent safety improvements while maintaining model utility. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31876v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: To improve safety in Large Language Models (LLMs) we can either perform post-training alignment or exploit refusal directions in the activation space. In this work, we relax this constraint and investigate whether textual refusal directions, extracted directly from the LLM backbone, generalize across modalities (i.e., image, video). These results reveal that safety-relevant structure is shared across modalities and that textual refusal directions are a powerful and underexplored foundation for multimodal alignment.
