items.title: Researchers find self-generated question-answer training for language models is fragile due to biased question selection and instruction compliance, propose fixes reducing bias and injection compliance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Self-Study Reconsidered: The Hidden Fragility of Learning from Self-Generated QA
items.summary:
Researchers have identified fragility in the process of training language models using self-generated question-answer (QA) pairs. They found that the question generation step is biased, focusing on certain salient parts of a document and influenced by local presentation, which can lead to artifacts like poorly cleaned markup dominating the training data. Additionally, models tend to comply with instruction-like passages embedded in the text when generating answers, especially under conflicting tasks, with larger models showing higher compliance.

The study reveals that these issues stem from the implicit policies in QA generation rather than the training loop itself. By linking each question to a fixed target and filtering out instruction-like spans before answering, the researchers significantly reduced bias and instruction compliance, lowering mean injection compliance from 88% to 13% while preserving most of the clean text. These findings suggest practical methods to improve the robustness of self-supervised training for language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.32002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models are increasingly taught from synthetic question--answer (QA) supervision: a model generates questions about a document, answers them from the same text, and the resulting pairs are used to fine-tune, distill, or compress knowledge into another model. We show that this generation step is not neutral preprocessing. It is an implicit policy that both selects which evidence becomes training signal and decides how that evidence is answered, and it is fragile at both stages. When choosing what to ask, generators do not scan a document uniformly. Coverage saturates early and concentrates on salient spans, diverse prompts converge on the same regions, and what looks question-worthy is driven by local presentation. As a result, salient artifacts such as poorly cleaned markup can hijack question generation across model families and scales. When answering, the model that produces the supervision tends to obey instruction-like passages embedded in the text. This compliance depends on the intent and surface form of the passage rather than its strictness, and is worst under task conflict, where larger models comply more often. These failure modes arise from choices made during QA generation, so they can be reduced without changing the training loop. Tying each question to a fixed target reduces biased selection, and filtering instruction-like spans before answering lowers mean injection compliance from $88\%$ to $13\%$ in our evaluation while retaining nearly all clean text.

items.title: Researchers present PolicyGuard, a neuro-symbolic framework converting organizational policies into executable compliance review engines using LLMs and symbolic evaluation for NDA contract analysis [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PolicyGuard: From Organizational Policies to Neuro-SymbolicCompliance Review Engines
items.summary:
Researchers have developed PolicyGuard, a neuro-symbolic framework that transforms organizational policies into executable compliance review engines. This system uses large language models (LLMs) to interpret documents and answer specific extraction questions, while a symbolic evaluator applies formal logic rules to assess compliance. PolicyGuard was tested on company-specific non-disclosure agreement (NDA) reviews, ensuring contract clauses adhere to internal negotiation policies.

By separating policy formalization, document interpretation, and compliance evaluation, PolicyGuard enhances transparency, maintainability, and testability in policy-grounded document reviews. This approach addresses limitations of end-to-end prompting with LLMs, where policy logic remains implicit and difficult to inspect or update.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.32004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Policy-grounded document review requires determining whether a target document complies with organization-specific policies, guidelines, or playbooks. While large language models can assist with policy interpretation and document analysis, end-to-end prompting leaves the applied policy logic implicit, making compliance decisions difficult to inspect, update, and test. We present PolicyGuard, a neuro-symbolic framework for policy-grounded document compliance review. PolicyGuard converts organizational policy guidance into an executable review engine consisting of typed relational logic rules and atom-level extraction questions. During review, LLMs answer these local questions using retrieved document evidence, and a symbolic evaluator applies the formal rules to detect non-compliance. We instantiate and evaluate PolicyGuard on company-specific NDA compliance review, where contract clauses must be checked against organization-specific negotiation policies. By separating policy formalization, local document interpretation, and symbolic compliance evaluation, PolicyGuard makes document review more explicit, maintainable, and systematically testable.

items.title: Researchers propose ASR-agnostic multimodal spectrotemporal model using Mel spectrograms for early dementia detection, achieving up to 93.7% accuracy on Slovak and Spanish datasets with cross-lingual validation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ASR-Agnostic Multimodal Spectrotemporal Modeling for Early Dementia Detection
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an ASR-agnostic multimodal model that uses Mel spectrograms to detect early signs of dementia, achieving up to 93.7% accuracy on Slovak and Spanish datasets. The model captures shifting spectral energy patterns as digital biomarkers of cognitive decline and integrates these with acoustic embeddings through a cross-attention mechanism and Transformer encoder. This approach avoids reliance on transcription and preserves temporal structure, addressing limitations of previous speech-based dementia detection systems.

The team trained independent models on English, Slovak, and Spanish corpora, finding that the Slovak model performed best, while the English baseline showed lower accuracy due to known recording artifacts. Cross-lingual studies revealed that the effectiveness of multimodal fusion depends on the dataset, being crucial when signals are distributed across modalities but less beneficial or even counterproductive when one modality dominates or no signal exists. The model's auxiliary temporal losses converged to language-invariant values, indicating architectural stability across languages.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30646v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Speech recruits the same executive, attentional, and working memory processes underlying instrumental activities of daily living, or IADLs, providing a non-invasive proxy for cognitive assessment. Yet most speech-based dementia detection systems depend on transcription, discard within-recording temporal structure, and are validated on a single English corpus with known recording artifacts. We propose an ASR-agnostic framework operating directly on Mel spectrograms. Our key contribution is extracting spectrotemporal displacement fields from consecutive spectrogram frames, capturing shifting spectral energy patterns as digital biomarkers of cognitive decline. These features are fused with CNN-ConvGRU acoustic embeddings via a learned cross-attention mechanism and aggregated using a Transformer encoder with learnable query pooling. A composite temporal loss enforces smoothness and contrastive coherence across segments. We train independent models on English DementiaBank, Slovak EWA-DB, and Spanish Ivanova corpora, using clinical elicitation protocols taxing IADL-relevant cognitive domains. The Slovak model achieves 83.9% accuracy, and Spanish achieves, while the English baseline yields 53.2%, confirming known artifacts. Cross-lingual ablation studies reveal distinct fusion regimes: removing cross-attention collapses Spanish performance to 53.7%, below unimodal models, while the Slovak audio encoder alone outperforms the full model, 93.7% vs. 83.9%, and all English configurations remain near chance. Thus, multimodal fusion's value is corpus-dependent: essential when signal is distributed across modalities, counterproductive when one dominates, and irrelevant when no signal exists. Auxiliary temporal losses converge to language-invariant values, indicating cross-lingual architectural stability.

items.title: Researchers present a physician-guided interactive machine learning framework for delirium detection using 3,862 hospital admissions, showing improved accuracy and temporal robustness [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Can Physician Expertise Improve Machine Learning Identification of Delirium?
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a physician-guided interactive machine learning framework to improve the detection of delirium in hospitalized patients. Using data from 3,862 admissions across six Toronto hospitals, the framework integrates clinical and administrative information with physician input to refine features and enhance model interpretability. This approach demonstrated better accuracy and temporal robustness compared to automated methods, highlighting clinically relevant signals through explainable AI techniques.

The study utilized the General Medicine Inpatient Initiative (GEMINI) dataset, incorporating variables such as laboratory results, medications, and radiology-derived text indicators. Physicians actively participated in feature selection and model evaluation, with Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) used to clarify feature contributions. The framework was tested using temporally separated holdout and validation cohorts, confirming its effectiveness over baseline classifiers.

These findings support the use of a human-in-the-loop machine learning approach as a practical tool for delirium detection in clinical settings, potentially aiding in earlier identification and improved patient care.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30651v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Delirium is common in hospitalized patients and is often missed in routine care. We present a user-centered interactive machine learning (UC-iML) framework for delirium detection support that combines physician-guided feature refinement with interpretable modeling. Using 3,862 labeled admissions from six Toronto hospitals in the General Medicine Inpatient Initiative (GEMINI), we integrate administrative variables, laboratory results, medications, and a radiology-derived text indicator. Physicians guide feature refinement and model evaluation, and Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) are used to summarize feature attribution. We evaluate standard supervised classifiers with temporally separated holdout testing and a later-phase validation cohort. Compared with automated and baseline variants, the proposed framework shows better overall discrimination and stronger temporal robustness, while the explanations highlight clinically meaningful signals. These results support UC-iML as a practical human-in-the-loop framework for clinically relevant delirium modeling.

items.title: Researchers propose a causal inference framework to estimate coupon timing effectiveness using natural randomized control trials, validated on onboarding and retention campaigns
items.originalTitle: Estimating the Effect of Timing on Coupon Effectiveness
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a causal inference framework to evaluate the impact of coupon timing on user engagement without the need for dedicated A/B testing. By leveraging "natural randomized control trials," the framework measures how delivering coupons at critical moments in the customer journey affects their effectiveness. The approach was validated through a user onboarding coupon campaign within the researchers' company and further tested on a publicly available dataset related to user retention.

This method addresses the challenge of implementing real-time event-triggered coupon distribution, which can be costly, by providing a data-driven way to assess timing effects using existing data. The framework's successful application in different campaign contexts demonstrates its potential for guiding marketing decisions and improving coupon strategies across various stages of the customer lifecycle.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30664v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The coupon incentive is one of the most common tools marketers use to court users to engage with a business at various stages of the customer life cycle. A variety of factors can affect the effectiveness of a coupon incentive on users, timing being one of them. We hypothesize that coupons can be more effective when delivered at critical times in the customer journey, right when a user is engaging with the platform. Verifying such a hypothesis would typically require real time event-triggered coupon distribution software that may be too expensive to implement. In this paper, we propose a framework in which we apply causal inference on "natural randomized control trial experiments" to measure the effectiveness of sending coupons at the right time to users without requiring a dedicated AB test. We demonstrate the usefulness of our framework in the case of a user onboarding coupon campaign held in our company and show how the results can lead to correct data-driven decisions for the business. Furthermore, in order to test the generalizability of our framework, and to make our research more reproducible, we apply our framework on a user retention campaign with a publicly available dataset.

items.title: Researchers show minimal LLM agent collectives spontaneously develop cooperative behaviors and evolving cultural artifacts using shared decaying text stores and simple tools [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Emergent Culture in Minimal LLM Systems
items.summary:
Researchers studied collectives of three large language model (LLM) agents operating with minimal context, prompting, and simple tools, allowing them to communicate and manipulate a shared, actively decaying text store. This setup introduced evolutionary pressure, leading the agents to spontaneously develop cooperative behaviors, storage management strategies, and complex evolving cultural artifacts without any top-down design. Analysis using dynamical systems tools revealed that these behaviors exhibited structured long-range coherence beyond the entropy limits of the decaying store, aligning with the concept of emergent culture as defined by Sperber.

The study draws inspiration from swarm engineering and demonstrates that even minimal LLM systems can generate sophisticated collective dynamics through simple interactions and shared resources. The findings suggest that such emergent cultural phenomena arise naturally from the agents' interactions with the decaying text environment, highlighting new possibilities for understanding and designing multi-agent AI systems.

items.title: Researchers propose a multimodal framework combining ASR embeddings and LLM-augmented linguistic features for early dementia detection, achieving over 89% F1-scores on ADReSS datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Listening Between the Lines: Joint Learning of ASR Embeddings and LLM-Augmented Linguistics for Dementia Detection
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a multimodal framework that combines acoustic speech representations and linguistic features enhanced by a large language model (LLM) to detect early signs of dementia. Using Whisper for automatic speech recognition, the system extracts both acoustic embeddings and transcripts, which are then analyzed through temporal networks and LLM prompts to capture diverse linguistic markers. This approach achieved F1-scores exceeding 89% on the ADReSS datasets, demonstrating effective integration of acoustic and linguistic data for dementia screening.

The framework employs attention pooling to convert variable-length acoustic sequences into fixed-dimensional embeddings, while the LLM extracts interpretable linguistic features such as lexical diversity, syntactic complexity, semantic coherence, and discourse patterns. A gated fusion network combines these modalities, and ablation studies confirm that the multimodal fusion outperforms using either acoustic or linguistic features alone, highlighting the benefit of integrating both types of biomarkers for improved detection accuracy.

items.title: Researchers propose a deep reinforcement learning method for locker-based truck-drone routing integrating pickups, deliveries, and no-fly zones to minimize operational costs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Locker-based Truck-Drone Routing with Integrated Considerations of Pickups, Deliveries, and No-Fly Zones
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a deep reinforcement learning approach to optimize locker-based truck-drone delivery systems, addressing the complex coordination of pickups, deliveries, drone battery constraints, and no-fly zones. Their method models the routing problem as a Markov Decision Process and employs a two-stage neural heuristic to minimize operational costs for fleets of drone-equipped trucks.

The first stage solves the truck-only routing problem using an attention-based encoder and a Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit decoder, while the second stage integrates a policy-transfer strategy with a hybrid dispatch heuristic to coordinate truck and drone routes effectively. Experiments demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing metaheuristic and neural heuristic methods across various scales, offering a scalable and efficient solution under practical delivery constraints.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30680v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Truck-drone delivery is an emerging last-mile logistics mode combining the long-haul capacity of trucks with the flexible service capability of drones. In locker-based operations, smart lockers serve not only as temporary parcel storage facilities but also as automated drone docking and service nodes. These automated nodes support drone takeoff, landing, parcel handover, and battery replacement, thereby significantly extending the service range and operational flexibility of drone-assisted delivery networks. However, practical locker-based delivery systems face complex real-world challenges, requiring the integrated coordination of not only parcel delivery, return pickup, battery-constrained and load-dependent drone flights, but also necessary detours around restricted airspace. To address this practical and multifaceted challenge, this paper introduces a locker-based truck-drone routing problem with integrated considerations of pickups, deliveries, and no-fly zones (LTDRP-PDNF), with the objective of minimizing the total operational cost of a fleet of drone-equipped trucks. We formulate the route construction process as a Markov Decision Process and develop a two-stage deep reinforcement learning-based neural heuristic. The first stage utilizes an attention-based encoder and a Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit decoder to solve the truck-only routing problem, formulated as a capacitated vehicle routing problem. The second stage combines a policy-transfer strategy with a hybrid dispatch assignment heuristic to construct fully coordinated truck and drone routes for LTDRP-PDNF. Experiments on instances of different scales demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms metaheuristic and neural heuristic baselines in most cases while maintaining exceptionally short computation times, offering an effective, scalable solution framework under practical operational constraints.

items.title: Researchers define a coherence-based training law for noisy U(1)-equivariant quantum neural networks, linking sector coherence to gradient trainability under decoherence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Coherence Law for Trainability in Noisy Equivariant Quantum Neural Networks
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a coherence-based training law that explains how gradients in U(1)-equivariant quantum neural networks remain trainable despite the presence of noise and decoherence. By analyzing brickwork circuits that conserve charge, they identified two key factors influencing gradient trainability: causality, which confines the gradient to a specific sector, and coherence, which governs the rate of gradient decay through off-diagonal sector modes observable by the readout. This work establishes a light-cone reduction and defines a coherence rate that predicts gradient behavior under noise.

The team validated their theoretical findings through density-matrix simulations, showing that gradient degradation under noise follows a predictable pattern based on noise depth and coherence contraction. Notably, their training law accurately predicted no gradient loss in a correlated-dephasing noise channel, outperforming standard diagnostic methods. This study highlights readout-visible sector coherence as the critical quantity linking equivariant quantum architectures, open-system dynamics, and the ability to train quantum neural networks in noisy environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30688v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Symmetry provides a quantum neural network structure, but on its own it does not keep the network trainable once noise is present. We ask which physical quantity decides whether the gradients of an equivariant circuit survive decoherence, and we answer with a compact training law. Working with U(1)-equivariant brickwork circuits that conserve a charge, we find that two distinct effects govern a trainable gradient. Causality fixes where the gradient can live, confining it to the backward light cone of the readout inside the active charge sector. Coherence then determines how fast it decays through the contraction of the off-diagonal sector modes that the projected readout can actually observe. We prove a light-cone reduction that pins the noiseless gradient to the sector-restricted cone with a lower bound independent of the total qubit number, and we define a readout-visible aligned coherence rate as a Rayleigh quotient of the noise generator along the gradient-carrying mode. A perturbative open-system analysis turns this rate into a leading-order training law. Density-matrix simulations then confirm that the finite-noise degradation follows a single accumulated variable built from noise depth and coherence contraction, with a coefficient of determination of 0.979. The sharpest test comes from a correlated-dephasing channel that has a large worst-case rate but a near-zero aligned rate. The law predicts no gradient loss for this channel, and none is seen. Sector coherence outperforms every standard channel diagnostic we compare it against, and the analysis identifies readout-visible sector coherence as the quantity that links equivariant architecture, open-system dynamics and noisy trainability.

items.title: Researchers present BEST-RQ-2, a two-step contextualize-then-predict approach for self-supervised audio representations that improves transfer performance on X-ARES benchmarks while maintaining inference efficiency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: BEST-RQ-2: Contextualize-Then-Predict, a Two-Step Approach for Self-Supervised Audio Representations
items.summary:
Researchers have developed BEST-RQ-2, an advanced self-supervised learning method for audio representation that improves transfer performance across various audio domains while maintaining efficient inference. This approach introduces a two-step process where a Vision Transformer (ViT) context encoder analyzes unmasked spectrogram regions, and a lightweight predictor estimates targets for masked regions, which is then discarded after pretraining. BEST-RQ-2 outperforms previous one-stage models on the X-ARES and XARES-LLM benchmarks, particularly enhancing performance in music and environmental sound recognition with minimal impact on speech tasks.

The method builds on the original BEST-RQ by retaining frozen random-projection-based discrete targets and replacing the Conformer encoder with a ViT, which shifts performance across domains. The key innovation lies in separating contextualization and prediction stages during masked audio modeling, leading to better overall transfer capabilities without increasing computational costs during inference. The researchers have made the code and model checkpoints publicly available to support further development in the field.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30700v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Self-supervised learning enables audio representations that transfer across domains and tasks. We present BEST-RQ-2, an evolution of BEST-RQ that retains frozen randomprojection-based discrete targets while introducing a two-step contextualize-then-predict pretraining scheme. A ViT context encoder processes only the unmasked spectrogram regions, and a lightweight predictor infers targets for the masked regions; the predictor is discarded after pretraining. Replacing the original Conformer encoder with a ViT shifts performance across domains, slightly reducing speech performance while improving music and environmental sounds, with comparable average scores. The main improvement comes from decomposing masked prediction into separate contextualization and prediction stages. On the X-ARES and XARES-LLM benchmarks, BEST-RQ-2 consistently outperforms one-stage baselines in overall transfer while keeping inference compute unchanged. Code and model checkpoints are publicly available.

items.title: Researchers introduce NHANES Accelerometry Cardiometabolic Benchmark using 1,381 adults' data to predict cardiometabolic risk biomarkers with uncertainty quantification and subgroup fairness analysis [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Accelerometry-Derived Digital Biomarkers for Cardiometabolic Risk: A Population-Representative Tabular Benchmark with Uncertainty Quantification
items.summary:
Researchers have developed the NHANES Accelerometry Cardiometabolic Benchmark using data from 1,381 adults collected between 2003 and 2006, including hip-worn accelerometry, fasting laboratory biomarkers, dietary intake, and anthropometric measurements. They evaluated three machine learning methods—ridge regression, XGBoost, and TabPFN v2—to predict cardiometabolic risk biomarkers such as glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c), fasting triglycerides, and C-reactive protein (CRP). TabPFN v2 showed the best overall predictive performance, particularly for HbA1c and CRP, while triglycerides remained difficult to predict, aligning with known genetic influences.

The study applied split conformal prediction to generate 90% prediction intervals and assessed fairness across demographic subgroups defined by sex and race/ethnicity. While overall coverage met the target for HbA1c and CRP, some subgroups, such as Mexican American participants for HbA1c, experienced undercoverage, highlighting challenges in achieving equitable clinical predictions. The benchmark and associated code are publicly available for further research and validation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30702v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Structured tabular data dominates clinical medicine, yet existing benchmarks fail to reflect real-world properties like complex survey sampling, demographic oversampling, and subgroup fairness. We introduce the NHANES Accelerometry Cardiometabolic Benchmark, derived from NHANES 2003-2006, comprising 1,381 adults with hip-worn accelerometry, fasting laboratory biomarkers, dietary intake, and anthropometrics. We evaluate three tabular learning methods -- ridge regression, XGBoost, and the foundation model TabPFN v2 -- to predict glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c), fasting triglycerides, and C-reactive protein (CRP) from activity phenotypes and lifestyle covariates. TabPFN v2 achieves the best overall performance (HbA1c R^2=0.156, CRP R^2=0.383), while triglycerides remain largely unpredictable (R^2 < 0.05), consistent with known genetic dominance. We apply split conformal prediction to generate distribution-free 90% prediction intervals and evaluate demographic coverage equity across sex and race/ethnicity subgroups. Marginal coverage aligns with the 90% target for CRP and HbA1c but falls below for triglycerides. At the subgroup level, we observe localized undercoverage (e.g., HbA1c for Mexican American participants), illustrating the gap between marginal guarantees and the conditional coverage required for clinical fairness. Code and data are at https://github.com/felizzi/nhanes-accel-cardiometabolic-benchmark.

items.title: Researchers identify geometric cause for failure of few-step deterministic generation on continuous text latents versus success on image latents, linking decoder sharpness to token flipping and proposing accuracy-depth-stiffness tradeoffs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Why Do Few-Step Text Latents Fail When Image Latents Work? Non-Commitment at Sharp Categorical Readouts
items.summary:
Researchers have identified a geometric reason why deterministic few-step generation works well on continuous image latents but fails on continuous text latents, leading to incoherent text output. They found that the failure is due to the inability of a smooth deterministic map to resolve discrete branch choices before a sharp categorical readout, making decoder sharpness the key factor rather than transport accuracy. Their analysis includes proofs showing how token flipping occurs near decision boundaries and introduces diagnostics that reveal continuous-text decoders amplify boundary perturbations significantly more than image decoders.

The study also explores mechanisms that can overcome these limitations, such as categorical commitment in autoregressive decoders and stochastic re-injection methods. Additionally, the researchers present theoretical results on the relationship between latent dimension, mode separation, and the required deterministic stiffness, outlining an accuracy-depth-stiffness tradeoff inherent in deterministic continuous models. These findings clarify fundamental constraints in text latent generation and suggest directions for improving model design beyond deterministic continuous approaches.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30705v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deterministic few-step generation succeeds on continuous image latents but collapses to incoherent text on continuous text latents, and we show the cause is geometric rather than a training or scaling deficiency: a smooth, regularity-limited deterministic map cannot resolve a discrete branch choice before a sharp categorical readout, so few-step failure is governed by decoder sharpness, not transport accuracy. In the overlapping regime of real text autoencoders, we prove (Theorem 3) that the posterior-mean terminal step flips tokens at the rate of the latent mass in an $O(s(t))$ tube around decision boundaries. Two diagnostics, DABI (readout sharpness) and CCI (categorical commitment), measured on published checkpoints show that four independently built continuous-text decoders amplify a boundary-aligned perturbation far beyond a norm-matched isotropic one (DABI from $5\times10^{2}$ to $>10^{5}$), while image decoders have DABI $\approx 1$. Two mechanisms escape the continuous bound: categorical commitment (autoregressive decoders succeed despite sharper readouts) and stochastic re-injection (deterministic ODE at $K=4$ gives PPL 294 versus SDE 50 on the same model). In the idealized separated regime we prove matching sharp transport laws, including a dimension phase diagram: the deterministic stiffness needed to separate $M$ modes grows as $\Theta(\sqrt{\log M})$ once the latent dimension is $\Omega(\log M)$ (and as $M^{1/n}$ in fixed dimension), with a depth-$B$ hierarchy giving a $\sqrt{B}$-smaller per-step peak (Theorems 5-7); a coarea identity links these to the overlapping tube (Theorem 17). The result is an accuracy-depth-stiffness tradeoff: within the deterministic-continuous class the cost is irreducible, and both escapes step outside it.

items.title: Researchers introduce Hierarchical Global Attention as a drop-in replacement for dense causal attention in pretrained long-context transformers, enabling 64K-token context on single RTX 5090 without retraining [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA)
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA), a method that replaces dense causal attention in pretrained long-context transformers without requiring retraining or changes to existing model parameters. Implemented on the Qwen3-30B model running on a single RTX 5090 GPU, HGA enables processing of up to 64,000 tokens by using a two-level hierarchical routing system that efficiently retrieves relevant token chunks and performs exact attention on a reduced subset. This approach significantly lowers GPU memory usage by storing most token data in host RAM or NVMe storage and transferring only a small working set to the GPU during attention.

HGA's hierarchical retrieval first selects relevant chunks using compact summaries aware of positional encoding, then refines this selection before applying token-level attention. This method maintains attention accuracy within 0.01 to 0.02 nats of dense attention across context lengths from 4,000 to 64,000 tokens, while using only about 3% of tokens in the routed attention. The results indicate that the minor approximation introduced by hierarchical routing has minimal impact on performance, with remaining quality differences likely due to positional encoding limitations rather than the routing technique itself.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30709v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hierarchical Global Attention (HGA) is a drop-in replacement for dense causal attention in pretrained long-context transformers. HGA preserves the original checkpoint parameters: the pretrained $W_Q$, $W_K$, $W_V$, and $W_O$ projections remain unchanged, no calibration parameters are introduced, and no retraining is required. Applied to Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507-FP8 on a single RTX~5090 (32GB), the patched model runs out of the box at a 64K-token context, where token-level K/V storage is not feasible on this hardware. Unlike previous sparse-attention methods, HGA performs hierarchical two-level routing. It first retrieves relevant chunks using compact RoPE-aware summaries and then refines the selection by routing only the most relevant groups before performing exact token-level attention. This hierarchical retrieval significantly reduces the number of fetched tokens while preserving exact attention over the retrieved token set, making RAM- and NVMe-backed storage practical. The full historical token K/V resides in host RAM or NVMe storage, while only a small routed working set is transferred to GPU memory during attention. Consequently, GPU memory consumption depends primarily on model weights and the routed working set rather than on the total context length. Across all tested context lengths (4K - 64K tokens), routed attention remains within approximately $0.01$--$0.02$ nats of dense attention while the sparsity used is just about 3%. These results suggest that the approximation introduced by hierarchical routing is small, and that the remaining quality gap is likely dominated by long-context positional encoding rather than by the routing algorithm itself.

items.title: Researchers deploy automated pipeline to optimize enterprise AI skill descriptions, matching manual accuracy with 32x less engineering effort and identifying limits of text-level fixes [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: A Single Rewrite Suffices: Empirical Lessons from Production Skill Description Optimization
items.summary: Researchers have developed an automated pipeline to optimize natural language skill descriptions used by enterprise AI agents to route user queries. This system addresses the problem of skill collision, where overlapping descriptions cause misrouting, by producing optimized descriptions that match the accuracy of manually tuned ones while reducing engineering effort by 32 times. The pipeline was tested on a production group chat agent with nine skills, achieving an average F1 score of 79.2%, comparable to the 79.4% from manual tuning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30775v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enterprise AI agents route user queries to specialized skills by matching queries against natural language skill descriptions. When two skills share overlapping descriptions, the routing LLM misroutes queries, a failure we term skill collision. As agents scale to dozens of skills, manually tuning descriptions to maintain routing accuracy becomes a significant engineering bottleneck. We deploy an automated description optimization pipeline on a production enterprise group chat agent (9 skills, 372 regression cases). The pipeline produces descriptions averaging 79.2% F1, matching manually tuned descriptions at 79.4% F1 (average per-skill difference -0.20%, within the 0.78% multi-seed noise floor), while reducing per-skill engineering effort from 120 minutes to 3.8 minutes (32 times speedup). We then examine which pipeline components actually drive this match. Systematic ablation on both the production system and ToolBench (16k tools) reveals that a single LLM rewrite using any available false-positive and false-negative cases captures most of the available improvement. Other design choices we tested (iteration budget, feedback signal composition, dual editing of confused pairs, and training set size) each affect final F1 by less than 0.5%. Description optimization addresses skill collisions caused by overlapping descriptions but cannot resolve cases where two skills intended scopes genuinely overlap. We identify a diagnostic (a large train-validation F1 gap) that flags the latter cases for architectural rather than text-level intervention.

items.title: Researchers introduce Indi-RomCoM benchmark to evaluate large language models on Romanized Indic-English code-mixed instructions across seven tasks and four languages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Indi-RomCoM: Code-Mixed Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Romanized Indic-English Instructions
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Indi-RomCoM, a new benchmark designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on Romanized Indic-English code-mixed instructions. This benchmark covers seven instruction-following tasks across four widely spoken Indic languages and includes varying levels of code-mixing intensity. The study reveals that LLMs generally underperform on these code-mixed instructions, with performance declining as the density of code-mixing increases.

The evaluation involved a range of LLMs, including proprietary, open-weight, and Indic-focused models, tested under zero- and few-shot settings. Notably, reasoning tasks showed less performance degradation compared to detection tasks like toxicity identification, likely because generated explanations provide additional context. Indi-RomCoM aims to support the development of more inclusive multilingual AI systems capable of handling the prevalent Romanized code-mixing communication style in multilingual communities.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30790v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Romanized Code Mixing (RCM), where bilingual speakers fluidly blend local languages with English in Roman script, has emerged as the dominant form of communication across multilingual communities. While Large Language Models (LLMs) perform strongly on monolingual and native-script benchmarks, their ability to follow instructions and reason over RCM-based content remains largely unexplored. To this end, we introduce the Indi-RomCoM benchmark for facilitating systematic evaluation on Indic Romanized Code-Mixed instructions. Our benchmark spans seven instruction-following tasks, four widely spoken Indic languages, and three controlled code-mixing intensity levels. We extensively evaluate a suite of LLMs covering proprietary, open-weight, and Indic-focused models under zero- and few-shot settings. LLMs consistently underperform on RCM instructions, with performance degrading as code-mixing density increases. Furthermore, reasoning tasks suffer less degradation than detection tasks (e.g., Toxicity) because the generated explanations offer necessary context. We believe Indi-RomCoM helps the community in developing inclusive multilingual systems.

items.title: Researchers introduce Gradient Smoothing, a depth-wise gradient augmentation method that improves optimization and generalization across diverse neural network architectures and training regimes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Gradient Smoothing: Coupling Layer-wise Updates for Improved Optimization
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Gradient Smoothing, a novel depth-wise gradient augmentation technique designed to enhance optimization and generalization in deep neural networks with repeated architectural blocks like transformers. This method transforms layer-wise optimizer updates along the depth dimension, improving training performance without altering model architectures or objectives. Gradient Smoothing is compatible with various base optimizers and incurs minimal computational overhead.

The approach was tested across diverse architectures and training scenarios, including language model pretraining, reinforcement learning post-training for large language models, diffusion modeling, and image classification with Vision Transformers. Results show consistent improvements in both optimization and generalization, alongside promoting more structured representation evolution across network depth, supporting its role as a structured depth-wise preconditioning method. This establishes Depth-wise Gradient Augmentation as a promising framework for leveraging cross-depth structure in neural network optimization.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep neural networks with repeated architectural blocks, such as transformers, often exhibit structured relationships across layers that emerge during training. Motivated by this observation, we introduce \emph{Depth-wise Gradient Augmentation}, a general optimization paradigm in which the update applied to each layer is obtained by transforming the collection of block-wise optimizer updates along the depth dimension. Within this framework, we study \emph{Gradient Smoothing}, a family of depth-wise smoothing methods, and instantiate it with a simple local \emph{Window Smoothing} operator. The resulting method operates directly on block-wise updates produced by arbitrary base optimizers (e.g., SGD, Adam, Muon), incurs minimal computational overhead, and is compatible with existing optimization pipelines. We evaluate Gradient Smoothing across a diverse set of architectures and training regimes, including language model pretraining, RL post-training of LLMs for reasoning, diffusion modeling, and image classification with Vision Transformers. Across these settings, Gradient Smoothing consistently improves optimization and generalization performance without modifying model architectures or training objectives. items.title: Researchers evaluate GPT-2 models trained on 'impossible' language variants, finding gradual grammatical sensitivity decline but significant generative failures linked to non-attestation in human languages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When transformers learn "impossible" languages, what do they learn?
items.summary:
Researchers investigated how GPT-2 style transformer models perform when trained on "impossible" variants of English—languages considered unlearnable by humans. They assessed two hypotheses: whether these models struggle due to reduced grammatical sensitivity or difficulties in generating language. The study found that while grammatical sensitivity declined gradually depending on the language's structure, the models showed significant failures in producing high-quality, longer sentences.

The experiments used BLiMP minimal pairs to measure grammaticality sensitivity and revealed that the models' generative capabilities deteriorated more sharply than their grammatical understanding. These findings suggest that the inability to generate coherent language may explain why such "impossible" languages do not appear in human linguistic systems, linking model behavior to linguistic non-attestation through generative deficiencies and transmission failures.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30815v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work suggests that transformer language models show a bias towards human languages over unnatural ("impossible") languages argued to be unacquirable by humans. However, this literature has largely based these claims on differences in sample efficiency and test-set perplexity, rather than on direct evaluations of the linguistic capacities that could plausibly explain non-attestation in human languages. We evaluate two theoretically motivated linking hypotheses: impossibility arising from deficiencies in grammatical sensitivity or generative production. Using GPT-2 style models trained on perturbed "impossible" variants of English, we measure sensitivity to grammaticality using BLiMP minimal pairs, finding that model performance exhibits only gradual degradation, mediated by the language's information locality. In contrast, these models exhibited pronounced failures in generation, producing substantially fewer high-quality sentences at longer lengths. Together, these results suggest generative deficiency and transmission failures as a plausible linking hypothesis between language model behaviour and non-attestation of impossible languages.

items.title: Researchers develop stationary-distribution theory modeling Random Forest ensemble size tuning as a birth-death Markov chain with stochastic plateau behavior [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Stationary-Distribution Theory for Triplet-Based Plateau Search in Random Forest Ensemble-Size Selection
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a stationary-distribution theory to model the tuning of ensemble size in Random Forest algorithms using a birth-death Markov chain framework. This approach addresses the plateau-based tuning method, which adjusts the number of trees by comparing out-of-bag scores at geometric triplets of tree counts. Instead of converging to a fixed value, the ensemble size fluctuates around a stationary regime, which the new theory characterizes mathematically.

The study models the central ensemble size as a birth-death Markov chain on a geometric grid and derives its stationary distribution through local balance equations. Using approximations such as the folded-normal and Gaussian models, the researchers describe the equilibrium behavior, variance, and spread of the ensemble size during tuning. Their findings reinterpret plateau-based Random Forest tuning as a stochastic process rather than a deterministic stopping rule, providing deeper insight into the dynamics of ensemble size selection.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The number of trees is a central computational parameter in Random Forests: increasing it reduces finite-ensemble variability but increases training and prediction cost. Plateau-based tuning adapts this parameter through local comparisons of out-of-bag scores at a geometric triplet of tree counts. After the remaining hyperparameters have stabilized, however, the central triplet point need not converge to a deterministic value; instead, it fluctuates around a stationary regime. This paper develops a stationary-distribution theory for this process. The central ensemble size $B_t$ is modeled as a birth-death Markov chain on a geometric grid, and its stationary distribution is derived through local balance. Under a leading centered folded-normal approximation, equilibrium equations are obtained for the original update rule and a symmetric modified variant, implying that the stationary center $B_*=O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$. The stationary spread is also characterized. A local Gaussian approximation and a Fokker-Planck interpretation give grid-level variance constants. After conversion to the ensemble-size scale, $\sigma_{B,*}=O(\varepsilon^{-2})$, while the variance is $O(\varepsilon^{-4})$. The leading relative spread is independent of $\varepsilon$ and controlled by the scale factor and update rule. These results interpret plateau-based Random Forest tuning as a stochastic process rather than a deterministic stopping rule.

items.title: Researchers introduce GradeSQL framework using Outcome Reward Models for test-time verification in Text-to-SQL, improving accuracy by up to 4.33% on BIRD and 2.10% on Spider benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Test-Time Verification for Text-to-SQL via Outcome Reward Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed GradeSQL, a new framework that uses Outcome Reward Models (ORMs) for test-time verification in Text-to-SQL tasks, enhancing the accuracy of large language models during inference. By training task-specific ORMs through automated candidate generation and execution-based labeling, GradeSQL enables effective verification without manual annotation. This approach outperforms traditional heuristic methods like Best-of-N sampling and Majority Voting, achieving accuracy improvements of up to 4.33% on the BIRD benchmark and 2.10% on the Spider benchmark.

The study evaluated GradeSQL across multiple open-source large language model families and demonstrated that ORM-based selection scales well with larger candidate sets and yields stronger gains on complex queries. These results suggest that ORM-based verification offers a simple, scalable, and more semantically informed alternative to existing test-time selection strategies for structured query generation in Text-to-SQL. The researchers have made their code, datasets, and models publicly available to support further development in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Improving the reliability of large language models (LLMs) at inference time is a central challenge in structured reasoning tasks such as Text-to-SQL. Common test-time inference strategies, including Best-of-N sampling and Majority Voting, rely on heuristic signals such as execution success or output frequency, which provide limited semantic discrimination across candidate outputs. In this work, we study Outcome Reward Models (ORMs) as learned semantic scoring functions for test-time verification in Text-to-SQL. While ORMs have been previously explored for test-time scaling and alignment, their application to structured query generation remains underexplored. We introduce GradeSQL, a scalable framework for training task-specific ORMs via automated candidate generation and execution-based labeling, enabling verifier training without manual annotation. We integrate ORMs into a verification-driven Best-of-N pipeline and evaluate our approach on the BIRD and Spider benchmarks across multiple open-source LLM families. ORM-based selection consistently outperforms execution-based Best-of-N and Majority Voting, with gains of up to +4.33% on BIRD and +2.10% on Spider. We further show that ORMs scale effectively with larger candidate sets and yield stronger improvements on complex queries. Overall, our results demonstrate that ORM-based verification provides a simple, effective, and scalable alternative to heuristic test-time selection strategies for Text-to-SQL. Code datasets and models are publicly available.

items.title: Researchers introduce Turing Test Network for zero-shot pseudo-label pruning, improving label accuracy and enabling task transfer across vision-language models with up to 44% F1-score gains [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: The Label Imitation Game: Turing Test Network for Zero-Shot Pseudo-Label Pruning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed the Turing-inspired Label Imitation Game (LIG) and its associated Turing Test Network (TTN) to improve the accuracy of zero-shot pseudo-labeling in vision-language models. This approach treats pseudo-label pruning as an adversarial process, using a task-agnostic network to evaluate labels within a dataset-wide context rather than relying on fixed thresholds. Experiments on four diverse datasets show that the TTN consistently enhances label accuracy across three state-of-the-art models without requiring additional supervision or retraining.

The TTN leverages learned semantic-contextual logic as an alternative to traditional spatial-geometric verification, enabling zero-shot task transfer where a model trained on image classification can effectively prune pseudo-labels for object detection. This method yields significant F1-score improvements, with gains of up to 44% after task-specific fine-tuning. Additionally, the TTN helps recover performance on classes that previously had zero recall by refining the training signal, a phenomenon termed Category Revival. The pre-trained TTN models and code have been made publicly available for further research and application.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30875v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Foundation model pseudo-labeling - labeling data strictly via zero-shot inference - enables massive scale, but performance is undermined by hallucinations that evade standard thresholds. To eliminate these errors, we introduce the Turing-inspired Label Imitation Game (LIG), a framework that formalizes pseudo-label pruning as an adversarial interrogation. Rather than filtering labels via isolated thresholds, we use the LIG to train a Turing Test Network (TTN), a task-agnostic "judge" that evaluates candidate pseudo-labels within a dataset-wide context. Experiments across four diverse datasets demonstrate the TTN's robustness, consistently enhancing label accuracy for three state-of-the-art vision-language models without costly supervision or retraining. Crucially, we demonstrate that learned semantic-contextual logic is a robust alternative to spatial-geometric verification, enabling a unique zero-shot task transfer capability - a TTN trained strictly on image classification datasets can effectively prune complex object detection pseudo-labels. This pruning yields F1-score gains of 28% for the worst-performing baseline categories and 44% with task-specific fine-tuning. Significantly, we also observe Category Revival, where the TTN pruning "detoxifies" the training signal for downstream models and enables them to recover from zero recall on transfer-vulnerable classes. The pre-trained TTN models and code are available at https://github.com/voxel51/ttn.

items.title: Researchers introduce TheraJudge and TheraAgent, multi-agent systems using human-aligned evaluation to improve therapeutic quality of mental health language models with strong clinician agreement [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Training Therapeutic Judges and Multi-Agent Systems for Human-Aligned Mental Health Support
items.summary:
Researchers have developed TheraJudge and TheraAgent, a two-stage multi-agent system designed to enhance the therapeutic quality of mental health language models by using human-aligned evaluation as an active control mechanism. TheraJudge is an open-source evaluator trained on human-annotated data to reliably assess responses across seven psychological dimensions, achieving strong agreement with clinician ratings. TheraAgent uses these evaluations to iteratively refine responses through specialized roles, resulting in significant improvements in therapeutic quality and safety.

TheraJudge demonstrated high intraclass correlation coefficients (0.87-0.95) with clinician assessments, outperforming existing supervised and closed-source evaluators, especially on critical factors like safety, relevance, and empathy. When applied, TheraAgent improved human-rated therapeutic quality by 0.43 points on a 5-point scale and effectively corrected low-quality responses, with a 94% recovery rate for unsafe outputs. The study highlights that aligning mental health language models effectively requires acting on human-aligned evaluations rather than solely enhancing generation capabilities. The researchers have made their code publicly available for further development and validation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30887v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models show promise for mental health support, yet therapeutic quality improves only when evaluation functions as an actionable control signal rather than a passive metric. We introduce a framework that formulates therapeutic response generation as a decision-refinement problem driven by multi-dimensional, human-aligned evaluation. In Stage I, we introduce TheraJudge, an open-source therapeutic evaluator trained via preference-based optimization on human-annotated data to produce reliable judgments across 7 psychological dimensions. In Stage II, we introduce TheraAgent, which operationalizes TheraJudge's evaluations through a coordinated refinement process with specialized Critic, Coach, and Therapist roles that translate evaluative signals into targeted response revisions. Empirically, TheraJudge achieves strong agreement with clinician ratings, with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC = 0.87-0.95), surpassing supervised baselines and strong closed-source judges, particularly on critical dimensions such as Safety, Relevance, and Empathy. Acting on these evaluations, TheraAgent yields a +0.43 improvement in human-rated therapeutic quality (on a 5-point scale) under blind evaluation, with 96\% clinician inter-rater reliability. Low-quality responses ($\leq 3$) improve by +2.45 points with a 94\% recovery rate, demonstrating targeted correction of unsafe outputs. items.title: Researchers prove on-policy distillation outperforms offline behavior cloning for imitation learning with noisy expert feedback, providing theoretical foundations and new algorithms [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Behavior Cloning is Not All You Need: The Optimality of On-Policy Distillation for Noisy Expert Feedback
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that on-policy distillation (OPD) outperforms offline behavior cloning in imitation learning scenarios where expert feedback is noisy. They introduced a noisy expert model to explain why online methods like OPD, which interact with the expert during learning, achieve better performance than offline methods such as supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Their findings reveal that offline learning from noisy expert trajectories requires exponentially more samples to match the performance of a clean expert, whereas OPD can achieve this with polynomial sample complexity relative to the task horizon.

The study provides theoretical foundations and new algorithms supporting these results, including conditions on the noise distribution that enable horizon-free sample complexity. The authors also extend their analysis to cases with unknown corruption when the clean expert is deterministic, offering insights into why OPD is more effective for training language models from imperfect teachers. This work bridges theoretical understanding and practical algorithm design for imitation learning under noisy expert conditions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30923v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Imitation Learning is a natural framework for learning in sequential decision-making systems and has emerged as the dominant paradigm through which we understand language model training. A central puzzle is that, while in theory offline IL can be horizon-free and optimal, in practice online methods such as on-policy distillation often outperform offline methods such as supervised fine-tuning. We propose a noisy expert model to explain this gap, in which the learner only has access to a noisy version of the expert's policy, but wishes to compete against the reward achieved by a clean expert, motivated by the fact that in many applications, e.g. training language models to perform long chains of thought, the expert is often imperfect. In this setting, we show a sharp separation between offline and online IL. Offline learning from noisy trajectories is fundamentally hard: to compete with the clean expert, the sample complexity must grow exponentially, in contradistinction to the clean expert setting where no explicit horizon dependence exists. In contrast, we prove that online interaction with the noisy expert via a novel variant of OPD enables polynomial dependence on the horizon in general. We further show that, under a natural condition on the expert noise distribution, which we show to be necessary for any horizon-free sample complexity, one can obtain such a guarantee, although our proposed algorithm sacrifices statistical efficiency in its dependence on the size of the policy class. Our analysis leads to an alternative loss function that is commonly considered empirically for LM training. We further provide algorithms and lower bounds, and extend our results to the more realistic setting of unknown corruption when the clean expert is deterministic, thereby providing a theoretical foundation for why OPD can outperform SFT when training language models from imperfect teachers.

items.title: Researchers develop physics-informed conditional normalizing flows for angles-only cislunar orbit determination using Near Rectilinear Halo Orbit data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Physics-informed Conditional Normalizing Flows for Angles-only Cislunar Orbit Determination
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a physics-informed approach using conditional normalizing flows to improve orbit determination in the cislunar environment. This method estimates the probability distribution of an object's initial state based on angles-only measurements collected over short observation periods, specifically focusing on Near Rectilinear Halo Orbits. By training on perturbed topocentric observations, the model can represent complex, multimodal posterior distributions and generate physics-consistent state hypotheses from new data.

The generated state estimates are further refined through nonlinear least-squares minimization, enhancing their accuracy and providing effective initial guesses for traditional orbit determination algorithms. This approach advances generative astrodynamics by combining machine learning techniques with physical modeling to address challenges in space navigation around the Moon.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative Astrodynamics is advanced in this work by extending generative modelling to an orbit determination problem in the cislunar environment. The task is formulated as conditional density estimation, aiming to infer the probability distribution of the initial state from angles-only measurements over short observation arcs. A normalising flow is trained on perturbed topocentric observations from Near Rectilinear Halo Orbits, enabling a flexible and potentially multimodal posterior representation. Given new measurements, the learned density is sampled to generate statistically consistent and physics-informed state hypotheses. These estimates are refined via nonlinear least-squares minimisation, providing a competitive warm start for classical algorithms.

items.title: Researchers propose a generative framework using compressed latent spaces for motion planning, demonstrating strong performance on nuPlan and Waymo Open Motion Dataset without task-specific training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Motion Planning in Compressed Representation Spaces
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new generative framework for motion planning that combines deep learning and model-based planning techniques. Their approach uses an autoencoder to compress motion data into a latent space of discrete tokens, enabling efficient search and optimization of motion plans directly within this compressed representation. This method allows for flexible objective functions at test time and produces realistic motion behaviors without requiring task-specific training.

The framework was tested on the nuPlan and Waymo Open Motion Dataset, demonstrating strong performance in closed-loop motion planning and multi-agent scenario synthesis. By leveraging the hierarchical structure of the latent space, the approach effectively balances the flexibility and efficiency of model-based planning with the data-driven capabilities of deep learning, offering a unified solution for complex robotic motion tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30940v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep learning methods have vastly expanded the capabilities of motion planning in robotics applications, as learning priors from large-scale data has been shown to be essential in capturing the highly complex behavior required for solving tasks such as manipulation or navigation for autonomous vehicles. At the same time, model-based planning algorithms based on search or optimization remain an essential tool due to their flexibility, efficiency, and the ability to incorporate domain knowledge via expert-designed algorithms and objective functions. We propose a new generative framework to unify these two paradigms. First, we learn an autoencoder with a high compression ratio and a latent space of hierarchically ordered, discrete-valued tokens. Leveraging both the dimensionality reduction and the hierarchical coarse-to-fine structure learned by this autoencoder, we then perform motion planning by directly searching in the latent space of tokens. This search can optimize arbitrary objective functions specified at test time, providing a large degree of flexibility while maintaining efficiency and producing realistic solutions by relying on the generative capabilities of the highly compressed autoencoder. We evaluate our method on nuPlan and the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, showing how latent space search can be used for a variety of guided behavior generation tasks, achieving strong performance for closed-loop motion planning and multi-agent guided scenario synthesis without requiring any task-specific training.

items.title: Researchers introduce Prost-RL, a reinforcement learning framework for micro-ultrasound prostate cancer detection achieving 79% AUROC on 6,607 biopsy cores across five clinical sites [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning Where to Look: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for Robust Micro-Ultrasound Prostate Cancer Detection
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Prost-RL, a reinforcement learning framework designed to improve prostate cancer detection using micro-ultrasound imaging. Prost-RL addresses challenges in training deep models due to sparse and noisy supervision by learning where to focus attention before decoding images. Tested on 6,607 biopsy cores from 693 patients across five clinical sites, the system achieved a 79% area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) for core-level detection, outperforming existing methods.

Prost-RL integrates a lightweight reinforcement-learning policy with an encoder-decoder model to generate interpretable spatial attention maps that guide cancer likelihood predictions and image classification. The approach includes Adaptive Policy Optimization to stabilize training and a noise-robust objective to handle weak-label noise and improve localization. The model's learned policy highlights biopsy-aligned regions, providing transparent, spatially grounded evidence alongside quantitative risk assessments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30951v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Micro-ultrasound ($\mu$US) is a new, emerging, and promising imaging modality for prostate cancer (PCa) detection, but accurate identification of suspicious tissue remains highly dependent on clinical experience, leading to substantial inter-observer variability. Machine-learning assistance can reduce this variability; however, training reliable deep models is challenging because supervision is sparse and noisy -- typically limited to core-level histopathology outcomes (e.g., cancer grade and its percentage in a biopsy core) without pixel-level lesion annotations and under severe class imbalance. We introduce Prost-RL, which reframes $\mu$US PCa detection as a spatially aware, policy-driven inference problem by learning where to look before decoding. Prost-RL integrates a lightweight reinforcement-learning policy into a foundation-model encoder-decoder to generate interpretable spatial attention maps that act as soft prompts for both cancer-likelihood heatmap prediction and image-level classification. We further propose Adaptive Policy Optimization (APO) to stabilize hybrid supervised-RL training and a noise-robust objective combining symmetric cross-entropy with negative-entropy regularization to mitigate weak-label noise and encourage sharp localization. On a cohort of 6,607 biopsy cores from 693 patients across five clinical sites, Prost-RL achieves $79.0\pm3.5$ AUROC with $64.6\pm6.3$% sensitivity at 80% specificity for core-level detection (+2.1 AUROC and +4.5 sensitivity points over the strongest baseline), and $79.3\pm5.8$ AUROC for clinically significant cancer classification. The learned policy highlights biopsy-aligned regions, providing transparent, spatially grounded evidence alongside quantitative risk predictions. Code is available at: https://github.com/DeepRCL/Prost-RL.

items.title: Researchers identify deductive stereotyping as a fairness failure in large language models and propose Fair-GCG to reduce bias and improve fairness in reasoning and generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Wait, am I Being Fair? Characterizing Deductive Stereotyping and Mitigating It with Fair-GCG
items.summary:
Researchers have identified a fairness issue in large language models (LLMs) called deductive stereotyping, where models apply broad population-level patterns to individual cases, resulting in logically consistent but socially biased conclusions. To address this, they propose a reasoning-time injection framework and introduce Fair-GCG, a method to discover effective phrases that guide models toward fairness-aware reasoning. 

Fair-GCG's injection phrases have been shown to improve performance on multiple fairness benchmarks, generalize across different model sizes, enhance fairness in reasoning, reduce bias in open-ended text generation, and transfer effectively to real-world tasks sensitive to fairness concerns.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.30989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Warning: This paper contains several toxic and offensive statements. While reasoning generally improves fairness in recent large language models (LLMs), failures persist. In this work, we identify a failure mode, deductive stereotyping, in which models apply population-level statistical regularities to individual cases, producing logically coherent yet socially biased inferences. We provide a statistical interpretation of this phenomenon. To steer models toward fairness-aware reasoning, we propose a reasoning-time injection framework. We further introduce Fair-GCG to systematically discover effective injection phrases. Injection phrases discovered by Fair-GCG improve performance across multiple fairness benchmarks, generalize from smaller to larger LLMs, improves reasoning-level fairness, reduces bias in open-ended generation, and transfer to real-world fairness-sensitive tasks.

items.title: Researchers propose OTCache, an Optimal Transport-based framework for geometry-aware caching in diffusion models achieving up to 4.7x acceleration and improved generation fidelity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OTCache: Optimal Transport for Geometry-Aware Caching in Diffusion Models
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced OTCache, a training-free framework designed to accelerate diffusion model sampling by predicting caching schedules using an Optimal Transport-based approach. OTCache addresses limitations in existing graph-based caching methods, which assume additive independence and struggle in low inference step regimes. items.title: Researchers distill knowledge from DeepSeek-R1 to Qwen2.5-7B using Chain-of-Thought training on John O'Bryan Mathematics Competition problems, improving student model accuracy by 4.76 points [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Knowledge Distillation from Large Reasoning Models to Compact Student Models: A Case Study on the John O Bryan Mathematics Competition
items.summary:
Researchers have successfully distilled knowledge from a large reasoning model, DeepSeek-R1, into a smaller student model, Qwen2.5-7B, using Chain-of-Thought training on problems from the John O'Bryan Mathematics Competition. This approach improved the student model's accuracy by 4.76 percentage points, raising it from 64.67% to 69.43% on the competition dataset, and also enhanced its performance on the MATH-500 benchmark to 73.1%. The study highlights the effectiveness of knowledge distillation and fine-tuning techniques in enhancing compact models for mathematical reasoning tasks.

The team created a training corpus from historical competition problems spanning 2011 to 2025 using a dual-agent framework and fine-tuned the student model with Low-Rank Adaptation on Apple Silicon hardware. Initial training runs showed overfitting after 200 iterations, leading to multiple shorter training runs to ensure stability. Additionally, the research examined how response length affects answer quality across six reasoning levels, finding that longer responses generally yield higher accuracy, with significant declines observed as response length decreases.

These findings demonstrate that Chain-of-Thought distillation can effectively improve the reasoning capabilities of smaller models, and that maintaining sufficient response length is critical for preserving answer quality in mathematical problem-solving. This work offers insights into optimizing compact AI models for complex reasoning tasks while managing computational resources.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates knowledge distillation from a large reasoning model (DeepSeek-R1) to a compact student model (Qwen2.5-7B). Using historical problems from the John O'Bryan Mathematics Competition at Northern Kentucky University (2011-2025), we build a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) training corpus through a dual-agent framework. The dataset is used to fine-tune the student model with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on Apple Silicon hardware using the MLX framework. The base Qwen2.5-7B model achieves 64.67% accuracy on competition problems, while the DeepSeek-R1 teacher achieves 91.40%. An initial 1,000-iteration training run revealed severe overfitting, with validation loss reaching a minimum at iteration 200 before rising steadily. Based on this finding, we ran five independent training runs each limited to 200 iterations with varied random seeds to assess result stability. Across these five runs, the fine-tuned student model achieves a mean accuracy of 69.43% (std dev 0.17%) on the competition dataset, a 4.76 percentage-point improvement over the base model, and generalizes to 73.1% (std dev 0.18%) on the MATH-500 benchmark. We further study how response length affects answer quality across six reasoning levels (R1-R6): accuracy declines consistently from 69.43% at R1 (mean 220 words) to 41.9% at R6 (mean 31.2 words), with the two-person speed section most sensitive to token reduction. These results demonstrate that CoT distillation improves compact student models and that response length is a critical factor in mathematical reasoning quality.

items.title: Researchers propose ADAPT framework to reduce hallucinations in multimodal large language models by aligning text-to-image cross-attention dynamics, achieving 40%-60% reduction across benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ADAPT: Attention Dynamics Alignment with Preference Tuning for Faithful MLLMs
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced ADAPT, a novel framework designed to reduce hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by directly addressing the degradation of text-to-image cross-attention during content generation. ADAPT employs three key strategies: a visual anchor for stable spatial grounding, an attention-supervised inference mechanism to detect and correct attention drift, and a Visual Attention Guidance method to align model preferences with visually grounded responses. This approach has demonstrated a 40% to 60% reduction in hallucination rates across multiple benchmarks while maintaining the models' general multimodal capabilities.

The study identifies progressive degradation of cross-attention as a core internal signature of hallucination, which leads to unfocused or biased attention patterns. Unlike previous outcome-driven methods, ADAPT intervenes at the attention dynamics level, providing a more targeted solution. Experiments confirm that each component of the framework contributes to improved fidelity in image-text alignment, marking a significant advancement in mitigating hallucinations in MLLMs.

By focusing on the internal behaviors of text-to-image cross-attention, this work offers a new perspective on enhancing the reliability of multimodal models. The researchers have made their code publicly available, facilitating further exploration and development in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31054v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are critically hampered by hallucination, generating content inconsistent with the provided image. In this paper, we identify an internal signature of hallucination: progressive degradation of text-to-image cross-attention during generation, leading to specific failure patterns like unfocused or biased attention. Existing mitigation strategies are largely outcome-driven and do not explicitly target this failure mode. To address this problem, we propose ADAPT (Attention Dynamics Alignment with Preference Tuning), an attention-based framework that intervenes directly on text-to-image cross-attention dynamics. We propose ADAPT with three key contributions: a cross-attention visual anchor refined from early decoding to provide stable spatial grounding, an attention-supervised inference mechanism that detects and corrects attention drift online, and a Visual Attention Guidance DPO that aligns preferences toward visually grounded responses. Experiments show that each component of ADAPT contributes to hallucination reduction, and the full framework achieves new best results across multiple hallucination benchmarks, reducing hallucination rates by 40%-60% across mainstream backbones while preserving general multimodal capabilities. Our work provides an attention-based perspective on mitigating hallucinations by exploring the model's internal text-to-image cross-attention behaviors. Code is available at https://github.com/yao-ustc/ADAPT
