items.title: Researchers propose Triospect, a three-dimensional statistical framework for robust AI-generated text detection, improving detection rates against 17 attacks across 12 domains and 17 source models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Triospect: A Three-Dimensional Framework for Robust Statistical AI-Generated Text Detection Against Diverse Attacks
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Triospect, a three-dimensional statistical framework designed to improve the detection of AI-generated text, particularly against various manipulation attacks. By analyzing content, core ideas, and stylistic elements, Triospect enhances robustness across 17 different attacks, 12 domains, and 17 source models, significantly outperforming existing detection baselines.

Testing on two benchmarks, including the Humanize-16K and adversarial RAID datasets, showed that Triospect increased detection accuracy by up to 22.3% in AUROC and 22% in true positive rate at a low false positive rate. This approach represents a novel statistical method to strengthen AI-generated text detection reliability, and the researchers have made their data and code publicly available for further study and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31074v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing AI-generated text detectors are vulnerable to attacks that manipulate textual characteristics. In this study, we propose a novel Triospect Detection Framework by using additional perspectives of content (core ideas) and expression (stylistic elements) within a given text. Experiments on two benchmarks involving 17 attacks, 12 domains, and 17 source models demonstrate that Triospect is robust against these attacks. It improves the strong baseline by a significant margin of 22.3% (AUROC) and 13% (TPR01) on the Humanize-16K after-attack subset, and by 9.1% (AUROC) and 22% (TPR01) on the adversarial RAID. This framework marks a pioneering effort in statistical methods to enhance detection reliability against attacks. We release our data and code at https://github.com/baoguangsheng/triospect.

items.title: Researchers propose Training-Free Gated Reranking to reduce computational costs by up to 80% and improve few-shot learning performance by up to 2% across 8 LLMs and multiple datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Reranking Hurts: Uncertainty-Based Gating for Few-Shot Reranking
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Training-Free Gated Reranking, a method that selectively applies reranking to few-shot learning examples based on model uncertainty. This approach challenges the common assumption that reranking always enhances performance, showing that it can sometimes degrade results. Experiments involving eight large language models across multiple natural language understanding and machine translation datasets demonstrated that this method reduces computational costs by 15% to 80% while improving average performance by up to 2%.

The study highlights that higher computational expense does not necessarily lead to better outcomes and that reranking is most effective when focused on instances where the model exhibits high uncertainty. This targeted strategy offers a more efficient and potentially more accurate approach to few-shot learning tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Few-shot selection typically assumes that reranking retrieved examples always improves performance. We challenge this view by identifying that the expensive reranking step can in fact degrade performance. Instead, we propose \emph{Training-Free Gated Reranking}, which decides whether to rerank the few-shot examples based on the model's uncertainty. Extensive experiments across 8 LLMs, covering 7 NLU datasets and 9 MT domain-language combinations, demonstrate that our approach reduces computational costs by 15\%-80\% while improving average performance by up to 2\%. These findings indicate that higher computational cost does not guarantee better performance, and that reranking is most beneficial when targeted at high-uncertainty instances.

items.title: Researchers probe autonomous driving policies to link internal prediction errors with ego vehicle planning, revealing limitations in near-collision predictions and improvements from correcting mistakes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What Probing Reveals about Autonomous Driving: Linking Internal Prediction Errors to Ego Planning
items.summary:
Researchers have investigated autonomous driving policies to understand how internal prediction errors affect the planning of the ego vehicle. Their study reveals that while driving policies perform well in typical scenarios, they often fail to predict the movements of surrounding vehicles accurately during near-collision events, which limits the effectiveness of the vehicle's planning. By probing these policies through imitation learning and reinforcement learning models, the researchers identified when predictive and planning capabilities emerge or fail.

The study used large datasets and simulation training to assess whether improvements in driving policies stem from better prediction and planning or simply from more effective heuristics. Targeted interventions demonstrated that correcting prediction mistakes leads to safer trajectory planning for the ego vehicle. This work highlights the importance of accurate prediction in autonomous driving and suggests that enhancing these internal signals can improve overall safety.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31106v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large-scale datasets and fast simulators have enabled improvements in driving policies that appear safe and robust, yet strong performance in nominal scenarios can still mask flawed reasoning and unsafe heuristics. Summary scores from closed-loop simulators do not give significant insight into the policy, making it difficult to determine whether they truly predict the motion of surrounding vehicles, how the ego vehicle generates future plans, or whether they merely rely on brittle heuristics that happen to succeed in nominal scenarios. To better understand the limits and weaknesses of driving policies, we focus on probing for forms of prediction, i.e., where surrounding vehicles will move next, and planning, i.e., understanding how to generate safe trajectories. We focus on these two capabilities because they reflect behaviors expected of effective driving policies, and use their presence or absence to assess policy quality across data-driven behavior cloning and simulation-driven reinforcement learning policies. To evaluate the presence of these capabilities, we investigate them as a function of scale, asking whether the closed-loop gains from larger datasets and longer simulation training reflect stronger prediction and planning or merely better behavioral heuristics. We use linear probing and targeted perturbations in both imitation learning and reinforcement learning models to track when these internal signals emerge, plateau, or fail. Despite good closed-loop performance, policies often fail to form timely surrounding-vehicle predictions during near-collision events, revealing a limitation in the predictive signals available for ego planning. Finally, causal intervention shows that correcting mistaken predictions improves ego planning toward safer trajectories.

items.title: Researchers introduce SkillSpotter, a pose-aware multi-view model that improves skilled action detection and grading in ego-exo videos, boosting mAP by 76% and accuracy on Ego-Exo4D and HoloAssist datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SkillSpotter: Pose-Aware Multi-View Skilled Action Detection and Grading in Ego-Exo Videos
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SkillSpotter, a pose-aware multi-view model designed to improve the detection and grading of skilled actions in ego-exo video settings. This system addresses the challenge of not only identifying what actions a person performs but also assessing how well they execute them, which is crucial for applications like real-time coaching in sports, cooking, or music. SkillSpotter enhances performance by integrating adaptive temporal suppression, gated 3D body pose fusion, and bidirectional cross-view attention, resulting in a 76% increase in mean average precision and improved accuracy on the Ego-Exo4D and HoloAssist datasets compared to existing methods.

The model builds on seven state-of-the-art temporal action detection architectures, extending evaluation protocols to separate detection from grading tasks. SkillSpotter's modules also demonstrate transferability to other temporal action detection models, showing consistent gains and generalizing beyond the initial datasets. The approach leverages body kinematics alongside visual features to better capture the nuances of skilled actions, effectively combining first-person and external camera views for comprehensive analysis.

SkillSpotter improves class-specific mAP from 12.40 to 21.82 (+76%) and balanced accuracy from 55.99% to 60.40% over the best baseline. SkillSpotter's modules transfer to other temporal action detection models with consistent gains, and our method generalizes beyond Ego-Exo4D to HoloAssist. items.title: Researchers propose UniSAE, a unified speech editing framework enabling composable speaker, emotion, and content modifications from sub-phoneme to word level using discrete phonetic posteriorgram modeling [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: UniSAE: Unified Speech Attribute Editing on Speaker, Emotion and Low-Level Content via Discrete Phonetic Posteriorgram Modelling
items.summary:
Researchers have developed UniSAE, a unified speech editing framework that enables flexible modifications of speaker, emotion, and content attributes within a single system. Unlike existing methods that focus mainly on word-level content changes and treat speaker and emotion editing separately, UniSAE supports composable edits from sub-phoneme to word level by using a Discrete Phonetic PosteriorGram (DPPG) representation. This approach breaks down speech content into discrete tokens capturing phoneme identity, pronunciation variants, and duration, allowing precise and granular editing.

The framework employs an autoregressive content transformer to predict edited DPPG sequences for higher-level content changes, while a diffusion-based acoustic decoder synthesizes the final speech conditioned on disentangled speaker and emotion features. Experimental results demonstrate that UniSAE effectively controls speaker and emotion attributes, supports multi-level content editing, and enables joint modification of all three attributes, offering a versatile tool for advanced speech editing applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31128v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Speech editing aims to modify specific portions of an utterance while preserving the remaining speech. Existing approaches primarily focus on word-level content modification and typically treat content, speaker, and emotion editing as separate tasks, limiting both editing granularity and flexibility. We propose UniSAE, a unified speech attribute editing framework which supports composable speaker, emotion and content editing from sub-phoneme to word level within a single architecture. UniSAE introduces a Discrete Phonetic PosteriorGram (DPPG) representation that factorizes speech content into discrete tokens encoding phoneme identity, pronunciation variants, and duration, enabling direct phoneme- and sub-phoneme-level editing. For higher-level modifications, an autoregressive content transformer predicts edited DPPG sequences for word-level content editing. The edited sequences are rendered into speech by a diffusion-based acoustic decoder, conditioned on disentangled speaker and emotion representations. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed unified framework supports precise speaker and emotion control, content editing at multiple granularities, and joint modification of all three attributes within a single framework.

items.title: Researchers propose PruneGround, a plug-and-play spatial pruning framework for 3D visual grounding that reduces computation and improves accuracy on major point cloud benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: PruneGround: Plug-and-play Spatial Pruning for 3D Visual Grounding
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced PruneGround, a plug-and-play framework designed to improve 3D Visual Grounding (3DVG) by focusing on relevant spatial regions within 3D scenes based on natural language descriptions. This approach reduces computational costs and enhances accuracy by pruning irrelevant areas, simplifying complex expressions, and aligning point cloud data with linguistic cues using a specialized language model. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on major point cloud benchmarks, including ScanRefer and Nr3D/Sr3D datasets.

PruneGround incorporates three main components: Language-Guided Spatial Pruning (LGSP) to narrow down search areas using a frozen Vision Language Model, MultiView-Conditioned Description Reformulation (MCDR) to break down complex language into simpler spatial relations, and LLM-Grounder, which adapts a detection-pretrained spatial language model for grounding tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness across multiple challenging 3DVG settings, with code and models made publicly available for further research and application.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31148v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: 3D Visual Grounding (3DVG) aims to localize target objects in 3D scenes given natural language descriptions. Existing approaches typically perform reasoning over the entire scene, leading to ambiguous predictions and high computational cost, especially in cluttered environments. We observe that many referential expressions rely on local spatial context and often correspond to restricted spatial regions rather than the full scene. Motivated by this insight, we propose PruneGround, an effective plug-and-play framework for 3DVG built upon three key components. First, we introduce Language-Guided Spatial Pruning (LGSP), which leverages a frozen Vision Language Model (VLM) to identify language-relevant regions, thereby reducing spatial computation and grounding candidates in the narrower search space. Second, we propose MultiView-Conditioned Description Reformulation (MCDR), which decomposes complex expressions into simplified target-anchor relations and augments missing spatial cues through multi-view reasoning. Finally, we propose LLM-Grounder, which repurposes a detection-pretrained spatial LLM into a language-conditioned grounding model by aligning point cloud and linguistic representations within the pruned region. Extensive experiments on the three most popular point cloud benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results on all three ScanRefer settings and on 9 out of 10 Nr3D/Sr3D settings. Code and models are publicly available: https://github.com/leduckhai/PruneGround

items.originalTitle: PPT-Eval: A Benchmark for Computer-Use Agents on PowerPoint Tasks
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced PPT-Eval, a new benchmark consisting of 120 PowerPoint tasks designed to evaluate AI agents' ability to create and edit presentations. The benchmark covers a range of content creation and editing scenarios and includes a rubric-based evaluation framework that awards partial credit and provides detailed feedback, addressing the complexity and multimodal nature of these tasks. Despite advances, leading AI models like Claude-4.5-Opus achieve only a 45% success rate, highlighting ongoing challenges in this domain.

The evaluation framework developed for PPT-Eval incorporates task-specific rubrics that penalize unnecessary changes and poor aesthetics while rewarding intermediate progress, resulting in a strong correlation with human judgments. This nuanced approach captures partial successes better than binary metrics, reflecting the varied valid solutions possible in PowerPoint tasks. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31154v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Creating and editing slides is a rich, multimodal activity that is ubiquitous in professional and educational settings, making it an ideal testbed for real-world computer-use agents. Microsoft PowerPoint is among the most widely adopted and feature-rich environments for presentation creation. We introduce PPT-Eval, a benchmark of 120 PowerPoint tasks across 12 files that cover both content creation and presentation editing scenarios, organized by difficulty. A central challenge in this domain is evaluation: tasks are complex, multimodal, and often admit many valid solutions. Moreover, today's agents frequently make only partial progress, which binary success metrics fail to capture. To address this, we design a robust evaluation framework to help create task-specific rubrics for PowerPoint tasks, taking inspiration from and building on past works for rubric-based evaluation. These rubrics award partial credit for intermediate steps, penalize unnecessary changes and poor aesthetics, and provide natural language feedback. This nuanced approach proves highly effective, achieving a Kendall's {\tau}-b correlation of 0.77 with human judgments. We find that existing frontier agents still struggle with solving PowerPoint tasks, with strong models like Claude-4.5-Opus achieving only a 45% success rate and an average partial score of 57%. The benchmark is located at: https://microsoft.github.io/ppteval.

items.title: Researchers propose AETDICE, an offline reinforcement learning algorithm unifying nonlinear multi-objective RL optimization through the Aggregation-Expectation-Transformation framework [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AETDICE: Unified Framework and Offline Optimization for Nonlinear Multi-Objective RL
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced AETDICE, a new offline reinforcement learning algorithm designed to optimize nonlinear preferences in multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL). This approach unifies two previously separate paradigms—Scalarized Expected Return (SER) and Expected Scalarized Return (ESR)—through the Aggregation-Expectation-Transformation (AET) framework, which decomposes scalarization into three components to provide a comprehensive foundation for nonlinear MORL.

AETDICE leverages DICE-style density-ratio estimation within an augmented state space, enabling effective sample-based optimization from static datasets. This method addresses longstanding challenges in nonlinear MORL by capturing the trade-offs inherent in the AET framework, which prior techniques have been unable to resolve.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optimizing nonlinear preferences in multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) is essential for capturing complex trade-offs like risk aversion or fairness. However, such non-linearity has historically bifurcated nonlinear MORL objectives into two distinct paradigms: Scalarized Expected Return (SER) and Expected Scalarized Return (ESR). While SER requires global-level optimization and ESR requires non-Markovian policies, leading to fragmented optimization strategies, we bridge this divide through the Aggregation-Expectation-Transformation (AET) framework. By unifying both criteria through a tripartite decomposition of scalarization, AET provides a principled foundation for general nonlinear MORL. Building on this framework, we propose AETDICE, a tractable offline RL algorithm for AET objectives. By utilizing DICE-style density-ratio estimation in an augmented state space, AETDICE enables sample-based optimization from static datasets. items.title: Researchers introduce Bayesian in-context experimenters using transformers to efficiently estimate average treatment effects with adaptive allocation and smoothness adaptation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Transformers as Bayesian In-Context Experimenters: Smoothness-Adaptive Efficient ATE Estimation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Bayesian in-context experimenters using transformer models to improve the efficiency of estimating average treatment effects (ATE) in adaptive experiments. These transformers are trained to mimic a Bayesian posterior Neyman teacher, which updates beliefs about potential outcomes based on experimental history to assign treatment probabilities. This approach converges to the optimal oracle design, enhancing statistical efficiency and valid inference in ATE estimation.

The method employs attention mechanisms and projected gradient descent to replicate Bayesian updating for Gaussian-series priors. To handle unknown outcome smoothness, the researchers use a mixture-of-experts transformer that adapts by focusing on near-optimal experts based on smoothness classes. The policy can be learned through supervised pretraining and empirical risk minimization, with experiments demonstrating accurate imitation of the teacher, adaptive allocation, and improved precision compared to baseline methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adaptive experiments for average treatment effects (ATE) require randomized allocations balancing valid inference with statistical efficiency. The oracle design is a covariate-dependent Neyman rule governed by unknown arm-conditional outcome variances. We investigate whether this sequential variance-estimation and allocation process can be amortized via in-context learning. We introduce Bayesian in-context experimenters: transformer policies trained to imitate a Bayesian posterior Neyman teacher. The teacher updates nonparametric beliefs over potential outcomes using experimental history to assign posterior Neyman treatment probabilities. This design converges to the oracle rule, supporting efficient ATE inference. Transformers constructively implement this mapping through attention-based sufficient statistics and projected gradient descent, imitating Bayesian updating for Gaussian-series priors. To address unknown outcome smoothness, we combine smoothness-indexed experimenters using a mixture-of-experts transformer. The gate acts as a hierarchical posterior over smoothness classes, concentrating on near-oracle experts. By bounding the complexity of the transformer class, we prove this amortized policy can be learned via empirical risk minimization using supervised pretraining. Experiments confirm accurate teacher imitation, adaptive allocation, and improved ATE precision over baselines.

items.summary: Researchers have developed a Multi-View Gated Graph Attention Network to detect Alzheimer's Disease using spontaneous speech. The model transcribes audio with Automatic Speech Recognition to create semantic, dependency, and co-occurrence graphs, capturing speech characteristics through a "content-structure-flow" framework. It incorporates Pointwise Mutual Information from a normative corpus to assess narrative coherence and linguistic deviations, and uses an adaptive gated fusion mechanism to handle clinical heterogeneity. Tested on the ADReSSo dataset, the approach achieved 90% accuracy, with ablation studies highlighting the importance of the PMI-based graph and heterogeneity-aware gating for robust classification. The source code for this method is publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spontaneous speech is a vital non-invasive biomarker for Alzheimer's Disease (AD), yet many systems overlook non-linear structural disruptions and clinical heterogeneity in pathological language. We propose a Multi-View Gated Graph Attention Network that transcribes audio via Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) to construct semantic, dependency, and co-occurrence graphs, characterizing speech through a "content-structure-flow" framework. Notably, the co-occurrence graph leverages Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) from a normative corpus to quantify narrative logic and linguistic deviation. To address symptomatic diversity, an adaptive gated fusion mechanism dynamically integrates these views. Evaluated on the ADReSSo dataset, our model achieves 90.00% accuracy. Ablation results confirm that the PMI-based graph and heterogeneity-aware gating are essential for robust classification across diverse clinical populations. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/opeacc/AD.

items.title: Researchers introduce PSALM framework to evaluate stylistic appropriation and copyright infringement risks in large language models under EU law, revealing limitations of current safeguards [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Probing Stylistic Appropriation using Large Language Models: An Evaluation Framework for Copyright Infringement under EU Law
items.summary:
Researchers have developed PSALM, a framework designed to evaluate the risks of stylistic appropriation and copyright infringement by large language models (LLMs) under European Union law. Unlike existing safeguards that focus mainly on verbatim copying, PSALM assesses broader aspects such as writing style, narrative structure, and creative elements, aligning with the EU's standard of substantial similarity. The framework was applied to Llama 3.2 models fine-tuned on historical Dutch literature, revealing that fine-tuning leads to systematic stylistic appropriation beyond literal memorization, and that current unlearning techniques reduce but do not eliminate these patterns.

PSALM uses ten evaluators to measure computational overlap, stylistic and content dimensions, and statutory exceptions like parody and quotation. The study found that instruction-tuned models already exhibit baseline stylistic similarities before exposure to specific corpora, and that fine-tuning amplifies these effects across multiple infringement-relevant dimensions. These findings highlight a significant gap in current copyright compliance methods, which focus narrowly on literal copying and overlook broader stylistic risks.

The framework offers a foundation for legally informed, auditable compliance evaluation, though the connection between automated similarity scores and legal infringement requires further validation by experts. This work bridges the gap between qualitative legal standards and quantitative technical measures, underscoring fundamental challenges at the intersection of generative AI and EU intellectual property law.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31250v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLM) trained on web-scale corpora generate output that may infringe copyright, yet existing technical safeguards focus narrowly on verbatim memorisation. EU copyright doctrine applies a broader standards: substantial similarity, which extends to stylistic choices, narrative structure, and creative elaboration. This mismatch between what current methods detect and what the law protects leaves a significant compliance gap. We introduce PSALM, an LLM-as-a-judge framework that operationalises EU copyright doctrine through ten evaluators assessing computational overlap, stylistic dimensions (writing style, narrative voice), content dimensions (character, plot, scene, world building), and statutory exceptions (parody, pastiche, quotation, sc\`enes \`a faire). Applying PSALM to Llama~3.2 models fine-tuned on translated historical Dutch literary works, we find that: 1) instruction-tuned models exhibit non-trivial baseline stylistic similarity prior to corpus exposure; 2) fine-tuning induces systematic stylistic appropriation across all infringement-relevant dimensions, extending beyond verbatim memorisation to abstract narrative patterns; 3) Negative Preference Optimisation unlearning substantially reduces similarity but leaves detectable residual stylistic patterns. These findings indicate that safeguards targeting literal copying alone are insufficient to mitigate broader copyright risks. PSALM provides infrastructure for auditable, legally informed compliance evaluation, though the relationship between automated similarity scores and infringement determinations requires validation by legal experts. This work bridges qualitative legal standards and quantitative technical measurement, exposing fundamental tensions between generative AI and EU intellectual property law.

items.originalTitle: TDGT: A Tabular Data Generation Toolkit supporting adaptive GPU-accelerated Bayesian mixture models, diffusion-based models, and latent-space generative modeling
items.summary:
Researchers have developed TDGT (Tabular Data Generation Toolkit), a web-based platform designed to generate synthetic tabular data with high fidelity while preserving privacy. TDGT features the Adaptive Bayesian Mixture Synthesizer (ABMS), which automatically optimizes the number of mixture components without manual tuning, and a hybrid model called VAE-ABMS that combines variational autoencoders with adaptive Bayesian mixtures to capture complex data distributions. The toolkit also includes a GPU-accelerated version for large datasets and evaluates synthetic data quality using multiple statistical metrics alongside privacy risk assessments.

The toolkit supports real-time data streaming and interactive visualizations, making it accessible for users across various domains such as healthcare, socioeconomic modeling, and cybersecurity. Evaluations demonstrate that TDGT consistently produces statistically coherent synthetic data across diverse feature types and scales, addressing the growing need for privacy-preserving data sharing in AI workflows.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31268v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing demand for privacy-preserving data sharing has positioned synthetic data generation as a critical component of responsible AI workflows. Despite notable advances in generative modeling, existing solutions often lack integration of adaptive generation strategies, multi-metric evaluation, and accessible end-to-end generators within a unified web-based toolkit. In this work, we introduce TDGT (Tabular Data Generation Toolkit), a web-based toolkit for synthetic tabular data generation and fidelity assessment. TDGT introduces the Adaptive Bayesian Mixture Synthesizer (ABMS), a novel algorithm that autonomously determines the optimal number of mixture components through iterative cluster quality optimization, eliminating the need for manual hyperparameter configuration. Building upon ABMS, we further propose VAE-ABMS, a hybrid architecture that couples Variational Autoencoder-based latent space learning with adaptive Bayesian mixture synthesis, enabling high-fidelity generation of complex, nonlinear tabular distributions. For large-scale scenarios, TDGT provides a GPU-accelerated variant of ABMS leveraging CUDA-based k-means clustering and Gaussian mixture fitting. Synthetic data fidelity is assessed through eleven statistical fidelity metrics spanning distributional divergence, structural correlation, and sample-level similarity, complemented by privacy risk indicators including k-anonymity scoring and disclosure rate estimation. The web-based toolkit supports a real-time streaming interface with interactive Plotly-based visualizations. TDGT is assessed across datasets from healthcare, socioeconomic modeling, and cybersecurity domains, demonstrating consistent generation fidelity and statistical coherence across heterogeneous feature types and data scales.

items.title: Researchers develop CSO-LLM, a class subspace orthogonalization method for post-training backdoor detection and trigger inversion in large language models across multiple architectures [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: CSO-LLM: Class Subspace Orthogonalization for Post-Training Backdoor Detection and Trigger Inversion in LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers have developed CSO-LLM, a novel method called class subspace orthogonalization, to detect and invert backdoor triggers in large language models (LLMs) after training. This approach addresses challenges unique to LLMs, such as the vast discrete input space and the difficulty of blacklisting tokens associated with targeted attack responses. CSO enhances the sensitivity and specificity of backdoor detection by implicitly penalizing tokens that align with the target class of an attack, improving detection accuracy without requiring comprehensive blacklists.

The method includes two complementary techniques: one that optimizes continuously in token embedding space and another that performs greedy token selection in discrete space. Tested across multiple LLM architectures and classification tasks, CSO-LLM demonstrated strong performance in both detecting backdoors and accurately recovering the original triggers, offering a robust framework for securing LLMs against post-training backdoor attacks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31309v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While post-training backdoor detection and trigger inversion schemes have been developed for AIs used e.g. for images, there is a paucity of such methods for LLMs. First, the LLM input space is discrete, with up to 150,000^k k-tuples to consider with k the token-length of a putative trigger. Second, one must blacklist tokens typical of the putative target response (class) of an attack, as such tokens may give false detection signals. However, a comprehensive blacklist is not available, in general, for a given domain. We develop a highly effective detection and inversion framework for LLMs treated as classifiers. Central to our approach is class subspace orthogonalization (CSO), a novel plug-and-play paradigm for backdoor detection that serves two fundamental roles when applied to LLMs: i) it enhances both sensitivity and specificity of a baseline detector; ii) it provides a form of implicit blacklisting, as it penalizes against inclusion, in a candidate trigger, of tokens that induce signal perturbations "in the direction of" the putative target class of an attack. One version of our detector performs continuous optimization in token embedding space, while a companion trigger-inversion and detection method performs greedy accretion in discrete token space. Our methods give both strong detection performance and accurate inversion of ground-truth triggers on several LLM classification domains, and for several different LLM architectures.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate AI-assisted visual analytics prototyping using Artifact-Transform Workflow Language, reducing development time from months to an afternoon [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Idea to Prototype in an Afternoon: Scaffolded, AI-Assisted Rapid VA Prototyping
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that using the Artifact-Transform Workflow Language (ATWL) combined with an AI assistant can significantly accelerate the prototyping of visual analytics ideas, reducing the process from months to just an afternoon. This approach was applied to a new method involving relaxing the Pareto frontier and grouping options into recurring types, resulting in a consistent workflow within minutes and a functional prototype in a few hours.

The study highlights three key findings: the importance of the scaffold provided by ATWL, the necessity of expert knowledge to achieve high-quality results beyond the initial AI-generated prototype, and the impact of how the scaffold is used. Controlled experiments showed that providing both a language definition and example library simultaneously can hinder creativity, and that scaffolds are most effective when introduced after an initial unconstrained design phase. The researchers suggest developing a typology of human knowledge injection that is both human-editable and machine-accessible to further enhance this process.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31311v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Testing a new visual-analytics idea usually takes months: one needs to find a realistic data set, clean it, and implement an interactive prototype. We describe a case where a workflow language and an AI assistant reduced this effort to one afternoon. The idea under test: relax the Pareto frontier with a tolerance and group the surviving options into recurring types -- ``constellations'' on a ``soft sky''. Using the Artifact--Transform Workflow Language (ATWL) as a scaffold, we obtained a consistent workflow in minutes and a running prototype in a few hours. We derive three lessons. The scaffold matters: without ATWL the assistant produced a naive workflow. The scaffold alone is not enough: the first implementation was only average, and expert knowledge injection was needed to reach state-of-the-art quality. Finally, the way the scaffold is used matters: controlled experiments show that a language definition and a library of examples support different aspects of the task, that providing both at once reduces quality because template following displaces creative content, and that scaffolds work best when introduced after an initial unconstrained design pass. We argue that the field needs a typology of human knowledge injection, in a form that is both human-editable and machine-accessible.

items.title: Researchers use sparse autoencoders to resolve superposition in AI models trained on 100,000 patient-derived neuronal images, enabling interpretable latent representations and cross-modal alignment with single-cell RNA sequencing data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Resolving superposition in AI for interpretability and cross-modal alignment in patient-neuronal images
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a method using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to address the issue of superposition in neural networks trained on over 100,000 multiplexed images of patient-derived neurons from Parkinson's disease and healthy controls. This approach improves interpretability by recovering the geometric fidelity of latent representations, which are then analyzed similarly to single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data. The team introduced GW-map, a technique that aligns these image-based representations with authentic scRNA-seq data using Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport, enabling the reconstruction of neuronal pathology pathways without relying on spatial transcriptomics.

The study highlights how superposition distorts the geometry of latent spaces in AI models and demonstrates that SAEs can effectively purify these representations. By treating the purified latent vectors as single-cell state vectors, the researchers adapted scRNA-seq analytical methods to image data, facilitating cross-modal alignment. This work establishes a scalable foundation for spatial biology and offers new tools for interpreting complex biological data through AI. The associated code has been made publicly available for further research and application.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31394v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming our capability to solve biological challenges. In dimensionality bottleneck regimes exacerbated by high-dimensional biological data, Neural networks force distinct concepts into the lower dimensions known as superposition. Although this superposition is widely known to hinder interpretability, its impact on corrupting the geometry of latent spaces remains critically overlooked. Here, we utilized sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on over 100,000 multiplexed images of patient-derived Parkinson's disease and healthy neurons to resolve superposition. This approach bypasses the mathematical non-uniqueness of feature attribution by shifting to interpretable latent representation analysis. We theoretically and empirically demonstrate that superposition contaminates representational metric spaces, and thereby SAEs successfully recover geometric fidelity. By treating these geometrically purified representations as single-cell state vectors, we adapted single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data analysis methodologies directly to the image domain. Finally, we introduce GW-map, utilizing Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport to align these image representations with authentic scRNA-seq data \emph{de novo}. This coupling reconstructs hierarchical neuronal pathology pathways such as Calcium-AIS scaffold, without reference spatial transcriptomics, establishing a scalable foundation for spatial biology. Code is available at https://github.com/jijihihi/Bio_superposition

items.title: Researchers introduce Mixture-of-Control, a state-aware fine-tuning framework for transformers that enables efficient cross-block communication and outperforms existing state-based methods with comparable memory and computational efficiency [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Mixture-of-Control: State-Aware Fine-Tuning for Transformer-based Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Mixture-of-Control (MoC), a novel fine-tuning framework for transformer models that enhances cross-block communication by integrating local and global control signals. Unlike traditional state-based fine-tuning methods that update controls only within individual blocks, MoC treats block-wise control states as experts in a sparse mixture-of-experts process, enabling efficient information exchange across transformer blocks. This approach maintains comparable memory and computational efficiency while improving representational adaptation.

MoC addresses the limitations of existing state-based methods, which often restrict inter-block communication or incur significant computational overhead when enabling it. Empirical evaluations across various transformer benchmarks demonstrate that MoC outperforms current state-based fine-tuning techniques, offering a more effective and efficient solution for adapting transformer-based models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31397v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: State-based fine-tuning has emerged as a compelling alternative to weight-based adaptation for transformers, updating lightweight controls into states rather than model weights, offering substantial memory savings while retaining parameter efficiency. However, most existing state-based methods typically apply only per-block control updates, which limits inter-block information exchange and restricts representational adaptation. Meanwhile, prior mechanisms that enable cross-block communication often introduce considerable computational overhead, reducing their practicality for efficient fine-tuning. We introduce Mixture-of-Control (MoC), a lightweight fine-tuning framework that adaptively integrates local and global control signals to enhance representation learning. MoC treats block-wise control states as experts in a sparse mixture-of-experts process, enabling efficient communication across transformer blocks. Empirical results across diverse transformer-based benchmarks demonstrate that MoC outperforms state-based methods while maintaining a comparable memory and computational efficiency.

items.title: Researchers propose Visual Semantic Entropy to measure visual ambiguity in vision-language models, outperforming existing uncertainty estimation methods across five VQA benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Visual Semantic Entropy: Do Vision Language Models Recognize Visual Ambiguity?
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Visual Semantic Entropy (VSE), a new method to measure visual ambiguity in vision-language models (VLMs). Unlike previous entropy-based approaches that rely on output diversity and can underestimate uncertainty due to overconfident visual embeddings, VSE perturbs only the image input while keeping the text query fixed. This approach clusters generated answers into semantic prototypes and calculates uncertainty based on their dispersion, effectively capturing visual ambiguity.

The team evaluated VSE across five modern vision-language models and five diverse visual question answering (VQA) benchmarks. Their results show that VSE outperforms existing uncertainty estimation methods, which often reflect sensitivity to textual changes rather than true visual ambiguity. This establishes VSE as a state-of-the-art technique for assessing uncertainty in VLMs, improving the reliability of their predictions on ambiguous visual inputs.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31407v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language models can produce confident answers on visually ambiguous inputs, resulting in biased predictions. Common entropy-based methods, such as Semantic Entropy (SE), rely on output diversity. Yet our analysis shows that overconfident visual embeddings suppress output diversity under stochastic decoding, causing SE to underestimate uncertainty in such cases. Recent methods instead probe output diversity through input perturbations, including textual paraphrasing or joint text-image perturbations, and show improved performance. We study these approaches and reveals that the resulting variability is often dominated by textual changes rather than visual evidence, causing uncertainty estimates to reflect prompt sensitivity rather than visual ambiguity. We therefore propose Visual Semantic Entropy (VSE), which perturbs only the image to probe nearby visual variations while keeping the text query fixed. VSE measures uncertainty by clustering generated answers into semantic prototypes and computing the mass-weighted dispersion among them. Extensive evaluation across five modern vision-language models and five diverse VQA benchmarks demonstrates that VSE effectively captures visual ambiguity, establishing a new state-of-the-art for VLM uncertainty estimation.

items.title: Team MKC proposes an LLM-based pipeline for analyzing mental health changes through social media timeline dynamics at CLPsych 2026 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Team MKC at CLPsych 2026: Capturing and Characterizing Mental Health Changes through Social Media Timeline Dynamics
items.summary:
Team MKC has developed a pipeline using Large Language Models (LLMs) to analyze mental health changes by examining the sequence of user posts on social media. Presented at the CLPsych 2026 shared task, this approach integrates both post-level evaluation and user-level temporal modeling to provide a comprehensive assessment of psychological well-being.

This work addresses the growing need for scalable computational tools to support early detection and ongoing monitoring of mental health, especially given the increasing prevalence of mental health disorders and limited access to professional care. By leveraging domain-specific datasets, the pipeline aims to enhance holistic mental health analysis through advanced AI techniques.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31464v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have motivated their adoption across a wide range of domains, including Artificial Intelligence (AI) for mental health. Given the growing prevalence of mental health disorders worldwide and the limited accessibility of professional care, there is an increasing demand for scalable computational approaches that can assist in early detection and continuous monitoring of psychological well-being. In this area, ongoing efforts have focused on curating domain-specific datasets and leveraging them to develop LLMs capable of supporting holistic mental health analysis. In line with this direction, we propose an LLM-based pipeline for comprehensive mental health analysis over sequentially ordered user posts, as part of the CLPsych shared task. Our pipeline offers a unified framework that jointly enables post-level assessment and user-level temporal modeling.

items.title: Researchers introduce FinPersona-Bench to measure mandate salience decay in autonomous financial agents using 18 LLMs across simulated market scenarios [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: FinPersona-Bench: A Benchmark for Longitudinal Psychometric Stability of Autonomous Financial Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed FinPersona-Bench, a simulation benchmark designed to measure Mandate Salience Decay (MSD) in autonomous financial agents powered by Large Language Models (LLMs). MSD refers to the gradual loss of influence of explicit behavioral mandates, such as capital preservation or avoiding speculative bets, as market context accumulates over time. The benchmark evaluates 18 leading LLMs across simulated market scenarios that separate observable prices from hidden fundamental values, testing agents' behaviors in calm markets, crashes, and speculative bubbles.

The study assigns each LLM one of three behavioral profiles ranging from conservative to aggressive and finds that MSD increases over time and varies by model. In crash scenarios, agents receiving periodic mandate re-grounding show a behavioral gap 4.4 times larger than static agents by the simulation's end. While re-grounding improves performance for conservative agents in low-signal markets, it can worsen outcomes for aggressive agents, indicating that effective long-term deployment requires selective, mandate-aware adjustments tailored to agent profiles and market conditions.
items.description:
Researchers have developed FinPersona-Bench, a simulation benchmark designed to measure Mandate Salience Decay (MSD) in autonomous financial agents powered by Large Language Models (LLMs). MSD refers to the gradual loss of influence of explicit behavioral mandates, such as capital preservation or avoiding speculative bets, as market context accumulates over time. The benchmark evaluates 18 leading LLMs across simulated market scenarios that separate observable prices from hidden fundamental values, testing agents' behaviors in calm markets, crashes, and speculative bubbles.

The study assigns each LLM one of three behavioral profiles ranging from conservative to aggressive and finds that MSD increases over time and varies by model. In crash scenarios, agents receiving periodic mandate re-grounding show a behavioral gap 4.4 times larger than static agents by the simulation's end. While re-grounding improves performance for conservative agents in low-signal markets, it can worsen outcomes for aggressive agents, indicating that effective long-term deployment requires selective, mandate-aware adjustments tailored to agent profiles and market conditions.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31522v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous financial agents initialized with explicit behavioral mandates such as "preserve capital" or "avoid speculative bets" that are meant to govern every decision throughout deployment. In practice, however, as market context accumulates over long horizons, these mandates gradually lose their behavioral influence, a phenomenon we formalize as Mandate Salience Decay (MSD). To measure MSD objectively, we introduce FinPersona-Bench, a simulation benchmark in which a synthetic market decouples observable price from hidden fundamental value, enabling falsifiable evaluation across three failure modes: trading without signal in calm markets, panic-selling during crashes, and ignoring fundamental value during speculative bubbles. Evaluating 18 leading frontier and open-source LLMs, each assigned one of three behavioral profiles ranging from strict capital preservation to aggressive growth, shows that MSD compounds over time and is model-dependent. In crash scenarios, the behavioral gap between static agents and those receiving periodic mandate re-grounding grows 4.4x from the first to the final quarter of the simulation. The effects of mandate re-grounding are not uniformly positive: it consistently helps conservative agents in low-signal markets but actively worsens behavior for aggressive agents in the same setting. These findings suggest that reliable long-horizon deployment requires selective, mandate-aware re-grounding based on agent profile and market regime.

items.title: Researchers propose SAIL-RevKL algorithm with reverse KL divergence penalty, proving global convergence and improved performance on LLM alignment and MuJoCo benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: On the Convergence of Self-Improving Online LLM Alignment
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced SAIL-RevKL, a new algorithm that enhances the Self-Improving Alignment (SAIL) method by incorporating a reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence penalty to address optimization challenges. This modification improves the algorithm's convergence properties, with the team proving that the regularized objective satisfies the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition, ensuring global convergence with near-linear sample complexity. Empirical tests show that SAIL-RevKL outperforms the original SAIL on both large language model alignment tasks and MuJoCo benchmarks.

The original SAIL algorithm tackled distribution shifts by simplifying a bilevel problem into a single-level approach but lacked formal convergence guarantees due to the non-strongly concave nature of its objective function. By adding the reverse KL divergence penalty, SAIL-RevKL improves the optimization landscape, enabling theoretical analysis and practical stability. This advancement offers a more reliable and efficient method for online alignment in machine learning applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31524v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Self-Improving Alignment (SAIL) algorithm addresses distribution shift by reducing a bilevel formulation of the problem to an efficient, single-level method. Empirically, SAIL has demonstrated strong performance on this task. However, a formal analysis of its convergence properties has been lacking. We identify a key theoretical challenge: the standard SAIL objective function is not guaranteed to be strongly concave due to unfavorable properties of its Hessian. To address this limitation, we propose a regularized objective, SAIL-RevKL, which incorporates a reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence penalty to improve the optimization landscape. Our central theoretical contribution is to prove that this regularized objective satisfies the Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition within a bounded parameter space. We establish global convergence guarantees, achieving a near-linear sample complexity. We further validate the effectiveness and stability of SAIL-RevKL through empirical evaluations, demonstrating that it outperforms the vanilla SAIL on both MuJoCo benchmarks and LLM alignment tasks.

items.title: Researchers find high-fidelity room-acoustic simulations reduce word error rate by up to 38% in multichannel speech enhancement training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Improving multichannel speech enhancement through accurate room-acoustic simulations
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that using high-fidelity room-acoustic simulations to augment training data significantly improves multichannel speech enhancement performance. By training the SpatialNet model on datasets generated with advanced acoustic modeling techniques, including a hybrid of wave-based and geometrical acoustics simulations, they achieved up to a 38% relative reduction in median word error rate compared to models trained on lower-fidelity geometrical acoustics data.

The study involved comparing different simulation methods and evaluating the resulting models on measured speech data. The findings highlight that more physically accurate room-acoustic simulations provide better training data for deep-learning-based speech enhancement, leading to more effective noise reduction and clearer speech recognition in multichannel audio systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31552v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Room-acoustic simulations are widely used to augment training data for deep-learning-based speech enhancement. While most pipelines rely on simplified geometrical acoustics, wave-based approaches offer greater physical accuracy. In this work, we examine how simulation fidelity affects multichannel speech enhancement performance. To this end, we train SpatialNet on datasets augmented with different room-acoustic simulation methods and evaluate the resulting models on measured data. We compare lower-fidelity datasets based on geometrical acoustics with a high-fidelity dataset using advanced acoustic modelling and a hybrid combination of wave-based and geometrical acoustics simulations. Training on the high-fidelity dataset results in an up to 38 % relative reduction in median word error rate compared to the lower-fidelity alternatives. These results show that augmentation with high-fidelity room-acoustic simulations directly translates into improved multichannel speech enhancement performance.

items.title: Researchers propose Physics-aware Neural Operator Transformer for real-time temperature field reconstruction of tungsten monoblock divertor on EAST fusion device [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Temperature Field Reconstruction of Tungsten Monoblock Divertor on EAST using Physics-aware Neural Operator Transformer
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a Physics-aware Neural Operator Transformer (PNOT) to enable real-time reconstruction of the temperature field in the tungsten monoblock divertor of the EAST fusion device. This approach addresses the limitations of traditional numerical methods like the Finite Element Method, which are too computationally intensive for real-time use. PNOT models boundary heat-flux relations as a structured graph and uses graph attention mechanisms to capture spatial physical dependencies, enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of temperature field predictions.

The model incorporates a physics-aware neural operator module that aggregates query points with similar physical conditions and simulates heat diffusion, supported by a gradient-constrained Sobolev regularization loss to maintain consistency between function values and their derivatives. Experimental results demonstrate that these physics-based constraints improve prediction accuracy while preserving physical consistency. The researchers plan to release the source code to facilitate further development and application in fusion device control.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31574v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate modeling of the divertor temperature field is essential for preventing material melting and damage and for extending the service life of fusion devices. However, conventional numerical methods, such as the Finite Element Method (FEM), are computationally expensive and therefore unsuitable for real-time applications. Therefore, a fast and generalizable method is required for real-time reconstruction of the divertor temperature field and subsequent real-time control. To address the above issue, we propose a Physics-aware Neural Operator Transformer (PNOT) to characterize the spatiotemporal evolution of the divertor temperature field. It models boundary heat-flux relations as a structured graph and employs graph attention to explicitly capture spatial physical dependencies. Inspired by physics-aware attention, we further develop a physics-aware neural operator module to aggregate query points with similar physical conditions via slicing and model heat diffusion, while a gradient-constrained Sobolev regularization loss enforces consistency between function values and their derivatives. Experimental results show that these physical constraints improve prediction accuracy while preserving physical consistency. The source code of this paper will be released on https://github.com/Event-AHU/OpenFusion

items.title: Researchers find optimiser choice drives a 7x variation in emergent misalignment in LLM fine-tuning, with spectral regularisation mitigating effects of EM-prone optimisers [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Evil Spectra: How Optimisers can Amplify or Suppress Emergent Misalignment
items.summary:
Researchers have identified that the choice of optimiser significantly influences emergent misalignment (EM) in large language model (LLM) fine-tuning, causing up to a sevenfold variation in misalignment rates. EM occurs when fine-tuning on a narrowly misaligned task leads to broadly misaligned behavior on unrelated prompts. Their study across multiple Qwen3 models, optimisers, datasets, and batch sizes found that optimiser choice outweighs model size in affecting EM severity, with model scale and family having negligible impact when using the Adam optimiser.

The team analyzed training dynamics and found that different optimisers follow distinct trajectories in loss-alignment space, with the optimiser becoming a stronger predictor of alignment than training loss after extensive training. The adaptive optimiser Muon was noted for preserving alignment best by implicitly regularizing the singular value distribution of the LoRA adapter. Introducing a spectral regularisation loss term to encourage a flatter singular value spectrum substantially improved alignment for EM-prone optimisers like Adam and Lion, without compromising training loss.

These findings highlight optimiser choice as a key factor in EM severity and demonstrate that spectral regularisation can effectively mitigate the negative effects of certain adaptive optimisers, offering a promising approach to improving alignment in LLM fine-tuning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31591v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Emergent misalignment (EM) is a recently discovered phenomenon in LLMs where fine-tuning on a narrow misaligned task, such as writing insecure code, leads to broadly misaligned behaviour on unrelated prompts. Previous work has noted that the severity of EM is highly sensitive to training choices; however, we still lack a systematic characterisation of this sensitivity. We perform a sweep over several Qwen3 models, optimisers, datasets, and batch sizes, and find that the choice of optimiser has the largest effect, producing a 7x spread in misalignment rate. Surprisingly, model size has a negligible effect within the Qwen3 family. An additional sweep over 12 models from three families using Adam confirms that model scale (1B-235B) and family have negligible effects for that optimiser. Analysing the loss-alignment relationship on Qwen3-8B, we find that final log training loss is a strong predictor of alignment, and that stratifying by optimiser captures nearly all the residual variance. Training dynamics reveal that each optimiser follows a different trajectory through loss-alignment space, and that after significant training, the optimiser becomes more important than training loss as a predictor of alignment. Muon, the adaptive optimiser that preserves alignment the best, implicitly regularises for a more uniform distribution of singular values of the LoRA adapter. We evaluate this insight by training with an additional loss term that incentivises a flatter singular value spectrum, and find that this substantially recovers alignment for the more EM-prone adaptive optimisers (Adam and Lion), with negligible cost to training loss. These results identify optimiser choice as a key factor in EM severity, but show that spectral regularisation can substantially mitigate the effects of EM-prone optimisers.

items.title: Researchers propose uncertainty-guided synthetic data augmentation using diffusion models to improve semantic segmentation on Cityscapes, UAVID, and BDD100K datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Preserve the Hard, Regenerate the Rest: Uncertainty-Guided Synthetic Training Data Augmentation with Diffusion Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an uncertainty-guided synthetic data augmentation method using diffusion models to enhance semantic segmentation performance on datasets such as Cityscapes, UAVID, and BDD100K. This approach targets uncertain semantic regions identified by a baseline segmenter's predictive entropy and inpaints only the surrounding visual context, preserving label accuracy and focusing training on challenging areas without relying on external models or broad heuristics. The method yields significant improvements in mean Intersection over Union (mIoU), especially for rare and difficult classes like buses, trains, and aerial-view cars.

The technique involves fine-tuning the segmentation model using synthetic data where the loss is computed solely over the original uncertain pixels, excluding the inpainted regions. This strategy efficiently maximizes the informativeness of each synthetic sample by presenting uncertain regions in novel contexts while maintaining label validity. The researchers provide code to facilitate adoption and demonstrate that uncertainty-guided context augmentation is an effective tool for improving segmentation on complex and diverse datasets.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31603v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Semantic segmentation models struggle with data sparsity and rare or visually diverse regions, e.g., dense regions or small objects in aerial or autonomous mobility data. While synthetic augmentation is an appealing solution, directly generating new labeled data risks misalignment of labels and generated pixels. Existing solutions to this problem often rely on external models, or employ coarse heuristics such as indiscriminately augmenting all foreground objects or entire backgrounds, which wastes capacity on uninformative pixels. To address this, we propose an uncertainty-guided synthetic context augmentation strategy that strictly preserves label validity and efficiently maximizes pixel informativeness per synthetic sample - no external guardrails required. Using a baseline segmenter's predictive entropy, we identify uncertain semantic regions and inpaint only the complementary visual context. When fine-tuning the segmenter on this synthetic data, we compute the loss only over the original pixels, excluding inpainted regions. This focuses learning on the unmodified, uncertain regions while presenting them in novel contexts. We demonstrate substantial mIoU gains on Cityscapes, UAVID, and BDD100K with the largest gains on rare and difficult classes such as buses, trains, or (from the aerial perspective) cars. items.title: Researchers propose ECHO, a selective turn-memory framework for agentic reinforcement learning that improves accuracy and traceable learning by compressing and reconstructing environment turns [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ECHO: Prune to act, trace to learn with selective turn memory in agentic RL
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced ECHO, a selective turn-memory framework designed to enhance agentic reinforcement learning for long-horizon language tasks. ECHO addresses limitations in existing context-management methods by compressing each environment turn into compact memory records and reconstructing policy contexts through selective retrieval. This approach improves accuracy and enables traceable learning by linking policy updates directly to the evidence supporting successful outcomes.

ECHO outperforms previous methods on the BrowseComp-Plus benchmark, achieving 43.4% held-out accuracy compared to 28.9% for GRPO and 36.1% for the rolling-summary baseline SUPO, while using fewer turns and less trajectory data. Additionally, the trained policy demonstrates improved zero-shot generalization across various tasks, including multi-objective question answering, code generation, and deep information-seeking, on both dense and mixture-of-experts model backbones.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31650v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon language agents must repeatedly interact with tools, accumulate evidence, and make decisions under bounded context windows. Existing context-management methods make such rollouts feasible by truncating distant history, folding past turns into summaries, or selecting compact memory states. However, these breakthroughs introduce two coupled limitations. First, as the number of turns grows, historical observations are progressively removed or collapsed into compressed states, making it harder for the policy to reuse fine-grained evidence. Second, once the original turns are no longer source-addressable, outcome-based RL loses an explicit path for aligning policy updates with the evidence that supported a successful final answer. To this end, we propose ECHO, a selective turn-memory framework that jointly addresses history collapse and traceable learning through source-indexed reconstruction. Specifically, ECHO compresses each completed environment turn into a compact memory record, reconstructs bounded policy contexts by selecting from these records, and reuses the selected source indices to route positive outcome credit to the evidence and selection actions that support successful answers. On BrowseComp-Plus, ECHO reaches 43.4% held-out accuracy, outperforming GRPO (28.9%) and the rolling-summary baseline SUPO (36.1%), while using fewer turns and lower trajectory volume than SUPO (Figure 1). Additionally, the trained policy improves zero-shot generalization across multi-objective QA, code generation, and deep information-seeking benchmarks on both dense and MoE backbones.

items.title: Researchers introduce AD-CERT, combining adversarial distillation with Interval Bound Propagation to improve certified robustness and achieve state-of-the-art performance on robustness benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Improving Certified Robustness via Adversarial Distillation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed AD-CERT, a new certified training method that combines adversarial distillation with Interval Bound Propagation (IBP) to enhance the certified robustness of neural networks. This approach leverages adversarial information distilled from a robust teacher model at the logit level, serving as an effective lower bound surrogate for certified training. AD-CERT achieves state-of-the-art performance on several robustness benchmarks, improving the balance between standard accuracy and certified robustness compared to previous methods.

Traditional certified training methods often sacrifice standard accuracy to ensure formal verification against adversarial perturbations, while adversarial training improves empirical robustness but is harder to certify. AD-CERT addresses this trade-off by integrating adversarial distillation with an IBP upper bound, effectively interpolating between lower and upper bounds of worst-case loss. The study also shows that logit-level adversarial distillation outperforms robust feature-space distillation by up to 5.40 percentage points in certified accuracy, marking a significant advancement in certified robustness training techniques.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31653v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Certified training aims to produce models whose predictions can be formally verified against adversarial perturbations, typically by optimising upper bounds on the worst-case loss over an allowed perturbation set. For neural networks, certified training methods based purely on tight relaxation bounds produce networks that are amenable to certification, but sacrifice standard accuracy. Conversely, adversarial training often yields stronger empirical robustness and standard accuracy, but the resulting models are generally difficult to certify with neural network verifiers. Recently, the literature has shown that better standard-certified accuracy trade-offs can be achieved by combining adversarial training objectives with loose over-approximations based on Interval Bound Propagation (IBP), effectively interpolating between lower and upper bounds of the worst-case loss. Building on this, we introduce AD-CERT, a certified training objective that combines adversarial distillation with an IBP upper bound. We show that distilling adversarial information over the logit space from an empirically robust teacher provides an effective lower bound surrogate for certified training, with AD-CERT achieving state-of-the-art certified performance on several robustness benchmarks. Furthermore, in a unified setup, distilling adversarial information at the logit-level is shown to improve certified accuracy over a robust feature-space distillation objective by up to 5.40 percentage points.

items.title: Researchers introduce Histogram-constrained Image Generation, a diffusion model control method enforcing user-specified distributional constraints via optimal transport for precise image generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Histogram-constrained Image Generation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Histogram-constrained Image Generation (HIG), a new method for controlling diffusion models in image generation by enforcing user-defined distributional constraints such as color histograms or latent token distributions. This approach uses optimal transport theory to guide the diffusion process, ensuring precise alignment with the specified histogram during sampling. HIG offers a control granularity between global semantic guidance and detailed local conditioning, addressing challenges in balancing overall coherence with local accuracy in generated images.

The method demonstrates versatility across various applications, including constrained image generation and high-capacity information embedding through histogram-level encoding. HIG is compatible with existing control mechanisms, enabling hybrid strategies for more flexible and interpretable control over image generation. This advancement broadens the toolkit for controllable generative modeling, enhancing the ability to produce images that meet specific distributional criteria.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31683v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as a dominant paradigm in generative modeling, enabling high-fidelity sampling from complex data distributions. Despite impressive capabilities, controlling diffusion models to produce outputs aligned with user intent remains an open challenge, especially when balancing global coherence with local precision. Existing control mechanisms vary in the granularity of their conditioning signals. For example, textual prompts guide generation globally through high-level semantics, while ControlNet-like approaches secure precise local structure via dense conditions. In this work, we introduce Histogram-constrained Image Generation (HIG), a novel control mechanism that falls into the middle ground of control granularity. Our framework enforces user-specified distributional constraints (e.g., color histograms or latent token distributions) during the generation process with exact precision. We model such control as an optimal transport (OT) problem and apply explicit guidance transformations during sampling, thereby driving the diffusion trajectory to align with the desired histogram. We demonstrate the versatility of HIG across diverse applications, including constrained generation via color/latent histograms and high-capacity information embedding through histogram-level encoding. Our findings underscore the promise of distributional control, a flexible and interpretable control scheme that is fully compatible with existing control mechanisms, diversifying the hybrid strategies for controllable image generation. Our project page is available at: https://maps-research.github.io/hig/.

items.title: Researchers propose a residual-overlap stopping rule for feature ranking truncation to select subsets with calibrated risk bounds, validated on high-dimensional genomic data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When to Truncate a Feature Ranking: A Residual-Overlap Stopping Rule for Subset Selection
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new stopping rule for feature ranking truncation in supervised feature selection, addressing the challenge of determining when to stop selecting features based on accumulated class-separation evidence. Their method uses the Bhattacharyya coefficient to measure marginal separation between class-conditional distributions and selects a global subset by retaining the shortest prefix of a ranking whose residual product overlap falls below a set threshold for all relevant class contrasts. This approach provides explicit risk-calibrated stopping criteria, moving beyond arbitrary or empirical thresholds commonly used in practice.

The team derived Bayes-risk bounds for both binary and multiclass cases and calibrated the residual-overlap threshold to target specific risk levels. Empirical tests on high-dimensional genomic datasets demonstrated that the method can reduce tens of thousands of variables to a few dozen while maintaining predictive performance comparable to using all features. Because the stopping rule relies only on one-dimensional marginal overlap estimates and scans a precomputed ranking, it is particularly suited for very high-dimensional settings where exhaustive subset search is impractical and interpretable feature selection is critical.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Feature rankings are widely used in supervised feature selection because they are simple, scalable and easy to interpret. Variables are first ranked by a relevance score, and a subset is then obtained by retaining the top-ranked variables. Although the first stage has been extensively studied, the second is often governed by an arbitrary cardinality, an empirical threshold or cross-validation, without a direct interpretation. This raises a basic question: given a feature ranking, when is there enough accumulated class-separation evidence to stop selecting features? This paper develops a distributional framework for transforming supervised feature rankings into class-independent subsets through an explicit risk-calibrated stopping rule. For each variable and each pair of classes, marginal separation is measured by the Bhattacharyya coefficient between the corresponding class-conditional distributions. The proposed method selects a single global subset shared by all classes by retaining the shortest prefix of a ranking whose residual product overlap falls below a prescribed threshold for every relevant class contrast. We derive binary and multiclass Bayes-risk bounds for the labelled product marginal problem, and obtain prior-dependent and prior-free calibrations of the residual-overlap threshold from a target all-pairs risk level. An empirical comparison on high-dimensional genomic datasets illustrates that the rule can reduce tens of thousands of variables to a few dozen while maintaining predictive performance statistically comparable to the all-features baseline. As the stopping rule only requires one-dimensional marginal overlap estimates and scans a precomputed ranking, it is well suited to very high-dimensional settings where exhaustive subset search is infeasible and interpretable truncation of feature rankings is essential.
