items.originalSummary: arXiv:2502.15845v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often hallucinate, limiting their reliability in sensitive applications. In black-box settings, several self-consistency-based techniques have been proposed for hallucination detection. We empirically show that these methods perform nearly as well as a supervised (black-box) oracle, leaving limited room for further gains within this paradigm. To address this limitation, we explore cross-model consistency checking between the target model and an additional verifier LLM. With this extra information, we observe improved oracle performance compared to purely self-consistency-based methods. We then propose a budget-friendly, two-stage detection algorithm that calls the verifier model only for a subset of cases. It dynamically switches between self-consistency and cross-consistency based on an uncertainty interval of the self-consistency classifier. We provide a geometric interpretation of consistency-based hallucination detection methods through the lens of kernel mean embeddings, offering deeper theoretical insights. Extensive experiments on QA-style hallucination detection benchmarks show that this approach maintains high detection performance while significantly reducing computational cost.

items.summary:
Researchers have introduced SAGE, a search-augmented evaluation framework designed to assess large language models (LLMs) on free-form question answering tasks without relying on fixed ground-truth answers. SAGE operates by actively retrieving and synthesizing external evidence through iterative web queries, summarization, and reflection, addressing limitations of traditional evaluation methods that depend on static references or ungrounded LLM judgments. This approach reduces dependence on costly and incomplete pre-annotated references and mitigates issues where LLMs as evaluators tend to accept incorrect answers or fabricate rationales. By dynamically gathering and refining information from external sources, SAGE offers a scalable and adaptive alternative for evaluating the factual accuracy of LLM outputs in open-ended question answering scenarios.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2504.07385v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become increasingly used for question-answering (QA), relying on static, pre-annotated references for evaluation poses significant challenges in cost, scalability, and completeness. Meanwhile, using LLMs themselves as evaluators without external grounding remains unreliable for objective tasks, as they systematically over-accept incorrect answers, fabricate supporting rationales, and degrade sharply on questions that fall outside their training data. We propose Search-AuGmented Evaluation (SAGE), a framework to assess LLM outputs without fixed ground-truth answers. Unlike conventional metrics that compare to static references or depend solely on LLM-as-a-judge knowledge, SAGE acts as an agent that actively retrieves and synthesizes external evidence. It iteratively generates web queries, collects information, summarizes findings, and refines subsequent searches through reflection. By reducing dependence on static reference-driven evaluation protocols, SAGE offers a scalable and adaptive alternative for evaluating the factuality of LLMs. Experimental results on multiple free-form QA benchmarks show that SAGE achieves substantial to perfect agreement with human evaluations.

items.title: Researchers propose TraCeS method to learn per-timestep constraint violation credit from sparse trajectory-level labels for safer reinforcement learning without known cost functions or thresholds [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: TraCeS: Learning Per-Timestep Constraint-Violation Credit from Sparse Trajectory-Level Labels
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced TraCeS (Trajectory-based Constraint Estimation for Safety), a new method designed to improve safety in reinforcement learning (RL) when explicit safety constraints are not directly measurable. TraCeS learns to assign per-timestep violation credit from sparse, trajectory-level labels that indicate whether an entire rollout meets an unknown safety threshold. This approach does not require a known cost function or threshold and integrates with standard continuous-control algorithms to enhance constrained policy optimization.

The method trains a sequential violation estimator that predicts the probability a trajectory has not violated safety constraints at each step, enabling more precise feedback from coarse supervision signals. The researchers provide theoretical analysis of the learning objective's approximation gap and demonstrate through experiments that TraCeS improves constraint satisfaction and feedback efficiency compared to baseline methods across various continuous-control benchmarks, including long-horizon tasks and scenarios with noisy or inconsistent labels.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2504.12557v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ensuring safe behavior in reinforcement learning (RL) is challenging when safety constraints are implicit and cannot be densely measured. In many settings, supervision is limited to coarse approvals or rejections of whole trajectories (e.g., whether a rollout remained within an unknown safety threshold). We propose TraCeS (Trajectory-based Constraint Estimation for Safety), a method for learning per-timestep violation credit from such sparse trajectory-level labels. TraCeS trains a sequential violation estimator whose per-step credits factorize the predicted probability that a trajectory has not yet violated the constraint, and integrates this learned signal into constrained policy optimization. The method requires neither a known cost function nor a known threshold, and remains compatible with standard continuous-control algorithms. We provide a theoretical analysis of the approximation gap introduced by the learning objective, and demonstrate empirically that TraCeS improves constraint satisfaction and feedback efficiency over baselines across multiple continuous-control benchmarks, including long-horizon tasks and settings with noisy or inconsistent labels.

items.title: Researchers present physics-constrained fine-tuning framework for flow-matching generative models to enforce PDE constraints and solve inverse problems in scientific systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Physics-Constrained Fine-Tuning of Flow-Matching Models for Generation and Inverse Problems
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a framework to fine-tune flow-matching generative models by incorporating physical constraints through partial differential equations (PDEs). This approach starts with models trained on low-fidelity or observational data and applies a differentiable post-training process to ensure physical consistency and boundary condition adherence without altering the learned data distribution. The method also includes a learnable latent parameter predictor to infer unknown physical inputs, enabling the model to solve inverse problems by producing physically valid solutions alongside estimates of hidden parameters.

The framework was validated on standard PDE benchmarks, showing improved compliance with PDE constraints and accurate recovery of latent coefficients. By combining generative modeling with scientific inference, this approach offers a data-efficient and physics-aware tool for simulation-augmented discovery and modeling of complex physical systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2508.09156v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a framework for fine-tuning flow-matching generative models to enforce physical constraints and solve inverse problems in scientific systems. Starting from a model trained on low-fidelity or observational data, we apply a differentiable post-training procedure that minimizes weak-form residuals of governing partial differential equations (PDEs), promoting physical consistency and adherence to boundary conditions without distorting the underlying learned distribution. To infer unknown physical inputs, such as source terms, material parameters, or boundary data, we augment the generative process with a learnable latent parameter predictor and propose a joint optimization strategy. The resulting model produces physically valid field solutions alongside plausible estimates of hidden parameters, effectively addressing ill-posed inverse problems in a data-driven yet physicsaware manner. We validate our method on canonical PDE benchmarks, demonstrating improved satisfaction of PDE constraints and accurate recovery of latent coefficients. Our approach bridges generative modelling and scientific inference, opening new avenues for simulation-augmented discovery and data-efficient modelling of physical systems.

items.title: Researchers introduce Quantum Flow Matching, a quantum-circuit method for efficient interpolation between density matrices enabling generative modeling and observable estimation on quantum computers
items.originalTitle: Quantum Flow Matching
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Quantum Flow Matching (QFM), a quantum-circuit method that efficiently interpolates between two density matrices, extending classical flow matching techniques to quantum systems. QFM enables systematic preparation of quantum states and sample generation for accurate observable estimation, and can be implemented on quantum computers without requiring costly circuit redesigns. This approach offers a unified framework for generative modeling in quantum computing.

The team demonstrated QFM's versatility through applications such as generating quantum states with specific magnetization and entanglement entropy, estimating nonequilibrium free-energy differences to test the quantum Jarzynski equality, and accelerating studies of superdiffusion. These results highlight QFM's potential to advance quantum generative modeling and facilitate various quantum physics investigations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2508.12413v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The flow matching has rapidly become a dominant paradigm in classical generative modeling, offering an efficient way to interpolate between two complex distributions. We extend this idea to the quantum realm and introduce the Quantum Flow Matching (QFM), a quantum-circuit realization that offers efficient interpolation between two density matrices. QFM offers systematic preparation of density matrices and generation of samples for accurately estimating observables, and can be realized on quantum computers without the need for costly circuit redesigns. We validate its versatility on a set of applications: (i) generating target states with prescribed magnetization and entanglement entropy, (ii) estimating nonequilibrium free-energy differences to test the quantum Jarzynski equality, and (iii) expediting the study on superdiffusion. These results position QFM as a unifying and promising framework for generative modeling across quantum systems.

items.originalTitle: One Shot vs. Iterative: Rethinking Pruning Strategies for Model Compression
items.summary:
Researchers conducted a systematic comparison of one-shot and iterative pruning methods for neural network compression, revealing that one-shot pruning is more effective at lower pruning ratios, while iterative pruning performs better at higher ratios. They provided rigorous definitions and benchmarks across various pruning settings and criteria, challenging the common preference for iterative pruning.

The study introduces a hybrid pruning approach based on patience-based pruning, which can outperform traditional methods in certain cases. This work offers valuable guidance for practitioners in selecting pruning strategies that best fit their specific goals and constraints, with source code made available for further exploration.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2508.13836v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pruning is a core technique for compressing neural networks to improve computational efficiency. This process is typically approached in two ways: one-shot pruning, which involves a single pass of training and pruning, and iterative pruning, where pruning is performed over multiple cycles for potentially finer network refinement. Although iterative pruning has historically seen broader adoption, this preference is often assumed rather than rigorously tested. Our study presents one of the first systematic and comprehensive comparisons of these methods, providing rigorous definitions, benchmarking both across structured and unstructured settings, and applying different pruning criteria and modalities. We find that each method has specific advantages: one-shot pruning proves more effective at lower pruning ratios, while iterative pruning performs better at higher ratios. Building on these findings, we advocate for patience-based pruning and introduce a hybrid approach that can outperform traditional methods in certain scenarios, providing valuable insights for practitioners selecting a pruning strategy tailored to their goals and constraints. Source code is available at https://github.com/janumiko/pruning-benchmark.

items.title: Researchers introduce SON-GOKU, a graph-coloring scheduler that partitions tasks to reduce gradient interference and improve multi-task learning performance across six datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Graph Coloring for Multi-Task Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SON-GOKU, a novel scheduler designed to improve multi-task learning by reducing gradient interference among conflicting tasks. The method constructs an interference graph based on gradient conflicts and uses greedy graph-coloring to group tasks that align well, activating only one group per training step. This approach ensures that tasks within each mini-batch update the model in compatible directions, enhancing convergence and overall performance without requiring additional tuning.

SON-GOKU dynamically updates task groupings as relationships evolve during training, allowing it to adapt to changing task interactions. Tested across six datasets, this interference-aware graph-coloring technique consistently outperforms existing baselines and state-of-the-art multi-task optimizers. The researchers also provide theoretical guarantees on descent, convergence, and the accurate identification of task conflicts and alignments, explaining why sequential updates and grouping improve multi-task learning outcomes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2509.16959v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When different objectives conflict with each other in multi-task learning, gradients begin to interfere and slow convergence, thereby potentially reducing the final model's performance. To address this, we introduce SON-GOKU, a scheduler that computes gradient interference, constructs an interference graph, and then applies greedy graph-coloring to partition tasks into groups that align well with each other. At each training step, only one group (color class) of tasks are activated, and the grouping partition is constantly recomputed as task relationships evolve throughout training. By ensuring that each mini-batch contains only tasks that pull the model in the same direction, our method improves the effectiveness of any underlying multi-task learning optimizer without additional tuning. Since tasks within these groups will update in compatible directions, multi-task learning will improve model performance rather than impede it. Empirical results on six different datasets show that this interference-aware graph-coloring approach consistently outperforms baselines and state-of-the-art multi-task optimizers. We provide extensive theory showing why grouping and sequential updates improve multi-task learning, with guarantees on descent, convergence, and the ability to accurately identify what tasks conflict or align.

items.summary:
Researchers have found that selectively forgetting specific time and frequency components in diffusion models enhances both the success of data unlearning and the quality of generated outputs. Unlike traditional methods that uniformly apply unlearning across all diffusion stages, this approach recognizes that forgetting is uneven across different phases and frequencies, leading to better performance in both conditional and unconditional generation settings.

The study provides theoretical support for the observed trade-off between forgetting effectiveness and utility, introducing an improved metric called SSCD to measure dissimilarity more accurately. These findings offer practical insights for refining data unlearning techniques in diffusion models, addressing challenges such as quality degradation and incomplete forgetting seen in previous methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2510.17917v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Data unlearning aims to remove the influence of specific training samples from a trained model. In fine-tuning methods, data unlearning relies primarily on loss maximization over forget samples, which often leads to quality degradation or incomplete forgetting. Existing methods perform unlearning uniformly across diffusion stages, ignoring diffusion dynamics from noise to data. Our systematic study of diffusion phases shows that forgetting in diffusion models is uneven across time and frequency, with theoretical justification of distributive distortion and forgetting-utility trade-off. By selectively forgetting time and frequency in diffusion models, we achieve both higher unlearning success rates and improved generation quality across diverse settings, including both conditional and unconditional scenarios. We also introduce an improved SSCD metric that measures dissimilarity using a normalized perturbation distance. Together, we provide practical insights for understanding and improving data unlearning in diffusion models.

items.title: Researchers introduce AutoPage, a multi-agent system for collaborative paper-to-webpage creation with human and AI verification, validated by the new PageBench benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Human-Agent Collaborative Paper-to-Page Crafting
items.summary:
Researchers have developed AutoPage, a multi-agent system designed to automate the creation of interactive project webpages from scientific papers. AutoPage breaks down the process into stages including narrative planning, multimodal content generation, and interactive rendering, with dedicated agents verifying each step against the source paper to reduce AI errors. The system also allows for human checkpoints to ensure the final webpage aligns with the author's intent, making it a collaborative tool rather than just an automated solution.

To evaluate AutoPage, the team introduced PageBench, the first benchmark for this task. Experiments demonstrated that AutoPage can produce high-quality, visually appealing webpages efficiently, completing the process in under 15 minutes at a low cost. The researchers plan to release the code and dataset to support further development in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2510.19600v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In the quest for scientific progress, communicating research is as vital as the discovery itself. Yet, researchers are often sidetracked by the manual, repetitive chore of building project webpages to make their dense papers accessible. While automation has tackled static slides and posters, the dynamic, interactive nature of webpages has remained an unaddressed challenge. To bridge this gap, we reframe the problem, arguing that the solution lies not in a single command, but in a collaborative, hierarchical process. We introduce $\textbf{AutoPage}$, a novel multi-agent system that embodies this philosophy. AutoPage deconstructs paper-to-page creation into a coarse-to-fine pipeline from narrative planning to multimodal content generation and interactive rendering. To combat AI hallucination, dedicated "Checker" agents verify each step against the source paper, while optional human checkpoints ensure the final product aligns perfectly with the author's vision, transforming the system from a mere tool into a powerful collaborative assistant. To rigorously validate our approach, we also construct $\textbf{PageBench}$, the first benchmark for this new task. Experiments show AutoPage not only generates high-quality, visually appealing pages but does so with remarkable efficiency in under 15 minutes for less than \$0.1. Code and dataset will be released at $\href{https://mqleet.github.io/AutoPage_ProjectPage/}{Webpage}$.

items.title: Researchers propose neighborhood-contextualized message-passing framework and SINC-GCN model to improve graph neural network expressivity and efficiency across benchmark datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Enhancing Graph Representations with Neighborhood-Contextualized Message-Passing
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a neighborhood-contextualized message-passing (NCMP) framework to enhance the expressivity and efficiency of graph neural networks (GNNs). Traditional message-passing GNNs typically consider only pair-wise interactions between a center node and its neighbors, overlooking the broader local neighborhood context. The NCMP framework addresses this limitation by integrating multiset neighborhood information, leading to the development of the Soft-Isomorphic Neighborhood-Contextualized Graph Convolution Network (SINC-GCN). This model demonstrates improved performance across various synthetic and benchmark datasets while maintaining computational efficiency.

The study builds on concepts from set-based aggregation and attentional GNN variants to generalize message-passing methods. SINC-GCN achieves a favorable balance between representational power and runtime complexity, outperforming baseline GNN models without incurring significant computational overhead. This approach offers a scalable and practical enhancement to classical GNN architectures by effectively capturing richer neighborhood context in graph representations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2511.11046v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have become an indispensable tool for analyzing relational data. Classical GNNs are broadly classified into three variants: convolutional, attentional, and message-passing. While the standard message-passing variant is expressive, its typical pair-wise messages only consider the features of the center node and each neighboring node individually. This design fails to incorporate contextual information contained within the broader local neighborhood, potentially hindering its ability to learn meaningful relationships within the entire set of neighboring nodes. To address this, the paper first refines the concept of neighborhood-contextualization within GNNs, leveraging ideas from set-based aggregation methods and a key property of the attentional variant. This then serves as the basis for generalizing the message-passing variant to the proposed neighborhood-contextualized message-passing (NCMP) framework. To demonstrate its utility, a simple, mathematically grounded method to parametrize and operationalize NCMP is presented, leading to the development of the proposed Soft-Isomorphic Neighborhood-Contextualized Graph Convolution Network (SINC-GCN). Across a diverse set of synthetic and benchmark datasets, SINC-GCN strikes a highly favorable balance between expressivity and efficiency. Notably, while more complex models incur significant computational overhead, SINC-GCN delivers substantial performance gains with considerable effect sizes over baseline GNN models while maintaining a highly efficient asymptotic runtime complexity, further underscoring the distinctive utility of neighborhood-contextualization. Overall, by integrating multiset neighborhood context, the proposed NCMP framework serves as a practical and scalable path toward enhancing the graph representational power of classical GNNs.

items.title: Researchers analyze self-consistency scaling in large language models and introduce Blend-ASC, a hyperparameter-free variant that improves sample efficiency by 4.8 times on average [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Optimal Self-Consistency for Efficient Reasoning with Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have conducted a comprehensive analysis of self-consistency (SC), a technique used in large language models to improve chain-of-thought reasoning by generating multiple responses and selecting the most frequent answer. They examined SC's scaling behavior and sample efficiency, introducing Blend-ASC, a new variant that dynamically allocates samples during inference. Blend-ASC achieves state-of-the-art sample efficiency, using on average 4.8 times fewer samples than traditional SC methods.

The study draws on mode estimation and voting theory to derive and validate power law scaling for SC across datasets. Unlike existing approaches, Blend-ASC is hyperparameter-free, supports batching, and can adapt to any sample budget, making it more practical and efficient for large-scale applications. This advancement offers a significant improvement in the efficiency of self-consistency techniques for large language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2511.12309v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-consistency (SC) is a widely used test-time inference technique for improving performance in chain-of-thought reasoning. It consists of generating multiple responses, or ``samples", from a large language model (LLM) and selecting the most frequent answer. This procedure can naturally be viewed as a majority vote or empirical mode estimation. Despite its effectiveness, self-consistency is prohibitively expensive at scale when naively applied to datasets, and it lacks a unified theoretical understanding of sample efficiency and scaling behavior. In this paper, we provide the first comprehensive analysis of SC's scaling behavior and its variants, drawing on mode estimation and voting theory. We derive and empirically validate power law scaling for self-consistency across datasets, and analyze the sample efficiency for fixed-allocation and dynamic-allocation sampling schemes. From these insights, we introduce Blend-ASC, a novel variant of self-consistency that dynamically allocates samples to questions during inference, achieving state-of-the-art sample efficiency. Our approach uses 4.8 times fewer samples than vanilla SC on average, outperforming both fixed- and dynamic-allocation SC baselines, thereby demonstrating the superiority of our approach in terms of efficiency. In contrast to existing variants, we note that Blend-ASC is hyperparameter-free, supports batching, and can fit any budget of samples, ensuring it can be easily applied to any self-consistency application.

items.title: Researchers propose a unified and stable risk minimization framework for weakly supervised learning covering multiple supervision patterns with theoretical generalization guarantees [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A Unified and Stable Risk Minimization Framework for Weakly Supervised Learning with Theoretical Guarantees
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a unified and stable risk minimization framework for weakly supervised learning that integrates various supervision patterns such as positive-unlabeled, unlabeled-unlabeled, complementary-label, partial-label, and similarity-unlabeled annotations into a single optimization objective. This approach eliminates the need for post-hoc corrections typically used to address instability in indirect supervision and provides theoretical guarantees through a non-asymptotic generalization bound based on Rademacher complexity.

The framework also addresses the impact of class-prior misspecification and establishes conditions for identifiability, ensuring the recoverability of the target risk. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent performance improvements across different class priors, dataset sizes, and class counts, while maintaining robustness against overfitting without relying on heuristic stabilization methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2511.22823v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Weakly supervised learning has emerged as a practical alternative to fully supervised learning when complete and accurate labels are costly or infeasible to acquire. However, many existing methods are tailored to specific supervision patterns -- such as positive-unlabeled (PU), unlabeled-unlabeled (UU), complementary-label (CLL), partial-label (PLL), or similarity-unlabeled annotations -- and rely on post-hoc corrections to mitigate instability induced by indirect supervision. We propose a principled, unified framework that bypasses such post-hoc adjustments by directly formulating a stable surrogate risk grounded in the structure of weakly supervised data. The formulation naturally subsumes diverse settings -- including PU, UU, CLL, PLL, multi-class unlabeled, and tuple-based learning -- under a single optimization objective. We further establish a non-asymptotic generalization bound via Rademacher complexity that clarifies how supervision structure, model capacity, and sample size jointly govern performance. Beyond this, we analyze the effect of class-prior misspecification on the bound, deriving explicit terms that quantify its impact, and we study identifiability, giving sufficient conditions -- most notably via supervision stratification across groups -- under which the target risk is recoverable. Extensive experiments show consistent gains across class priors, dataset scales, and class counts -- without heuristic stabilization -- while exhibiting robustness to overfitting.

items.title: Researchers introduce HydroGym, a solver-independent reinforcement learning platform for fluid dynamics with 61+ environments enabling transferable flow control and drag reduction up to 90% [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: The HydroGym Reinforcement Learning Platform for Fluid Dynamics
items.summary:
Researchers have developed HydroGym, a solver-independent reinforcement learning platform designed to advance fluid dynamics control. HydroGym features over 61 validated environments covering a wide range of flow conditions from laminar to turbulent, supporting various computational solvers. The platform enables reinforcement learning agents to discover effective flow control strategies that significantly reduce drag, with reductions exceeding 90% in standard test cases.

HydroGym's standardized infrastructure allows for transferable control intelligence across different flow regimes, demonstrated by agents trained on simplified flows achieving substantial drag reduction on complex, unseen geometries without additional training. This zero-shot transfer capability suggests that the agents learn fundamental fluid dynamics principles rather than configuration-specific solutions. The platform offers a scalable and extensible resource for research in fluid dynamics, machine learning, and control engineering.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2512.17534v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modeling and controlling fluids is critical across science and engineering. Effective flow control can increase lift, reduce drag, enhance mixing, and attenuate noise, potentially unlocking new technologies. Yet controlling fluids is hard: the dynamics are high-dimensional, nonlinear, and multiscale. While reinforcement learning (RL) has recently succeeded in robotics and protein folding through shared benchmarks, fluid dynamics has resisted such progress: each controller is typically tuned to a single geometry and operating point, making results hard to accumulate, transfer, and compare. We introduce HydroGym, a solver-independent RL platform for flow control, and show that standardized infrastructure unlocks transferable control intelligence across flow regimes. HydroGym provides 61+ validated environments spanning laminar to turbulent flows, with systematic Reynolds number progressions up to Re=400,000 and Mach number variations in 2D and 3D. It supports diverse backends, including finite-volume, spectral-element, finite-element, lattice-Boltzmann, and fully differentiable solvers for gradient-enhanced optimization. Across environments, RL agents consistently discover robust control principles, such as boundary-layer manipulation, acoustic-feedback disruption, and wake reorganization, yielding drag reductions exceeding 90% in canonical configurations. Critically, we demonstrate zero-shot transfer: agents trained only on a simplified channel flow achieve 38% friction-drag reduction on an unseen 3D wing section at chord Reynolds number Re=200,000 reducing exploration costs by four orders of magnitude versus direct on-wing optimization. This suggests RL agents uncover essential physics rather than configuration-specific patterns, pointing toward generalizable control. HydroGym offers extensible, scalable community infrastructure for fluid dynamics, machine learning, and control research.

items.title: Researchers propose sequence truncation for efficient reasoning distillation, retaining 91% performance on math benchmarks while halving training time, memory, and FLOPs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Distilling the Essence: Efficient Reasoning Distillation via Sequence Truncation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a method to improve the efficiency of knowledge distillation from large reasoning models to smaller student models by selectively truncating training sequences. Their approach focuses on distilling only the chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens, which contain the essential reasoning steps, while omitting parts of the prompt and answer sections when these are encompassed by the CoT. This selective training reduces computational costs significantly without greatly sacrificing performance.

The team established a truncation protocol that balances computation and quality, finding that training on just the first 50% of tokens in each sequence retains approximately 91% of the full-sequence performance on math benchmarks. This approach cuts training time, memory usage, and floating-point operations by about half, making the distillation process more resource-efficient. The researchers have made their code publicly available to support further exploration and application of this technique.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2512.21002v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Distilling the capabilities from a large reasoning model (LRM) to a smaller student model often involves training on substantial amounts of reasoning data. However, knowledge distillation (KD) over lengthy sequences with prompt (P), chain-of-thought (CoT), and answer (A) sections makes the process computationally expensive. In this work, we investigate how the allocation of supervision across different sections (P, CoT, A) affects student performance. Our analysis shows that selective KD over only the CoT tokens can be effective when the prompt and answer information is encompassed by it. Building on this insight, we establish a truncation protocol to quantify computation-quality tradeoffs as a function of sequence length. We observe that beyond a specific length, longer training sequences provide marginal returns for downstream performance but require substantially higher memory and FLOPs. To this end, training on only the first $50\%$ of tokens of every training sequence can retain, on average, $\approx91\%$ of full-sequence performance on math benchmarks while reducing training time, memory usage, and FLOPs by about $50\%$ each. Codes are available at https://github.com/weiruichen01/distilling-the-essence.

items.title: Researchers present InfiniteWeb, a system that generates scalable, functional web environments to improve GUI agent training and outperform commercial coding agents in website construction [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: InfiniteWeb: Scalable Web Environment Synthesis for GUI Agent Training
items.summary:
Researchers have developed InfiniteWeb, a system that automatically generates scalable and functional web environments to enhance the training of graphical user interface (GUI) agents. These agents, designed to interact with graphical interfaces on behalf of users, face training challenges due to the lack of suitable environments. InfiniteWeb addresses this by creating realistic, multi-page websites using unified specifications, task-centric test-driven development, and a combination of website seeds with reference design images to ensure diversity.

The system also produces verifiable task evaluators that provide dense reward signals for reinforcement learning. Experimental results demonstrate that InfiniteWeb outperforms commercial coding agents in constructing realistic websites, and GUI agents trained on these generated environments show significant performance improvements on benchmarks such as OSWorld and Online-Mind2Web, highlighting the system's effectiveness in advancing practical AI assistant capabilities.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2601.04126v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: GUI agents that interact with graphical interfaces on behalf of users represent a promising direction for practical AI assistants. However, training such agents is hindered by the scarcity of suitable environments. We present InfiniteWeb, a system that automatically generates functional web environments at scale for GUI agent training. While LLMs perform well on generating a single webpage, building a realistic and functional website with many interconnected pages faces challenges. We address these challenges through unified specification, task-centric test-driven development, and a combination of website seed with reference design image to ensure diversity. Experiments show that InfiniteWeb surpasses commercial coding agents at realistic website construction, and GUI agents trained on our generated environments achieve significant performance improvements on OSWorld and Online-Mind2Web, demonstrating the effectiveness of proposed system.

items.title: Researchers develop AI framework using class-aware Mahalanobis distance for pixel-level anomaly detection in rodent liver histopathology to improve preclinical toxicity assessment [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Toxicity Assessment in Preclinical Histopathology via Class-Aware Mahalanobis Distance for Known and Novel Anomalies
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an AI-based framework that uses class-aware Mahalanobis distance for pixel-level anomaly detection in whole-slide images of rodent liver histopathology. This approach aims to improve preclinical toxicity assessment by accurately identifying healthy tissue, known pathologies, and flagging unknown anomalies as out-of-distribution (OOD). The method was tested on challenging categories such as apoptosis and staining artifacts, demonstrating high accuracy with minimal false positives and false negatives.

The framework involves fine-tuning a pre-trained Vision Transformer with Low-Rank Adaptation for segmentation, followed by OOD detection using class-specific thresholds. The study reports that only 0.16% of pathological tissue was misclassified as healthy, and 0.35% of healthy tissue as pathological, reflecting a safety-first approach to avoid overlooking lesions. This work highlights the potential for AI to enhance preclinical workflows and increase efficiency in drug development by automating detailed histopathological analysis.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.02124v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Drug-induced toxicity is a leading cause of preclinical and early-clinical failure, making early detection critical. Histopathology is the gold standard for toxicity assessment but relies on expert pathologists, creating a bottleneck for large-scale screening. We introduce an AI-based anomaly detection framework for whole-slide images (WSIs) of rodent liver that identifies healthy tissue and known pathologies (anomalies) and flags samples without training data as out-of-distribution (OOD). We evaluate OOD detection on two held-out categories: apoptosis (single-cell, near-OOD) and staining/processing artifacts (heterogeneous, far-OOD). We build a novel pixelwise-annotated dataset and fine-tune a pre-trained Vision Transformer (DINOv2) via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) for segmentation, then use the Mahalanobis distance for OOD detection with class-specific thresholds. Optimizing the false positive rate subject to a predefined constraint on the false negative rate yields only 0.16% of pathological tissue classified as healthy and 0.35% of healthy tissue classified as pathological. Our false negative rate does not penalise cross-type errors, reflecting the safety-first objective of never overlooking a lesion; under the stricter correct-class criterion our method assigns 93.93% of ID and 89.38% of OOD findings to their own class. The study demonstrates technical feasibility of pixel-level anomaly detection for mouse liver histopathology, indicating possible applications in improving preclinical workflows and drug development efficiency.

items.title: Researchers propose a novel Bellman operator formulation for static CVaR objectives in MDPs enabling dense rewards and contracting properties, with risk-averse algorithms and convergence guarantees [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reward Redistribution for CVaR MDPs using a Bellman Operator on L-infinity
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a new formulation of the static conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) objective for Markov decision processes (MDPs), addressing limitations in traditional approaches that rely on state augmentation and result in sparse rewards and degenerate fixed points. Their method produces a Bellman operator with dense per-step rewards and contracting properties across all bounded value functions, enabling more effective risk-averse policy learning.

Building on this theoretical framework, the team developed risk-averse value iteration and model-free Q-learning algorithms that use discretized augmented states. They provide convergence guarantees and bounds on approximation errors due to discretization. Empirical evaluations show that these algorithms successfully learn CVaR-sensitive policies, achieving a balance between performance and safety in decision-making tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.03778v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Tail-end risk measures such as static conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) are used in safety-critical applications to prevent rare, yet catastrophic events. Unlike risk-neutral objectives, the static CVaR of the return depends on entire trajectories without admitting a recursive Bellman decomposition in the underlying Markov decision process. A classical resolution relies on state augmentation with a continuous variable. However, unless restricted to a specialized class of admissible value functions, this formulation induces sparse rewards and degenerate fixed points. In this work, we propose a novel formulation of the static CVaR objective based on augmentation. Our alternative approach leads to a Bellman operator with: (1) dense per-step rewards; (2) contracting properties on the full space of bounded value functions. Building on this theoretical foundation, we develop risk-averse value iteration and model-free Q-learning algorithms that rely on discretized augmented states. We further provide convergence guarantees and approximation error bounds due to discretization. Empirical results demonstrate that our algorithms successfully learn CVaR-sensitive policies and achieve effective performance-safety trade-offs.

items.summary: Researchers have developed DeXposure-FM, a novel time-series graph foundation model designed to measure and forecast credit exposures and systemic risk across over 4,300 decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols on 602 blockchains. This model addresses the complex interdependencies in DeFi, where credit exposure is often implicit and token-mediated, potentially leading to significant contagion effects. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2602.03981v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Credit exposure in Decentralized Finance (DeFi) is often implicit and token-mediated, creating a dense web of inter-protocol dependencies. Thus, a shock to one token may result in significant and uncontrolled contagion effects. As the DeFi ecosystem becomes increasingly linked with traditional financial infrastructure through instruments, such as stablecoins, the risk posed by this dynamic demands more powerful quantification tools. We introduce DeXposure-FM, the first time-series, graph foundation model for measuring and forecasting inter-protocol credit exposure on DeFi networks, to the best of our knowledge. Employing a graph-tabular encoder, with pre-trained weight initialization, and multiple task-specific heads, DeXposure-FM is trained on the DeXposure dataset that has 43.7 million data entries, across 4,300+ protocols on 602 blockchains, covering 24,300+ unique tokens. The training is operationalized for credit-exposure forecasting, predicting the joint dynamics of (1) protocol-level flows, and (2) the topology and weights of credit-exposure links. The DeXposure-FM is empirically validated on two machine learning benchmarks; it consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches, including a graph foundation model and temporal graph neural networks. DeXposure-FM further produces financial economics tools that support macroprudential monitoring and scenario-based DeFi stress testing, by enabling protocol-level systemic-importance scores, sector-level spillover and concentration measures via a forecast-then-measure pipeline. Empirical verification fully supports our financial economics tools. The model and code have been publicly available. Model: https://huggingface.co/EVIEHub/DeXposure-FM. Code: https://github.com/EVIEHub/DeXposure-FM.

items.title: Researchers propose swap-adversarial framework to improve domain generalization in electrocorticography-based Parkinson's disease classification, validated across ECoG and EEG datasets with new rat model benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A swap-adversarial framework for improving domain generalization in electrocorticography-based Parkinson's disease classification
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a novel swap-adversarial framework to address challenges in electrocorticography (ECoG) data analysis for Parkinson's disease classification, focusing on reducing inter-subject variability and overcoming the high-dimensional, low-sample-size problem. This approach combines robust preprocessing, a bio-inspired inter-subject balanced channel swap (ISBCS) method for cross-subject data augmentation, and domain-adversarial learning (DAL) to minimize subject-specific biases, enhancing domain generalization across both ECoG and electroencephalography (EEG) datasets.

The ISBCS technique swaps functionally corresponding brain channels between subjects based on a brain map, while DAL encourages the model to learn shared, task-relevant features. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this framework outperforms existing methods across cross-subject, cross-session, and cross-dataset scenarios, showing particularly strong performance in variable environments. Additionally, the researchers introduced a new reproducible ECoG benchmark dataset derived from long-term recordings of rat models with Parkinson's-like conditions, annotated with neural responses before and after electrical stimulation.

items.title: Researchers present TVF, a 24k-parameter, interpretable, low-latency IIR filter-based denoiser for on-device assistive hearing with real-time noise tracking and adjustable suppression control [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: An Interpretable, Controllable Time-Varying IIR Denoiser for On-Device Assistive Hearing
items.summary:
Researchers have developed TVF (Time-Varying Filtering), a compact and interpretable speech enhancement model designed for real-time, on-device assistive hearing. The model uses a lightweight neural controller to predict coefficients for a cascade of 35 second-order IIR filters, enabling it to track non-stationary noise while maintaining an explicit and adjustable equalizer curve rather than relying on opaque transformations. With only 24,000 parameters and a 10.7ms latency, TVF operates within hearing aid constraints and processes audio entirely on-device to ensure privacy.

TVF offers an explicit control over the trade-off between noise suppression and speech preservation, adjustable during both training and inference without retraining. Performance metrics for hearing aids show that TVF closely matches larger models with significantly fewer computational resources, demonstrating its potential as an efficient, interpretable, and controllable denoiser for assistive hearing devices.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2603.02794v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present TVF (Time-Varying Filtering), an interpretable, low-latency speech enhancement model for real-time, on-device assistive hearing. A lightweight neural controller predicts, in real time, the coefficients of a differentiable cascade of 35 second-order IIR filters (biquads), so the model tracks non-stationary noise while keeping a fully interpretable processing chain: every spectral modification is an explicit, adjustable equalizer curve rather than an opaque `black-box' transform. Because the biquad cascade carries the signal processing, the controller can be made very small, driving the cascade with only 24k parameters at a 10.7ms algorithmic latency, within hearing-aid budgets, and running entirely on-device so that audio never leaves the device. We also expose the suppression-versus-preservation trade-off as an explicit control: it can be set during training through the loss weighting, and adjusted at inference, with no retraining, by mixing the noisy input with the denoised output. On hearing-aid metrics (HASPI/HASQI) the 24k model stays within about 0.02 of DFNet3 (2.3M parameters, almost two orders of magnitude larger) while using about 29X fewer multiply-accumulates, although larger black-box models still lead on reference metrics such as PESQ. We present TVF as a proof of concept for a compact, interpretable, and controllable denoiser for on-device assistive hearing.

items.title: Researchers propose finite difference flow optimization for reinforcement learning post-training of text-to-image diffusion models, achieving faster convergence and improved image quality and prompt alignment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Finite Difference Flow Optimization for RL Post-Training of Text-to-Image Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new reinforcement learning (RL) method for post-training text-to-image diffusion models that improves image quality and alignment with prompts. Their approach treats the entire sampling process as a single action and reduces variance in model updates by comparing paired trajectories, leading to faster convergence and better results than existing techniques.

The team tested their method using both advanced vision-language models and standard quality metrics for rewards, evaluating outputs across multiple criteria. This novel RL variant demonstrates enhanced efficiency and effectiveness in optimizing diffusion-based image synthesis models, offering a promising direction for future improvements in AI-generated imagery.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2603.12893v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a standard technique for post-training diffusion-based image synthesis models, as it enables learning from reward signals to explicitly improve desirable aspects such as image quality and prompt alignment. In this paper, we propose an online RL variant that reduces the variance in the model updates by sampling paired trajectories and pulling the flow velocity in the direction of the more favorable image. Unlike existing methods that treat each sampling step as a separate policy action, we consider the entire sampling process as a single action. We experiment with both high-quality vision language models and off-the-shelf quality metrics for rewards, and evaluate the outputs using a broad set of metrics. Our method converges faster and yields higher output quality and prompt alignment than previous approaches.

items.title: Researchers propose VLC, a neuro-symbolic method combining vision-language models with circuit-based symbolic reasoning to improve robustness on visual deductive reasoning tasks under distribution shifts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Can VLMs Reason Robustly? A Neuro-Symbolic Investigation
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced VLC, a neuro-symbolic approach that integrates vision-language models (VLMs) with circuit-based symbolic reasoning to enhance robustness in visual deductive reasoning tasks under distribution shifts. Their study reveals that while fine-tuned VLMs perform well on in-distribution data, they struggle to generalize when perceptual inputs change but underlying logical rules remain constant. VLC addresses this by separating perception from reasoning, compiling task rules into symbolic circuits that operate precisely on concepts recognized by VLMs.

Experiments on three distinct visual deductive reasoning tasks demonstrate that VLC consistently outperforms other reasoning methods in accuracy on out-of-distribution data. This suggests that combining VLM-based concept recognition with exact symbolic execution can improve reasoning robustness. The researchers have made their code publicly available to support further exploration in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2603.23867v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have been applied to a wide range of reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether they can reason robustly under distribution shifts. In this paper, we study covariate shifts in which the perceptual input distribution changes while the underlying prediction rules do not. To investigate this question, we consider visual deductive reasoning tasks, where a model is required to answer a query given an image and logical rules defined over the object concepts in the image. Empirically, we find that VLMs fine-tuned through gradient-based end-to-end training can achieve high in-distribution accuracy but fail to generalize under such shifts, suggesting that fine-tuning does not reliably induce the underlying reasoning function. This motivates a neuro-symbolic perspective that decouples perception from reasoning. However, we further observe that recent neuro-symbolic approaches that rely on black-box components for reasoning can still exhibit inconsistent robustness across tasks. To address this issue, we propose VLC, a neuro-symbolic method that combines VLM-based concept recognition with circuit-based symbolic reasoning. In particular, task rules are compiled into a symbolic program, specifically a circuit, which executes the rules exactly over the object concepts recognized by the VLM. Experiments on three simple visual deductive reasoning tasks with distinct rule sets show that VLC consistently achieves higher task accuracy on out-of-distribution data than other reasoning paradigms. Code is available at https://github.com/uiuctml/VLC.

items.title: Researchers present RARE, a redundancy-aware retrieval evaluation framework for high-similarity corpora, revealing robustness gaps in retrievers on Finance, Legal, and Patent datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: RARE: Redundancy-Aware Retrieval Evaluation Framework for High-Similarity Corpora
items.summary:
Researchers have developed RARE, a redundancy-aware retrieval evaluation framework designed to address the limitations of existing QA benchmarks that assume minimal document overlap. This framework targets real-world retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems operating on highly redundant corpora such as financial reports, legal codes, and patents, where traditional evaluations may undervalue retrievers due to unaccounted redundancy. RARE decomposes documents into atomic facts for precise redundancy tracking and enhances data generation reliability using a method called CRRF.

Applying RARE to Finance, Legal, and Patent datasets, the researchers introduced RedQA, revealing significant drops in retriever performance compared to standard benchmarks, highlighting robustness gaps that current evaluations miss. This framework enables the creation of domain-specific RAG benchmarks that more accurately reflect real-world deployment conditions, improving the assessment of retriever effectiveness in high-similarity document collections.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.19047v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Existing QA benchmarks typically assume distinct documents with minimal overlap, yet real-world retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems operate on corpora such as financial reports, legal codes, and patents, where information is highly redundant and documents exhibit strong inter-document similarity. This mismatch undermines evaluation validity: retrievers can be unfairly undervalued even when they retrieve documents that provide sufficient evidence, because redundancy across documents is not accounted for in evaluation. On the other hand, retrievers that perform well on standard benchmarks often generalize poorly to real-world corpora with highly similar and redundant documents. We present RARE (Redundancy-Aware Retrieval Evaluation), a framework for constructing realistic benchmarks by (i) decomposing documents into atomic facts to enable precise redundancy tracking and (ii) enhancing LLM-based data generation with CRRF. RAG benchmark data usually requires multiple quality criteria, but LLMs often yield trivial outputs. CRRF scores criteria separately and fuses decisions by rank, improving the reliability of generated data. Applying RARE to Finance, Legal, and Patent corpora, we introduce RedQA, where a strong retriever baseline drops from 66.4% PerfRecall@10 on 4-hop General-Wiki to 5.0-27.9% PerfRecall@10 at 4-hop depth, revealing robustness gaps that current benchmarks fail to capture. RARE enables practitioners to build domain-specific RAG evaluations that faithfully reflect real-world deployment conditions.

items.title: Researchers develop Lyapunov-certified switching linear system framework for Q-learning error analysis using joint spectral radius to determine convergence rates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Lyapunov-Certified Direct Switching Theory for Q-Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a novel framework for analyzing Q-learning, a key algorithm in reinforcement learning, by modeling its error dynamics as a switching linear system (SLS). This approach enables a finite-time error analysis using the joint spectral radius (JSR) of the SLS model, which precisely characterizes the worst-case exponential convergence rate. This study represents the first to express the leading exponential convergence rate of standard Q-learning through the JSR, offering potentially sharper bounds than traditional row-sum methods when those are conservative.

The framework derives a stochastic SLS representation of the Q-learning error, linking the convergence rate directly to the intrinsic worst-case behavior of the system. This connection provides a more accurate and theoretically grounded understanding of Q-learning's convergence properties, which could inform future algorithmic improvements and analyses in reinforcement learning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2604.19569v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Q-learning is a fundamental algorithmic primitive in reinforcement learning. This paper develops a new framework for analyzing Q-learning from a switching linear system (SLS) viewpoint. In particular, we derive a stochastic SLS representation of the Q-learning error, and a finite-time error analysis through the joint spectral radius (JSR) of the corresponding SLS model, where the JSR is the exact worst-case exponential rate of the associated SLS. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first convergence rate analysis of standard Q-learning whose leading exponential rate is expressed through the JSR. The resulting rate is tied to the intrinsic worst-case exponential rate of the direct SLS representation and can be sharper than row-sum upper bounds when those bounds are conservative.

items.summary:

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.04057v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper focuses on a key challenge in Neural Architecture Search (NAS): integrating established architectural knowledge while exploring new designs under expensive evaluations. Large language models (LLMs) are a promising assistant for NAS because they can translate rich architectural and coding priors into executable code edits. However, in practice, seemingly local revisions often propagate into non-local behavioral and performance shifts because a single edit can inadvertently couple multiple interacting functional factors, a phenomenon we refer to as functional entanglement. To make LLM knowledge usable under such entanglement, we propose Structured Progressive Knowledge Activation (SPARK), which activates relevant priors by explicitly selecting the functional factor to modify and conditioning the edit on that factor. This factor-conditioned editing reduces entangled side effects and yields more targeted, reliable architecture modifications. On CLRS-DFS, SPARK achieves a 28.1x sample-efficient architecture evolution speedup and yields a 22.9\% relative improvement in OOD accuracy. Our code is available at https://github.com/AIM-ResearchLab/SPARK.

items.title: Researchers analyze instability in MeanFlow training for one-step generative models, derive optimal variance reduction coefficient, and reveal mismatch between variance and quality optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: On Variance Reduction in Learning Mean Flows
items.summary:
Researchers have investigated the instability issues in MeanFlow training, a method used in one-step generative modeling for diffusion and flow-matching models. They identified that the instability arises from an incorrect use of the conditional velocity field, which serves dual roles in the loss function. By deriving the optimal variance reduction coefficient, the study unifies various existing fixes and explains why MeanFlow experiences non-decreasing loss and unbounded gradient variance.

The team conducted experiments on two-dimensional benchmarks and a latent Diffusion Transformer, confirming the predicted bias-variance trade-offs. Their findings also revealed a mismatch between minimizing gradient mean squared error and optimizing generation quality, measured by the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID). This indicates that the coefficient minimizing variance does not necessarily yield the best generative performance, providing new insights into improving training stability and model quality in generative modeling.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.09235v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: One-step generative modeling has emerged as a leading approach for amortizing the inference cost of diffusion and flow-matching models. Among distillation-free methods, MeanFlow training is notoriously unstable, with non-decreasing loss and unbounded gradient variance. In this work, we establish a theory that attributes this pathology to a misuse of the conditional velocity field. We show that the conditional velocity plays two distinct statistical roles in the loss: both as an unbiased regression target and as a Monte Carlo control variate in a Jacobi-vector product, with the original MeanFlow loss assigning the wrong coefficient to the latter. We derive the optimal coefficient in closed form and show that a family of fixes in concurrent works corresponds to different practical realizations of the same optimum. A controlled sweep of this coefficient on two-dimensional benchmarks and on a latent Diffusion Transformer recovers the predicted bias-variance ordering. Our DiT experiment also reveals a quantitative FID-MSE landscape mismatch. Specifically, although the gradient-MSE is minimized at an interior coefficient value near $\beta\!=\!0.94$, the coefficient that minimizes FID prefers to use conditional velocity directly at the unbiased corner. Our analysis therefore explains why MeanFlow is unstable and unifies its concurrent remedies, and shows that the variance-optimal coefficient need not coincide with the quality-optimal one.

items.title: Researchers find typed knowledge graphs improve GPT-4 accuracy from 65% to 83% and enable near-perfect reasoning in industrial asset operations scenarios [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Knowledge Graphs as the Missing Data Layer for LLM-Based Industrial Asset Operations
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that integrating typed knowledge graphs as a data layer significantly improves the accuracy of GPT-4 in industrial asset operations scenarios, raising performance from 65% to over 82%. By using a typed knowledge graph to structure data and guide query generation, the approach enables near-perfect reasoning, achieving up to 99% accuracy on graph-answerable cases without relying solely on the language model. This method also incorporates generation-augmented knowledge to handle missing information, ensuring comprehensive and auditable responses.

The study, based on the AssetOpsBench benchmark with 139 industrial maintenance scenarios, highlights that the data model underlying the tools is a critical factor in enhancing reasoning capabilities. The researchers employed a combination of LLM-generated Cypher queries for structured retrieval, native graph operations, and provenance-tagged graph nodes to materialize missing facts. This inverted use of LLMs—constraining them to query generation and enrichment while letting the graph execute deterministically—proved effective in addressing non-deterministic and previously unanswerable scenarios.

These findings suggest that for structured operational domains, the primary improvement lever lies in the data layer rather than the orchestration of language models. The typed knowledge graph serves as a robust grounding substrate, bridging raw industrial data and LLM reasoning, which could lead to more reliable and auditable AI-driven asset management solutions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2605.26874v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLM-based agents for industrial asset operations show limited accuracy when reasoning over flat document stores. AssetOpsBench (KDD 2026) establishes that GPT-4 agents achieve 65% on 139 industrial maintenance scenarios, and compares LLM orchestration paradigms (Agent-As-Tool vs. Plan-Execute) on a fixed data layer. We ask the orthogonal question: how much does the data model behind the tools matter? We treat a typed knowledge graph as a grounding substrate and route each question by how it is best answered: (i) LLM-generated Cypher for structured retrieval, which lifts the same GPT-4 model from 65% to 82-83%; (ii) native graph and optimization primitives, with no LLM, reaching 99% on graph-answerable scenarios; and (iii) generation-augmented knowledge (GAK) for answers absent from the data -- the engine's agent materializes the missing facts as provenance-tagged graph nodes, then answers. A recurring theme is inverted LLM usage: we constrain the LLM to query generation or one-shot enrichment from a typed schema and let the graph execute deterministically. On the 88 real AssetOpsBench failure-mode scenarios the benchmark itself flags non-deterministic -- ten equipment types absent from the graph -- GAK lifts answerability from zero to 100% of equipment types and answers 81.8% of scenarios, every materialized fact tagged source:LLM-derived for auditability. We also contribute 40 graph-native scenarios. For structured operational domains the data layer -- not the LLM orchestration -- is the primary lever, and a typed knowledge graph serves as a grounding substrate between raw industrial data and LLM reasoning.

items.title: Researchers introduce BenGER benchmark to evaluate 12 LLM systems on subsumption-based legal reasoning in German law using 1,127 exam-style and doctrinal tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: BenGER: Benchmarking LLM Systems on Subsumption-Based Legal Reasoning in German Law
items.summary:
Researchers have developed BenGER, a benchmark and dataset designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on subsumption-based legal reasoning within German law. The dataset includes 1,127 tasks, combining 596 exam-style free-text legal case problems and 531 short doctrinal reasoning tasks, covering multiple levels of legal education. The evaluation involved 12 contemporary LLM systems, including closed flagship, efficiency-oriented, and open-weight models, assessed using a rubric-aligned LLM-as-a-Judge approach validated against multi-rater human grading.

The study features a controlled validation subset with timed human-written solutions under both unaided and human-AI co-creation conditions. Results show that closed-flagship systems lead performance across all task sets, and human-AI collaboration improves outcomes compared to unaided human efforts. The LLM judge's assessments correlate strongly with human grading, demonstrating stable system rankings across different judge families and meeting established benchmarks for replacing single human reviewers on human-authored solutions.

items.title: Researchers propose COM-as-Action paradigm for professional software manipulation, introduce ComCADBench benchmark and ComActor agent achieving state-of-the-art results in industrial CAD tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: ComAct: Reframing Professional Software Manipulation via COM-as-Action Paradigm
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a new paradigm called COM-as-Action to improve professional software manipulation by treating interactions as deterministic program synthesis rather than relying on fragile GUI-based control. They developed ComCADBench, the first benchmark for agents operating industrial CAD software, revealing that COM-based execution significantly outperforms existing GUI-based models. To enhance accuracy, they created ComActor, a self-correcting agent trained through a three-stage framework, supported by ComForge, a scalable training platform.

Extensive testing shows that ComActor achieves state-of-the-art results on ComCADBench, demonstrating strong resilience in complex, long-horizon tasks where other models fail. It also generalizes well to external CAD benchmarks, indicating its potential for broader application in professional software environments.

items.originalTitle: Same-Origin Policy for Agentic Browsers
items.summary:
Researchers have identified that agentic browsers, which integrate autonomous AI agents to perform web tasks via natural language, frequently violate the same-origin policy (SOP), a key security mechanism designed to prevent unauthorized cross-origin data flows. To systematically study this issue, they developed SOPBench, a benchmark for evaluating SOP violations in these browsers, revealing frequent breaches both in normal use and under attack scenarios. To address this, the team proposed SOPGuard, a tailored enforcement mechanism implemented in the open-source agentic browser BrowserOS, which effectively enforces SOP with minimal impact on performance and usability.

The study highlights that agentic browsers themselves can act as automated channels for cross-origin data flows, posing new security challenges. SOPGuard was extensively evaluated and demonstrated to maintain browser utility while imposing only a small runtime overhead. The researchers have made their code and data publicly available to support further development and security improvements in agentic browsing technology.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.14027v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Agentic browsers integrate autonomous AI agents into web browsers, enabling users to accomplish web tasks through natural-language instructions. The same-origin policy (SOP) is a fundamental browser security mechanism that prevents unauthorized automated cross-origin data flows induced by scripts. However, whether SOP remains effective in agentic browsers is an open question that has not been systematically studied. In this work, we bridge this gap. We first observe that an agentic browser can itself serve as an automated channel for cross-origin data flows, potentially leading to SOP violations. To investigate this phenomenon, we construct SOPBench, a benchmark for evaluating SOP violations in agentic browsers. Our evaluation shows that existing agentic browsers frequently violate SOP, both in benign settings and under attacks. To address this problem, we propose SOPGuard, an SOP enforcement mechanism tailored to agentic browsers. We implement SOPGuard in BrowserOS, an open-source agentic browser. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that SOPGuard effectively enforces SOP while preserving utility and incurring only a small runtime overhead. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/wxl-lxw/BrowserOS-SOPGuard.

items.title: Researchers propose Entropy-Gated Latent Recursion, a deterministic decoding method that expands language model rollout diversity by recursively reapplying top decoder layers, improving math reasoning accuracy by over 8 percentage points [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Entropy-Gated Latent Recursion
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Entropy-Gated Latent Recursion (EGLR), a deterministic decoding method that enhances language model reasoning by recursively reapplying the top decoder layers at tokens with high uncertainty. This approach expands rollout diversity beyond traditional stochastic token-level sampling by adding a new axis based on the layer span, producing distinct rollouts without randomness. EGLR, combined with temperature sampling, creates a richer set of candidate outputs, significantly improving math reasoning accuracy by over 8 percentage points on benchmarks like MATH-500.

The method operates without additional training, iteratively refining predictions until convergence, and has been tested across multiple instruction-tuned models and math reasoning tasks. The complementary nature of the layer-based and temperature-based sampling axes allows EGLR to capture a broader range of problem-solving strategies. This expanded rollout pool benefits downstream processes such as self-consistency checks, best-of-N selection with verifiers, and reinforcement learning training, offering a new direction for inference-time scaling that does not rely on stochastic noise.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.16620v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Inference-time scaling has become the dominant lever for improving language-model reasoning, but existing methods derive rollout diversity from a single source: stochastic token-level sampling. We argue that this single-axis sampling space is fundamentally limiting, and identify a second, fully deterministic and complementary axis: the layer span $L$ at which a frozen model's top decoder layers are recursively re-applied at high-uncertainty tokens. Different choices of $L$ produce distinct rollouts that solve different subsets of problems, with no stochasticity. We instantiate this axis through Entropy-Gated Latent Recursion (EGLR), a training-free decoding procedure that re-applies the top-$L$ layers for at most $K_{\max}$ iterations until the next-token distribution converges. Combined with $T$ temperature samples, EGLR turns a single-axis stochastic rollout pool into an $L\times T$ Cartesian sampling space at almost the same per-rollout cost. We characterize this space across $8$ instruction-tuned models and $6$ math reasoning benchmarks, and show that the $L$-axis is genuinely complementary to temperature: on MATH-500 with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, the joint $L\times T$ oracle reaches $91.6\%$, $+8.2$ percentage points beyond the temperature-only oracle ($83.4\%$) and $+10.4$ points beyond the layer-only oracle ($81.2\%$), confirming that the two axes capture genuinely complementary problems. The expanded rollout pool provides richer per-prompt candidates for any downstream procedure that consumes rollouts, including self-consistency, best-of-$N$ with verifiers, and group-relative RL training (GRPO), opening a new direction for inference-time scaling that does not rely on stochastic noise.

items.title: Researchers introduce Topological Neural Dynamics, a neuron-wise sequence modeling framework that outperforms RNN, LSTM, and Transformer baselines in behavior cloning tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Topological Neural Dynamics: A Neuron-wise Framework for Sequence Modeling
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Topological Neural Dynamics (TND), a novel sequence modeling framework that shifts from traditional layer-wise dynamics to neuron-wise dynamics, allowing individual neurons to evolve independently within a directed neuron graph. This approach contrasts with existing models like RNNs, LSTMs, and Transformers, which use shared operators for all neurons in a layer. TND was tested on a behavior cloning task in single-player Pong, where it outperformed several baseline models by achieving the highest catch rate and an average of 17.47 consecutive catches per round, more than triple the best baseline performance.

TND models neural systems as discrete-time graph-coupled dynamical systems, where collective computation arises from interactions defined by explicit graph topology. This neuron-wise dynamic framework provides a new inductive bias for sequence modeling, inspired by complex dynamical systems where global behavior emerges from locally evolving units. The results suggest that allowing neurons to evolve independently within structured connectivity can enhance sequence modeling capabilities beyond traditional layer-wise approaches.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.21295v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Existing sequence models, including RNNs, LSTMs, continuous-time networks, and Transformers, share a common structural principle: layer-wise dynamics, where all neurons in the same layer co-evolve through a shared parameterized operator, leaving individual neurons no freedom to evolve independently. Yet in many complex dynamical systems, rich global behavior emerges precisely from locally evolving units interacting through structured connectivity. Inspired by this principle, we introduce Topological Neural Dynamics (TND), a sequence modeling framework that shifts computation from layer-wise to neuron-wise dynamics. TND represents a neural system as a directed neuron graph, an interaction operator, and a local dynamics function, where each neuron evolves independently and collective computation emerges from interactions through the explicit graph topology. We instantiate TND as a discrete-time graph-coupled dynamical system and evaluate it as a case study on a behavior cloning task in single-player Pong. Compared with Vanilla RNN, Sparse RNN, LSTM, Closed-form continuous-time neural network (CfC), and Transformer baselines, TND achieves the best catch rate and a mean of 17.47 consecutive catches per round, more than three times that of the strongest baseline. These results suggest that shifting from layer-wise to neuron-wise dynamics provides an effective inductive bias for sequence modeling.
