items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31174v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Production large language-model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed not as lone problem-solvers but as managers: a main model creates specialized subagents, delegates work, and orchestrates their parallel, asynchronous returns through dynamic workflows. Whether one model can actually run such a team is largely unmeasured: existing benchmarks score a policy's own task-solving or a fixed multi-agent system's emergent behavior, but none isolate the management ability of the single LLM acting as leader. We introduce ClawArena-Team, a benchmark of 41 multi-turn, multimodal, multi-directory scenarios spanning 258 evaluation rounds and 72 staged updates that measures this management ability. The main agent is deliberately constrained: it natively perceives only text and directly accesses only part of the workspace. It commands a fixed, locally served subagent pool, so score differences reflect management skill, not raw capability. All scoring is execution-based with no LLM judge: an overall score -- the Subagent-Management Score (SMS) -- multiplies task correctness by a least-privilege and modality-routing factor. Across twelve proprietary, community-hosted, and self-hosted models, experiments show that the management bottleneck is privilege granting rather than perception (no model exceeds 50% workspace-permission precision); that cost and management quality are decoupled (API cost spans over 100 times while the overall score spans under 4 times, with the cheapest open models on the Pareto frontier); and that most leaderboard scores cluster within a 9.9-point band while orchestration behaviors diverge by more than an order of magnitude. Code and data will be released.

items.title: Researchers use AI dual-agent system to discover tighter convex relaxations, improving certified lower bounds on two optimization constants in 2026 study [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AI-Assisted Discovery of Convex Relaxations via Dual Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an AI-driven dual-agent system to discover tighter convex relaxations, which improve certified lower bounds on two important optimization constants. The system uses a coding agent to propose constraints and a theory agent to verify them and search for counterexamples, ensuring each bound is rigorously certified. This approach enhanced the lower bounds for the first autocorrelation inequality and the Erdős minimum-overlap constant, advancing the precision of these mathematical constants.

The study builds on previous work that used large language model agents to find upper bounds by searching for extremal constructions. By focusing on the complementary problem of establishing lower bounds through convex relaxations, the researchers applied an autoresearch paradigm that combines automated proposal and verification. Their method was validated using explicit dual-feasible points checked with interval arithmetic, demonstrating improved bounds from 1.28 to 1.2937 and from 0.379005 to 0.37912, respectively, for the two constants studied.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31182v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work shows that LLM agents can improve sharp-constant inequalities by searching for extremal constructions, which yield upper bounds. We address the complementary side: a lower bound holds for every admissible function and follows from a convex relaxation of the nonconvex problem, with tighter relaxations giving stronger bounds. We instantiate the autoresearch paradigm to discover such relaxations: a coding agent proposes valid tightening constraints, a theory agent verifies each one and searches for counterexamples, and every reported bound is certified by an explicit dual-feasible point checked in rigorous interval arithmetic. On two optimization constants studied by \citet{tao2025alphaevolve} - the first autocorrelation inequality ($C_{6.2}$) and the Erd\H{o}s minimum-overlap constant ($C_{6.5}$) - we improve the certified lower bounds from $1.28$ to $1.2937$ and from $0.379005$ to $0.37912$, respectively.

items.title: Researchers present Agentic RAG-VLM, a robotic grasping framework integrating affordance-aware retrieval, scene graph reasoning, and self-reflective planning, achieving 78.3% success on a 12-task benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Agentic RAG-VLM: Affordance-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Self-Reflective Planning for Robotic Grasping
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Agentic RAG-VLM, a novel robotic grasping framework that combines affordance-aware retrieval, scene graph reasoning, and self-reflective planning to improve manipulation in cluttered environments. This system integrates vision-language models with retrieval-augmented generation and adaptive planning to better understand object properties like material fragility and graspability, enabling more effective and robust grasp execution.

Agentic RAG-VLM features three key components: a Hierarchical Affordance-Aware RAG that retrieves grasp strategies based on functional compatibility rather than visual similarity; a Scene Graph Constraint Reasoner that adjusts grasp parameters using spatial relationships; and an Agentic Self-Reflective Pipeline that refines grasp attempts through failure analysis and adaptive retries. Tested on a 12-task benchmark involving various grasping scenarios, the framework achieved a 78.3% success rate, significantly outperforming baseline methods that rely solely on vision-language models.

The results demonstrate that combining affordance-based retrieval, spatial reasoning, and closed-loop recovery is essential for reliable robotic manipulation in complex, unstructured settings. This approach advances the deployment of manipulators in human environments by addressing challenges posed by densely packed and physically diverse objects.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31200v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generalizable robotic grasping in cluttered environments is essential for deploying manipulators in unstructured human spaces, yet existing VLM-based methods rely on visual similarity for object matching, neglecting physical affordances such as handle graspability and material fragility, and operate open-loop without spatial reasoning or failure recovery, limiting their effectiveness when objects are densely packed or physically diverse. We present Agentic RAG-VLM, a unified framework that bridges VLM-based semantic understanding and physically grounded grasp execution by integrating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with vision-language models (VLMs) and agentic self-reflective planning. Agentic RAG-VLM introduces three tightly coupled components: (1) a Hierarchical Affordance-Aware RAG (HAA-RAG) that encodes four-dimensional affordance descriptors, including type, material, fragility, and graspable region, and retrieves strategies by functional affordance compatibility rather than visual appearance; (2) a Scene Graph Constraint Reasoner that constructs spatial relationship graphs from VLM perception and translates proximity, occlusion, and support constraints into concrete grasp parameter adjustments; and (3) an Agentic Self-Reflective Pipeline with a 14-type failure taxonomy and three-level adaptive retry for closed-loop grasp refinement. Evaluated on a 12-task benchmark spanning single-grasp, interactive, and long-horizon scenarios with 360 trials per configuration, Agentic RAG-VLM achieves 78.3 percent overall success, a 53.3 percentage-point absolute gain over VLM-only baselines, demonstrating that affordance-aware retrieval, scene graph reasoning, and agentic recovery are jointly essential for robust manipulation.

items.title: Study analyzes elderly mobility patterns in Jersey City bike data, finds majority-trained models misrepresent elderly behavior and highlights need for demographic representation in urban mobility modeling [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Towards Inclusive Mobility Modeling: Characterizing and Evaluating Elderly Trajectory Patterns in Urban Systems
items.summary:
A study analyzing Jersey City bike data from 2016 to 2020 reveals that elderly riders exhibit distinct mobility patterns compared to younger riders, including smaller activity spaces, lower mobility entropy, and different temporal usage. The research highlights that mobility models trained predominantly on majority populations misrepresent elderly behavior, particularly in spatial metrics, leading to biased synthetic trajectory generation.

Using both a first-order Markov chain and a fine-tuned large language model, the study compares models trained on the full population, young riders only, and elderly riders only. Results show that models trained specifically on elderly data produce more accurate representations, while higher-capability models do not necessarily improve subgroup fidelity when demographic data is limited. These findings emphasize the need for inclusive demographic representation in urban mobility modeling to avoid systematic biases affecting underrepresented groups.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31207v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid advance of smart cities increasingly depends on trajectory data mining, yet underrepresented demographic groups, particularly the elderly, are often sparsely represented in public mobility datasets. This underrepresentation can introduce systematic bias into mobility modeling and downstream urban planning. Using the 2016-2020 Jersey City subset of the Citi Bike System Data, this study quantitatively examines how the absence of underrepresented subgroups' mobility signatures affects mobility modeling, using synthetic trajectory generation as a case study. The analysis reveals that elderly riders exhibit a structurally distinct mobility signature, including localized activity spaces (958 m vs. 1,189 m for young riders), lower mobility entropy (1.82 vs. 4.15), and asymmetric off-peak temporal patterns. To demonstrate that relying on majority-dominated training data yields biased synthetic outcomes, we further evaluate both a first-order Markov chain and a Qwen3-4B model fine-tuned with QLoRA across three demographic training settings: the full population, young riders only, and elderly riders only. Results show that models trained on majority-dominated populations systematically misrepresent elderly mobility behavior, particularly for spatial mobility metrics. The Markov model trained on the full population overestimates elderly step length by 4.5% and dwell time by 8.9%, whereas the elderly-specific model achieves substantially lower errors across most metrics. Comparisons between the Markov and LLM-based frameworks further show that higher-capability models do not necessarily improve subgroup-level fidelity under limited demographic data. These findings underscore the importance of demographic representation in mobility modeling and its downstream applications for underrepresented populations.

items.title: Researchers introduce RosettaSim, a structured autoregressive model for long-term multi-agent traffic simulation achieving state-of-the-art results on Waymo Open Sim Agent Challenge [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Long-term Traffic Simulation via Structured Autoregressive Modeling
items.summary:
Researchers have developed RosettaSim, a structured autoregressive model designed for long-term multi-agent traffic simulation, which achieves state-of-the-art results on the Waymo Open Sim Agent Challenge. The model leverages the architectural strengths and statistical priors of large-scale sequence models, such as Large Language Models, to effectively handle dynamic multi-agent interactions over extended periods. RosettaSim encodes scene topology, agent states, and spawning intents into a variable-length autoregressive stream, enabling both accurate short-term predictions and stable long-term simulation fidelity.

To evaluate extended simulations where direct agent correspondence diminishes over time, the team introduced Retrieval-based Traffic Evaluation (RTE), a method that uses semantically similar real-world scenarios as reference points. Experiments demonstrate that RosettaSim outperforms existing approaches in both short- and long-term traffic simulation, with RTE showing a stronger correlation to standard metrics, indicating improved alignment with real-world traffic dynamics.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31209v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interactive traffic simulation is a vital world model for autonomous driving. A central challenge in long-horizon simulation is modeling sustained multi-agent interactions, which is further exacerbated by dynamic token cardinality as agents continuously enter and exit the scene. In this work, we propose that the solution lies in the synergy between the architectural inductive biases and statistical priors of large-scale sequence models, e.g., Large Language Models (LLMs). Our probing experiments reveal that the transferability of attention mechanisms and the distributional consistency between motion tokens and natural language enable small-scale, heavily frozen LLMs to rapidly adapt to traffic modeling. Building on this insight, we introduce RosettaSim, a unified framework that projects scene topology, agent states, and spawning intents into a structured autoregressive stream with variable length, achieving both strong short-term accuracy and stable long-horizon simulation fidelity. Furthermore, evaluating extended rollouts presents yet another hurdle, as one-to-one agent correspondence inevitably fades over time. To address this, we introduce Retrieval-based Traffic Evaluation (RTE), which retrieves semantically similar real-world scenarios as context-aware reference anchors. Experiments on the Waymo Open Sim Agent Challenge (WOSAC) demonstrate that RosettaSim achieves state-of-the-art performance in both short- and long-term simulation. Furthermore, RTE exhibits a stronger correlation with standard metrics ($r=0.83$) than existing approaches ($r=0.74$), indicating improved alignment with long-horizon simulation fidelity.

items.title: Researchers introduce PEC-CIR, a training-free multi-stage reasoning framework for zero-shot composed image retrieval that improves query construction and retrieval stability through planning, execution, and self-criticism [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Thinking Before Retrieving: Robust Zero-Shot Composed Image Retrieval via Strategic Planning and Self-Criticism
items.summary:
Researchers have developed PEC-CIR, a training-free, multi-stage reasoning framework designed to improve zero-shot composed image retrieval. This approach enhances query construction and retrieval stability by breaking down the process into three stages: planning, execution, and self-criticism. Unlike existing single-pass methods that combine reference images and textual modifications into one description, PEC-CIR uses a Planner to extract constraints, an Executor to generate multiple candidate queries, and a Critic to evaluate these candidates for compliance, reducing semantic errors and improving retrieval accuracy.

By structuring query construction as a staged inference process rather than a single-step output, PEC-CIR addresses challenges such as semantic distortions and attribute preservation conflicts that degrade retrieval precision. This framework operates within a frozen vision-language embedding space at inference time, enabling more robust and stable retrieval without additional training.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31222v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Composed image retrieval requires identifying a target image from a gallery by integrating a reference image with a textual modification instruction. In a training-free zero-shot setting, this task relies on constructing a retrieval-oriented textual query within a frozen vision--language embedding space at inference time. Existing approaches predominantly rely on a single-pass generation strategy that fuses the reference context and modification text into a unified description. This strategy makes it difficult to detect or correct semantic distortions and omissions during generation. Consequently, the preservation of reference attributes and the integration of textual requirements interfere with each other, which degrades retrieval precision. To address these challenges, we introduce PEC-CIR, a training-free framework that structures query construction as a multi-stage reasoning pipeline. The framework operates through a Planner--Executor--Critic architecture where the Planner extracts explicit constraints, the Executor generates multiple candidate target descriptions, and the Critic evaluates these candidates based on constraint compliance. By reframing query construction as a staged inference process instead of a single-pass output, PEC-CIR reduces the propagation of generative errors by explicitly evaluating candidate queries before retrieval, thereby improving retrieval stability.

items.title: Researchers propose Agentic-Ideation framework with Oracle-Guided Data Synthesis to improve sample efficiency and quality of scientific ideation agents by over 10 times and 11.9% respectively [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Agentic-Ideation: Sample Efficient Agentic Trajectories Synthesis for Scientific Ideation Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Agentic-Ideation, a new framework designed to enhance scientific ideation agents by significantly improving sample efficiency and output quality. This approach combines an automated trajectory synthesis pipeline with a specialized agentic large language model (LLM) trained for scientific ideation, addressing limitations of previous methods that relied on rigid workflows and faced high data synthesis costs. The framework incorporates a comprehensive set of tools and employs an Oracle-Guided Data Synthesis strategy that uses reference ideas to guide multi-agent systems in generating more directed and efficient reasoning paths.

The method trains the agent on synthesized trajectories with a masking strategy to focus on decision-making logic, avoiding interference from external feedback. Experimental results show that Agentic-Ideation outperforms state-of-the-art workflow-based baselines by 11.9% in overall quality and achieves over a tenfold increase in sample efficiency for high-quality data synthesis. This advancement offers a promising direction for more flexible and cost-effective automated scientific discovery processes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31229v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ideation plays a pivotal role in scientific discovery. Recent LLM, especially AI Scientist systems, show promising potential for automated ideation. However, existing approaches predominantly rely on pre-defined agentic workflows. This constraint severely limits the flexibility required to navigate the vast search space of scientific literature and the complex action space of research reasoning. Recently, training Agentic LLMs has emerged as a promising direction, offering flexible reasoning frameworks and the capability for autonomous tool utilization. However, there remains a non-trivial challenge: applying previous agentic data synthesis methods to scientific ideation suffers from prohibitively high data synthesis cost. To bridge this gap, we propose Agentic-Ideation, a novel framework comprising an automated trajectory synthesis pipeline and a specialized agentic LLM trained for scientific ideation. Specifically, we first define a comprehensive tool space incorporating three external tools and three cognitive tools. Then we introduce an Oracle-Guided Data Synthesis strategy. By leveraging a reference idea as oracle guidance, this approach steers the multi-agent system to efficiently reconstruct the logical reasoning and tool invocation paths, transforming aimless trial-and-error into directed trajectory generation. Finally, we train the agent on these synthesized trajectories, employing a masking strategy on tool execution results. This ensures the model focuses on decision-making logic without interference from external feedback. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms the SOTA workflow-based baseline by \textbf{11.91\%} in overall quality. Furthermore, our approach improves the sample efficiency of high-quality data synthesis by \textbf{over 10$\times$}.

items.title: Researchers propose Delta-JEPA, a reconstruction-free world model using latent difference action decoding to improve action-sensitive planning in visual continuous-control tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Delta-JEPA: Learning Action-Sensitive World Models via Latent Difference Decoding
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Delta-JEPA, a novel reconstruction-free world model designed to enhance action-sensitive planning in visual continuous-control tasks. This model incorporates a Latent Difference Action Decoder (LDAD) that reconstructs executed actions from the latent displacement between consecutive observations, ensuring that latent representations remain sensitive to actions and avoid collapse into action-insensitive forms. Delta-JEPA relies solely on latent prediction and action reconstruction, bypassing traditional pixel reconstruction and distribution-matching methods.

Tested across four visual continuous-control tasks, Delta-JEPA demonstrated improved planning performance compared to existing JEPA-based and representation-learning world models. The approach's displacement-based action decoding proved more effective than endpoint concatenation, and analyses confirmed clearer action-conditioned latent responses. These findings suggest that supervising latent differences offers a straightforward and effective strategy for developing collapse-resistant, action-sensitive world models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31232v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning visual world models for planning requires compact latent dynamics that remain sensitive to actions, yet reconstruction-free joint-embedding objectives can collapse to action-insensitive representations. We propose Delta-JEPA, an end-to-end reconstruction-free world model that augments latent forward prediction with a Latent Difference Action Decoder (LDAD). Unlike inverse decoders that infer actions from concatenated endpoint embeddings, LDAD reconstructs the executed action from the latent displacement between consecutive observations. This displacement-level supervision directly regularizes transition geometry: adjacent embeddings cannot collapse without losing action information, and different actions are encouraged to induce distinguishable latent changes for rollout-based planning. Delta-JEPA uses only latent prediction and action reconstruction, avoiding pixel reconstruction and distribution-matching regularizers. Across four visual continuous-control tasks, Delta-JEPA improves planning over JEPA-based and representation-learning world model baselines. Ablations show that displacement-based action decoding is consistently more effective than endpoint concatenation, and action-sensitivity analyses show clearer action-conditioned latent responses. These results indicate that supervising latent differences is a simple and effective mechanism for collapse-resistant and action-sensitive world model learning.

items.title: Researchers present Embodied CAD, solver-grounded large language model agents for parametric B-Rep assembly modeling with iterative action selection and solver feedback, evaluated on multi-step industrial tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Embodied CAD: Solver-Grounded LLM Agents for Parametric B-Rep Assembly Modeling
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Embodied CAD, a system that integrates large language models with solver-grounded feedback to improve parametric boundary representation (B-Rep) assembly modeling in computer-aided design (CAD). Unlike traditional methods that generate complete scripts in one step, this approach iteratively selects actions from a hierarchical CAD skill library, executes them in a CAD backend, and uses solver feedback to refine planning and repair processes. This method ensures that every feature and assembly relation is validated by an exact geometric kernel, maintaining editability and precision.

The framework combines action grammar constraints, deterministic parameter resolution, and solver-derived rewards to enhance learning and execution. Evaluations on complex mechanical and industrial assembly tasks demonstrate that solver-grounded planning successfully completes all benchmark workflows, while learned controllers achieve high executable rates, highlighting the gap between valid tool usage and precise long-term policy prediction. This advancement offers a promising direction for reliable and editable industrial CAD modeling driven by AI.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31252v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models can write plausible CAD scripts, but reliable industrial CAD modeling requires more than syntactically valid code: every feature, placement, and assembly relation must be accepted by an exact geometric kernel while remaining editable as parametric boundary representation geometry. We present Embodied CAD, solver-grounded LLM agents for parametric B-Rep assembly modeling. Instead of generating a complete script in one pass, the agent iteratively selects actions from a stratified L0-L4 CAD skill library, resolves them into typed geometric operations, executes them in a CAD backend, and uses solver feedback to plan, repair, and learn. The framework combines action grammar constraints, deterministic parameter resolution, and solver-derived rewards for supervised warm-up and GRPO-style refinement. We evaluate Embodied CAD on multi-step mechanical, industrial equipment, and mold-oriented assembly tasks using solver-aligned metrics: executable rate, skill accuracy, operation-family accuracy, exact policy accuracy, and task completion success. The results show that solver-grounded planning executes all strong-planner workflows in the current benchmark, while learned controllers reach high executable rates and expose the remaining gap between valid tool calls and exact long-horizon policy prediction.

items.title: Researchers introduce modality switching between language and symbolic grids to improve spatial reasoning in large language models by up to 42% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Spatial Reasoning via Modality Switching Between Language and Symbolic Representation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a method to enhance spatial reasoning in large language models (LLMs) by enabling them to switch between natural language and symbolic grid representations. This approach is based on the observation that human reasoning often involves multiple modalities, such as diagrams or grids, to better understand complex problems. The study introduces a switching metric that helps the model decide when to use language-based reasoning and when to rely on structured spatial representations, leading to performance improvements of up to 42% in reasoning tasks.

The research focuses on grounding multi-hop textual-spatial stories into geometry-aware modalities like layouts or grids, comparing this to traditional natural language inference. By assessing trustworthiness and complexity signals, the model can determine the most effective modality for a given problem. This work represents a step toward more principled modality selection in LLM reasoning, highlighting the significant impact of modality choice on reasoning outcomes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31285v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Human reasoning is inherently multimodal: when problems become difficult, we rarely think in words alone. We often externalize our reasoning by sketching diagrams or drawing grids to understand the underlying conceptual structure and avoid mistakes. Building on this premise, our research investigates: (a) whether grounding multi-hop textual-spatial stories into geometry-aware modalities, such as layouts or grids, improves reasoning compared to natural language-based inference; and (b) whether a model can decide when to rely on natural language reasoning and when to switch to a structured modality. We address these questions by introducing a switching metric based on trustworthiness and complexity signals, which estimates when grounding a spatial story into structure is likely to improve performance. This takes a first step toward principled modality selection in Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning. Across our settings, switching from natural language-based reasoning to a grid-based representation improves LLM performance by up to 42\%, highlighting the importance of modality choice in shaping reasoning outcomes.

items.title: Researchers benchmark 14 large language models on floating-point error classification using InterFLOPBench with 1,130 test samples across six error categories, finding top models exceed 0.88 F1-score [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Floating-Point Error Classification
items.summary:
Researchers have evaluated the ability of 14 large language models (LLMs) to detect and classify floating-point errors in software code using a new benchmark called InterFLOPBench. This benchmark includes 1,130 test samples from 90 C kernels and covers six categories of floating-point errors: cancellation, comparison, division by zero, overflow, underflow, and NaN. The study treats error detection as a multi-label classification task and measures performance with the F1-score metric, finding that the latest models achieve overall F1-scores above 0.88.

The evaluation revealed variation in model performance across different error types, with explicit errors like division by zero scoring higher (average F1-score of 0.85) compared to more subtle numerical issues such as underflow and cancellation, which had lower average scores around 0.61. Top-performing models include Qwen 3 32b, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Phi 4 Reasoning, DeepSeek R1T2, and gpt-oss variants, demonstrating strong capabilities in static floating-point error classification.

items.summary:

The creation of HistoriQA-ThirdRepublic involved careful selection and alignment of heterogeneous historical sources, question validation, and integration of metadata. While focused on French historical documents, the methodology used to build the corpus can be adapted to other languages and national archives. items.title: CryoACE introduces an atom-centric framework for automated, accurate protein model building from cryo-EM density maps, enabling dynamic atomic-level conformations without pre-built static structures [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: CryoACE: An Atom-centric Framework for Accurate and Automated Model Building in Cryo-EM
items.summary:
CryoACE is a new automated framework designed to build accurate protein models directly from cryo-EM density maps, addressing challenges in maintaining physicochemical validity and handling conformational variability. It introduces an atom-centric approach that samples density features at atomic coordinates and iteratively refines structures, replacing traditional voxel-based methods for more efficient data fusion. Additionally, it employs a training-free guidance system using local resolution predictions to resolve dynamic ambiguities.

Tested on a high-quality dataset, CryoACE outperforms existing methods on static structure benchmarks and uniquely reveals atomic-level dynamic conformations in complex real-world datasets without relying on pre-existing static models. This advancement offers a significant step forward in modeling both homogeneous and heterogeneous protein structures from cryo-EM data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31332v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Protein automodeling from cryo-EM density maps faces unique challenges in enforcing physicochemical validity and managing conformational heterogeneity. Current solvers are often limited to static predictions or require computationally intensive heuristic searches. We present CryoACE, an end-to-end framework that reconstructs precise atomic graphs for both homogeneous and heterogeneous structures. Our method features two key innovations: an atom-centric reconstruction paradigm, where density features are sampled directly at atomic coordinates and iteratively recycled to refine structures, replacing expensive voxel convolutions for efficient multimodal fusion; and a training-free guidance mechanism that leverages predicted local resolution priors to resolve dynamic ambiguity. Validated on a newly constructed high-quality dataset, CryoACE significantly outperforms existing baselines on static benchmarks and, for the first time, unveils atomic-level dynamic conformations on complex real-world datasets like EMPIAR-10345 without relying on pre-built static structures.

items.title: Survey of 78 joint OFDM-RIS optimization algorithms for 6G networks classifies methods from convex relaxation to foundation models and identifies six open challenges [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Optimization Algorithms for Joint OFDM Waveform Design and RIS Configuration in 6G Networks: From Convex Relaxation to Foundation Models
items.summary:
A comprehensive survey reviews 78 studies on joint OFDM-RIS optimization for 6G networks, addressing challenges such as sum-rate maximization, energy efficiency, fairness, and peak-to-average power ratio constraints. The research categorizes existing methods into four paradigms: model-based convex relaxation, heuristic/metaheuristic search, deep reinforcement and unsupervised learning, and emerging approaches including foundation models and quantum optimization. The survey highlights that machine learning techniques achieve near-model-based spectral efficiency with significantly faster runtimes, and identifies a critical scaling advantage of neural network inference over iterative solvers.

The study notes the absence of standardized benchmarks, making cross-comparison difficult, and presents a tutorial benchmark revealing runtime invariance in GPU-based neural network methods across different problem sizes. It also outlines six key open challenges, including the need for standardized benchmarking, real-world hardware constraints, optimization for complex channel conditions, multi-objective trade-offs, safety concerns with large language models in network control, and the limited gains from standalone heuristics. This work provides a roadmap for future research and practical deployment of joint OFDM-RIS optimization in 6G systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31334v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Joint OFDM-RIS optimization for 6G is a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem covering sum-rate maximization, energy efficiency, max-min fairness, and peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR)-constrained objectives. Seventy-eight joint OFDM-RIS optimization works published between 2021 and 2026 are surveyed. No standardized benchmark exists, and cross-paper comparisons remain infeasible. This survey classifies these works into four paradigms: (I) model-based convex relaxation, (II) heuristic and metaheuristic search, (III) deep reinforcement and unsupervised learning, and (IV) emerging methods including foundation models (FM), diffusion-based generative AI, and quantum optimization. A literature synthesis of self-reported benchmarks shows that ML-based methods (Paradigm~III) report 95-99\% of model-based spectral efficiency at 10^2-10^4 x faster per-inference runtime (method-pair dependent; literature values are self-reported and exclude ML pre-training cost). A companion tutorial benchmark at N=16, N=64, and N=128 reveals a critical scaling property: GPU-based neural network inference (DDQN, PPO, graph neural network (GNN), unsupervised DL) is N-invariant, with identical runtime at N=16 and N=128, while iterative solvers (AO+SCA, PSO) scale polynomially. Energy efficiency (P2) and PAPR-constrained (P4) benchmarks are deferred to future work with standardized power models and waveform generators. Six open challenges emerge from the synthesis: the cross-paradigm benchmark deficit, real-world hardware-constrained deployment, joint waveform-RIS optimization for doubly-dispersive channels, multi-objective PAPR trade-offs, LLM safety in live network control, and diminishing returns of standalone heuristics. We specify requirements for a standardized benchmark. This study serves as a roadmap for researchers and practitioners working on joint OFDM-RIS optimization in 6G networks.

items.title: Researchers compare independent multi-agent reinforcement learning methods for decentralized smart charging of large electric vehicle fleets under dynamic pricing and grid constraints [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Smart charging of large fleets of Electric Vehicles: Independent Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning approaches
items.summary:
Researchers have compared two independent multi-agent reinforcement learning methods—contextual combinatorial bandits and policy gradient algorithms—for decentralized smart charging of large electric vehicle fleets. Their study addresses challenges posed by increased peak demand and grid constraints due to EV integration, aiming to optimize charging schedules under dynamic electricity pricing and network limitations. The evaluation was conducted in a realistic simulation where autonomous agents make decisions based on local information such as price signals, battery state, and timing constraints.

The research tested these approaches across different congestion levels and heterogeneous agent groups, using dynamic pricing derived from real photovoltaic energy production data. This work highlights the potential of decentralized coordination among electric vehicles to minimize user costs and prevent grid overloads while accommodating renewable energy variability.

items.title: Researchers introduce ReGRPO, a reflection-augmented policy optimization framework that improves tool-using vision-language agents by learning reflection-guided corrections, outperforming open-source baselines on GTA and GAIA tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ReGRPO: Reflection-Augmented Policy Optimization for Tool-Using Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ReGRPO, a reflection-augmented policy optimization framework designed to enhance the performance of tool-using vision-language models (VLMs) in solving complex multimodal tasks. ReGRPO addresses limitations in existing methods by learning reflection-guided corrections, enabling agents to recover from tool failures more effectively. The approach involves collecting failure observations through near-miss actions and creating Reflection-of-Thought triplets that guide corrective actions, which are optimized jointly to improve task success.

The framework was tested on GTA and GAIA benchmarks, where it consistently outperformed strong open-source baselines using the same backbone and tool suite. ReGRPO incorporates a reflection-cost term to minimize unnecessary reflection, balancing correction with efficiency. The researchers have made their code and reflection data publicly available, supporting further development in tool-augmented vision-language agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31392v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-augmented vision-language models (VLMs) can solve multimodal, multi-step tasks by calling external tools, yet they remain fragile in practice. Existing works have two common gaps. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is built mostly on successful trajectories and offers little signal for recovery after tool failures, while sparse trajectory-level RL rewards provide limited guidance on which step failed and how to repair it. We introduce ReGRPO (Reflection-augmented Group Relative Policy Optimization), a framework that learns reflection-guided correction in tool-using agents. ReGRPO starts with a structured reflective data engine: we execute near-miss actions to collect grounded failure observations, then build Reflection-of-Thought triplets (ErrorType, Evidence, FixPlan) paired with corrected actions for warm-start SFT. We then optimize reflection tokens and corrective actions jointly within local trajectories using group-relative advantages, and include a reflection-cost term to reduce unnecessary reflection. items.title: Researchers identify phase transition causing sudden world-model collapse in long-horizon language agents, revealing a measurable bottleneck in agent performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: World-Model Collapse as a Phase Transition
items.summary:
Researchers have identified a phase transition in long-horizon language agents that leads to a sudden collapse of their implicit world models. This phenomenon occurs when small changes in parameters, such as state load or horizon length, push the agent past a critical boundary, causing a rapid degradation in world-state fidelity despite maintaining valid actions. The study, conducted on a deterministic task family with exact per-step gold state, reveals a phase diagram with distinct regions of stable performance, transition, and collapse, highlighting a measurable bottleneck in agent performance.

The research involved a comprehensive grid search over various factors including state cardinality, dependency density, horizon, branching, observation mode, and mutation rate. Findings show that stronger models shift the critical boundary but do not eliminate the qualitative transition, indicating that world-model collapse is an inherent challenge for long-horizon agents. This insight advances understanding of the limitations in agent world modeling and may guide future improvements in their design and robustness.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31399v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Water looks unchanged as it warms, then at a critical point it boils. We ask whether long-horizon language agents show an analogous transition in their implicit world models. In some parameter settings, changing state load by a small amount, or adding a single step of horizon, leaves behavior nearly unchanged; near a critical boundary, the same small change causes a sudden world collapse. We study this effect in a deterministic task family with exact per-step gold state. A large grid search over state cardinality, dependency density, horizon, branching, observation mode, and mutation rate reveals a phase diagram: a solved plateau, a narrow transition band, and a collapse floor. Per-step traces show the mechanism: world-state fidelity fails before action validity, so the agent is not merely choosing a bad action; it is acting from a corrupted world. Stronger models translate the critical boundary but do not remove the qualitative transition. These results make world-model collapse a measurable bottleneck for long-horizon agents.

items.title: Researchers investigate artificial swarm intelligence in large language models, finding up to 37% error reduction across GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Claude Sonnet 4.5 in estimation tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Wisdom Of The (AI) Crowd: Investigating Artificial Swarm Intelligence In Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have explored whether large language models (LLMs) can replicate the collective accuracy of human swarm intelligence through artificial swarms. In a controlled study involving 960 prompts across three models—GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Claude Sonnet 4.5—they tested both intra-model sampling and inter-model aggregation on eight estimation tasks, finding error reductions of up to 37% in mean absolute percentage error (MAPE). The study also identified correlations between confidence interval widths and estimation errors, indicating that LLMs may have metacognitive awareness when evaluating uncertainty.

The experiment demonstrated consistent improvements in accuracy through aggregation strategies within and across models, suggesting that artificial swarms of LLMs can enhance decision-making processes. These findings provide valuable insights for applying LLM swarms in organizational contexts, potentially overcoming limitations of human swarm intelligence related to cost, coordination, and scalability.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31404v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Human swarm intelligence demonstrates remarkable collective accuracy but faces scalability constraints in cost, coordination, and time. We investigate whether large language models (LLMs) can approximate swarm intelligence effects through artificial swarms, addressing a critical gap in understanding AI-based aggregation mechanisms. We conducted a controlled experiment with 960 manually executed prompts across three proprietary models (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.5), testing intra-model sampling and inter-model aggregation on eight estimation tasks. Results reveal consistent error reduction through intra- and inter-model aggregation, with significant error reductions up to 37 percentage points in MAPE across different aggregation strategies. We observed small to large effect sizes for positive correlations (Spearman's $\rho=0.242-0.568$, all $p<0.001$) between relative confidence interval widths and relative estimation errors, suggesting LLMs possess metacognitive awareness when assessing uncertainty. We discuss implications for research and practice, providing actionable insights for deploying LLM swarms in organizational decision-making.

items.title: Xiaomi releases Xiaomi-GUI-0, a multimodal GUI agent trained and evaluated on real mobile devices achieving over 72% success on RealMobile and 78.9% on AndroidWorld benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Xiaomi-GUI-0 Technical Report
items.summary:
Xiaomi has introduced Xiaomi-GUI-0, a multimodal graphical user interface (GUI) agent designed to operate in real mobile environments. Unlike previous GUI agents trained on simulated data, Xiaomi-GUI-0 is developed and evaluated using real devices, achieving success rates of 72.0% on the RealMobile benchmark and 78.9% on AndroidWorld. This approach addresses the gap between benchmark performance and real-world usability by incorporating physical devices into its training and evaluation loop, enhancing execution stability and abnormal-state recognition.

The agent is built on a hybrid infrastructure that prioritizes real-device execution supported by sandboxes, enabling data collection and training that closely mirror actual deployment conditions. Its training involves diverse data sources covering common tasks, long-tail intents, and capabilities like reflection and memory, alongside an error-driven data flywheel that refines the model through corrected actions and recovery demonstrations. Xiaomi-GUI-0 undergoes a progressive training pipeline including supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning stages to improve its performance in complex, real-world mobile interactions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31410v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents build on vision-language models to complete user tasks end-to-end in real applications through interface actions such as tapping, swiping, text entry, and navigation. However, existing GUI agents are trained and evaluated largely on offline trajectories, simulated environments, and standardized benchmarks. These differ substantially from real applications in interface layout, interaction logic, and abnormal-state distribution, and cannot faithfully characterize execution stability in real-world use, where account states, permission dialogs, payment authentication, and risk control continually reshape the state distribution and open a persistent gap between benchmark scores and real usability. To close this gap, we propose Xiaomi-GUI-0, a native multimodal GUI agent for real mobile environments, trained and evaluated within a real-device closed loop. At its core is a real-device-dominant hybrid infrastructure, where physical devices are the primary execution environment and sandboxes provide auxiliary support, so that data collection, training, rollout, and evaluation share an execution distribution close to real deployment. We construct multi-source training data spanning high-frequency head tasks, high-generalization data for long-tail intents, and capability-enhancement data for reflection and memory, and introduce an error-driven data flywheel that turns failure trajectories into corrected actions, reflective explanations, and recovery demonstrations. The model is trained through a progressive three-stage pipeline of supervised fine-tuning, step-level reinforcement learning, and agentic reinforcement learning. Evaluated on public benchmarks and our in-house RealMobile, Xiaomi-GUI-0 achieves 72.0% success on RealMobile and 78.9% on AndroidWorld, while substantially improving execution stability and abnormal-state recognition in real-world tasks.

items.title: Researchers propose BP-TTA method combining balanced sampling and prototype-guided adaptation to address class imbalance and continual domain shifts in dynamic test-time scenarios [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: BP-TTA: Balanced and Prototype-Guided Test-Time Adaptation in Dynamic Scenarios
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced BP-TTA, a new method for Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) that addresses both class imbalance and continual domain shifts in dynamic test-time scenarios. BP-TTA combines balanced batch sampling with prototype-guided adaptation to improve model performance when adapting to unlabeled test data streams that exhibit changing distributions and uneven class representation.

The method constructs balanced adaptation batches by mixing current samples with high-confidence historical data, reducing bias toward dominant classes and stabilizing online updates. It also maintains evolving class prototypes during inference, using prototype similarity to guide adaptation and enhance the reliability of pseudo-labels. Experiments show that BP-TTA outperforms existing TTA approaches in handling dynamic, real-world test-time streaming conditions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31420v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) enables models trained on a source domain to adapt online to unlabeled test data under distribution shifts. While recent TTA methods have moved beyond static settings and begun to consider continual domain shifts, they primarily address distribution drift and fail to account for class imbalance in dynamic scenarios. In real-world test-time streams, class imbalance and continual domain shifts often occur at the same time and interact with each other. In this paper, we propose a novel Balanced and Prototype-Guided Test-Time Adaptation (BP-TTA) method, which combines batch-balanced sampling with prototype-guided adaptation to handle the class imbalance and continual domain shift problems. BP-TTA constructs balanced adaptation batches by integrating current samples with high-confidence historical instances, effectively mitigating bias toward dominant classes and stabilizing online updates. Meanwhile, BP-TTA maintains evolving class prototypes during inference and leverages prototype similarity as a constraint for model adaptation, thereby improving the reliability of pseudo-labels and enhancing the stability of online updates under persistent domain shifts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BP-TTA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art TTA methods in dynamic test-time streaming settings.

items.title: Researchers introduce a budgeted environment probing method for calibrating world models in long-horizon language agents to reduce terminal errors during task planning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Ask the World Before Acting: Budgeted Environment Probing for World-Model Calibration
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a budgeted environment probing method called \method to improve the calibration of world models used by long-horizon language agents during task planning. This approach allows agents to query the environment selectively about specific belief fields before taking actions, helping to correct model drift and reduce errors that could lead to task failures. By treating environment interaction as a limited resource for calibration rather than just task progression, the method enhances the agent's decision-making accuracy over extended sequences of actions.

The study distinguishes between different types of beliefs within the agent's model, such as procedural beliefs related to tool dependencies and spatial beliefs concerning object locations and relationships. Targeted environment probes can effectively repair procedural beliefs, while spatial beliefs require structural cues due to challenges like off-screen changes. Controlled experiments demonstrate that incorporating mid-planning environment feedback following the task's structure significantly lowers terminal errors in the world model, highlighting the value of strategic probing in complex task environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.31422v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon language agents do not only choose actions; they carry a private model of the world from one decision to the next. When that model drifts, a later failure can be decided before the failing action is ever taken. We study a direct repair mechanism: before committing to the next task action, an agent may ask the environment about one belief field and write the answer back into its world model. This makes environment interaction a scarce calibration resource, not merely a way to advance the task. We introduce \method, a budgeted probing operator for structured belief tables. The useful probes are not the same everywhere. Procedural beliefs, such as tool dependencies, can often be repaired by targeted checks, but those checks spend steps that the task may need. Spatial beliefs, such as object locations and graph edges, rely more on structural cues; the agent's own confidence can be a poor guide when the world changes off-screen. A type-stratified analysis formalizes this probe-action frontier, and controlled experiments show that mid-planning environment evidence reduces terminal world-model error when the probe policy follows the structure of the task.
